REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible
for implementation of various programmes of national importance like family welfare,
primary health care, prevention, control and eradication of major diseases which form the
main plank of our development efforts. Apart from these, the Ministry also takes special
care for preventing the spread of diseases assuming the dimension of epidemic. The
Department of Health, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is
committed to achieve the goal of health for all by the year 2000 A.D. is responsible for |
evolving broad policies for the health sector and provides financial and technical assistance
to State Governments in critical areas through the implementation of important health
programmes.

1.2 Broadly, the objectives of the Department are to undertake National Health
Programmes, to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to
prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs, to provide primary health care at the door
steps of the people, to take steps for better implementation of health care programmes for
tribal and other weaker sections of the society and also to collaborate with member countries
of United Nations and international agencies like WHO, UNICEF, etc. in matters relating
to health promotion and development.

1.3 The Department finances the State and Union Territory Administrations for
Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being implemented by them and includes national
programmes for prevention control and eradication of diseases. Some of the schemes which
are financed to the tune of 100% by the Central Government are National Schemes for
Prevention of Visual Impairment and Blindness including ‘Trachoma, National Leprosy
Eradication Programme, National Guinea Worm Eradication Programme and National
AIDS Control Programme. While for some other programmes like National Malaria
Eradication Programme (Rural and Urban), National Sexually Transmitted Diseases Control
Programme, National 1.8. Control Programme, Kala-Azar Control Programme it is on a
50:50 basis by the Central and State Governments.

1.4 The Department also finances, wholly or substantially,the following autonomous
institutions engaged in patient care andor research; All India Institute of Medical Sciences
and Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences, New Delhi, Post-Graduate
Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, All India Institute of Speech and
Hearing, Mysore., Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

2.1. The Department of Health has been allocated Rs. 1122.16 crores on the Plan side
and Rs. 654.52 crores on the Non-Plan side, for the year 1998-99.

2.2 As compared to total outlay of Rs. 920.20 crores in 1997-98 outlay of Rs. 1122.16
crores for medical and public health for 1998-99 shows a quantum jump. Major portion of
the outlay is meant for National Programmes for control of Communicable Diseases and
other diseases implemented through State Governments on the health side. Maximum
allocation has been made for National Malaria Eradication Programme (Rs. 287.00 crores),

Programme, National Trachoma and Blindness Control Programme, National Leprosy
Eradication Programme, National TB Control Programme and Kala-Azar Control Prog-
ramme. On the medical side the emphasis is on the development of medical sciences
including medical education, training and research for which an outlay of Rs. 254.01 crores
have been provided during 1998-99.

2.3 Commenting on the budget allocation, the Secretary stated that when compared
with the Eighth Plan figure of Rs. 2,825 crores, the Ninth Plan figure of Rs. 4,995.59 crores
including a foreign aid component of Rs. 1,497 crores, signifies a 75% increase. However, in
real terms, it has increased by 35 per cent only.

2.4 The Secretary informed the Committee that the allocation made to the Department
is insufficient to ¢arry“Oi its activities: With this allocation,” the Secretary stated that the
Department’ may ot be~ able 10 start the programme for testing -hepatitis, for which the
Department would be short by Rs. 68 crores. The Committee feels that testing hepatitis
should be started in a big way and necessary funds may be provided at the RE stage.
Another area which needs immediate attention and the Department may not be able to
attend to, is immunisation for Hepatitis-B as part of immunisation programme for which
there is a need for Rs. 600 crores. The Committee is of thé opinion that immunisation for
Hepatitis-B should be started in a phased manner in view of paucity of funds. Funds will not
be sufficient for setting up a trauma Centre at AIIMS, for which a minimum of Rs. 100
crores is required. The Committee was also informed that there is shortage of funds for
construction of quarters for the faculty of AIIMS.

2.5 The Committee feels that the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance
should take a realistic view of the needs of the Department and try to provide more funds to
attain the goal of Health for All by 2000 A.D.

गा, CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME

3.1 The Plan allocation for CGHS was reduced from Rs. 9 crores in BE 1997-98 to
Rs. 5 crores in RE 1997-98. However, it has been stepped up to Rs. 9 crores in BE 1998-99.
When the Department was asked to explain the reason for the increase, the department
stated that the increase is for expansion of CGHS to new cities and for opening of new
Allopathic / Homoeopathic / Ayurvedic / Unani dispensaries and for creation of more posts.

3.2 The Secretary, during the course of the evidence stated that at present C.G.H.S.
caters to about 44 lakh beneficiaries in 18 cities of the country. The Secretary assured the
Committee that action would be taken for expansion of this scheme on receipt of fresh SIU
study of CGHS dispensaries from Ministry of Finance by July, 1998. The Committee
recommends that the expansion of CGHS as envisaged during the year be undertaken.

IV. HOSPITALS

4.1 The Central Government hospitals are suffering from resource crunch which leads to
appalling conditions, sub-standard services, overcrowding, etc. Staff scarcity and lack of
basic amenities are a regular feature in all the hospitals. The Secretary pointed out a number
of difficulties being faced in the smooth functioning of the Central Government Hospitals. In
order to strengthen the casualty of three Central Government Hospitals i.e. Safdarjung,
Lady Harding and Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospitals, the Department had planned to
privatise. some of the services. This was duly approved by the Expenditure Finance
Committee in February, 1998. However, there has been a lot of resistance from the Group
‘C’ and ‘D’ Unions against these efforts of privatisation or for even having contract labour.
The Committee feels that the indisciplines approach of all the staff working in these Central

very stringent conditions have been laid down by the Medical Council of India for grant of
recognition to private medical colleges. Not only this, now every medical college is to have
its own building and hospital before it is recognised. The Committee fails to understand how

8.3 The Committee is also equally worried about the brain drain that is taking place in

X. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME

10.1 T.B. continues to be a major health problem in the country. It affects mainly
people in their most productive years of life and is commonly associated with poverty,
overcrowding and malnutrition. Lack of education, environmental pollution and poor
sanitation compound the problem. The Secretary informed the Committee that the
Department is seized of the magnitude of the problem of T.B. morbidity and mortality in
the country. The Committee was informed that the Prevalence rate of T.B. is around 1.5.%
i.e. about 1.5 crores T.B. patients are presently there in the whole of the country. Control of
’T.B. has become all the more important due to the emerging dangers from HIV/TB co-
- infection. The Secretary further informed that the department is presently adopting revised
DOT Strategy (Directly Observed Treatment Short-Course Chemotherapy) to fight against
T.B. under a World Bank funded project which has been implemented in 102 districts in the
Country and already 42,741 cases have been treated under the project till 31st March, 1998.
Apart from this; support from World Bank to 203 other districts is also being given for
strengthening of State T.B. Cells/Training and Demonstration Centres/Labs as well as
training and for IEC. For the remaining 154 district of the country, the project intervention
is in the form of strengthening of State TRB Cell/Training and Demonstration Centre and
supply of conventional drugs.

10.2 This year the allocation for the programme has been substantially raised :
Rs. 90 crores BE 1997-98 to Rs. 125 crores in BE 1998-99. However, the Committee would
like to point out, that inspite of a well planned strategy for control of T.B., financial targets
could not be achieved in the entire Eighth Plan period. Not only this, in 1997-98, only
Rs.32.05 crores could be utilised against the allocation of Rs.90 crores in BE 1997-98. This
has been mainly due to delay in the delivery services as a result of lengthy World Bank
procedures. All these procedures have now been streamlined and also supply of drugs ‘has
also been decentralised, the Department clarified. The Committee recommends that th
Department should take effective steps for full utilisation of allocated funds.

successful programme and it is due to the effect of the recent drugs which have entered in

12.1 The Programme.was launched by the Government in 1976 to reduce the blindness

“from 1.4% to.0.3%. by-2000-A.D. The Committee was informed by the Secretary that a World

of stock level in the States funded under the World Bank Project were the main reasons cited by

13.1 Out of the total allocation of Rs. 297 crores for Malaria Control in BE 1998-99, Rs.137
crores have been earmarked for National Malaria Eradication Programme. The allocation for
Kala-azar Control is Rs. 10 crores and under Externally Aided Component (EAC) for the

Control Programme has been retained at the same level as in 1997-98 there has been substantial

support from Rs.50 crores in 1997-98 to Rs.150 crores, in 1998-99. Out of this, the Committee
was told, Rs.105 crores have been kept for Insecticides, Larvicidés, Drugs Material and
Equipments.

XIV. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME

14.1 In order to prevent and control the HIV infection and to reduce its impact the
Government of India launched a scheme on September 23rd, 1992 at an estimated cost of
Rs. 267.88 crores during Eighth Plan period with assistance from International Development
Association and technical support from World Health Organisation.

14.2 The expected outcome of National AIDS Control Programme are:—

Reduction of HIV transmission and better clinical care and management of
HIV/AIDS patients.

Elaborating on the programme, the Secretary stated that as per the projections made by
WHO, India has the largest number of HIV cases in the world. Recently, a Nation wide
survey was conducted all over the country except Bihar in the month of February and March
1998. The results gave a mixed picture. The prevalent rate of the disease is different in
different States in varying forms. The most affected part of the country is the Southern and
the Western region. There is no State in India which has not reported HIV/AIDS. The
Department is working with each individual State to provide, the management capability,
strengthening the delivery system and for proper execution of the programme.

14.3 Blood safety, production of safe blood, control of sexually transmitted diseases and
large scale information campaign are the measures through which efforts are being made to
contain the disease. The Department informed about 1850 Blood Banks have been
modernised in pursuance of Supreme Court directions in this regard.

14.4 Under the Supreme Court direction, a National Blood Transfusion Council has
been formed. Not only this, a draft Blood Policy has been announced and it will be brought
before the Cabinet very soon, Prevention of Human Rights of the people who are already

very important component of AIDS Control Programme as it increases the risk of
transmission by almost ten times. Information, education and communication was another

14.5 The Committee was also informed that the awareness level in urban areas is
something like 62% and in the rural areas it is 30% to 35%. The Committee feels that to

XV. DISEASE SURVEILLANCE SYSTEM

15.1 The Department initiated a pilot project in 1997-98 for strengthening the disease
surveillance system in the country. The Committee was informed that the main objective of
the programme is to develop and strengthen surveillance activities to promote early detection
of outbreaks and appropriate field action for prevention and control of outbreaks by capacity
building at district and State level. It was also informed that the Surveillance System is being
strengthened through training of medical and para-medical personnel, upgradation of
laboratories, communication and data processing system. The programme is being
implemented by the State Health Authorities with districts as the focal points. It is being
implemented in 11 States,.i.e. 2 districts in each State have been selected for the purpose.

15.2 The programme envisages to develop IEC material for use by community leaders at
sub-district levels (especially Gram. Panchayat) for facilitating their active support in disease
surveillance activities, For Ninth, Year: Plan an amount'of Rs. 30.00 crores have been
earmarked for the programme, the Committee was informed out of which Rs. 2.90 crores and
Rs. 4.55 crores have been allocated in 1997-98 and 1998-99 respectively.

9

15.3 The Committee was also infromed by the Secretary that the World-Bank is very
responsive to the ide2 and WHO has in fact given some funds for the purpose. The
Committee welcomes the idea at the first instance. The Committee is of the opinion that
priority should be given to the districts where there is frequent recurrence of outbreaks
under the Comprehensive Disease Surveillance System and steps should be taken to expand
this system aff over the country.

XVI. HOSPIPAL WASTE MANAGEMENT

16.1 Hospital Waste is one of the biggest health hazards that is being faced by every
citizen of this country. The Committee points out that all the projects of the Department are
envisaged and implemented to cure disease, but it will remain a dream if abundant caution is
not taken to dispose of the waste while curing the disease.

16.2 Explaining the subject the Secretary informed that in the wake of a Supreme Court
judgement that all the hospitalgin Delhi having more than fifty beds would have to have an
incinerator in accordance with the specifications of Central Pollution Control Board, the
Ministry of Environment and Forests has brought out the Draft Biomedical Waste Rules
inviting objections from the public. These rules would be made applicable to every hospital
having more than 50 number of beds. This would be monitored by the Central Pollution
Control Board.

16.3 The Committee is of the opinion that although responsibility is not of the
Department of Health alone, it should take some initiative and evolve a comprehensive
approach to waste management in consultation with the Ministries of Urban Affairs, Rural
Development and Water Resources etc. The Committee feels that strengthening of
preventive aspects in respect of water borne and masquito-borne diseases like Dengue,
malaria, plague etc. is very essential as the origin of all such diseases is waste.

16.4 The Committee feels that considering the enormity of the problem, the Bio-
medical Waste rules must be brought into force without further delay. The Committee is
also of the opinion that the issue of Hospital waste should not be restricted to Delhi alone
Steps should be taken for gradual coverage of Hospitals all over the country.

XVII, ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH AND SANITATION

17.1 The Committee feels that lack of sanitation, absence of hygienic habits and
accumulation of garbage and filth leads to frequent epidemic outbreaks in the Country.

17.2 The Committee was given to understand that in the wake of plague in 1994, a
Committee of four Ministries namely Ministry of Urban Development, Ministry of’ Rural
Development, Ministry of Environment and Forests and the Ministry of Health under the
convenorship of Health Secretary was set up to look into this problem. The report spelling
out what should be done in the area of environmental health and sanitation was submitted
and the proposal contained in the report was to be included in the Ninth Plan Projections of
the individual Ministries. The Department of Health took the view that a Technology
Mission on environmental health and sanitation should be set up in collaboration with
concerned Ministries. However nothing concrete has emerged so far.

17.3 The Committee feels that the Department in co-ordination with the concerned
Ministries should make all efforts to form a Technology Mission on the issue. Local bodies
should also be alert on this important, aspect.

XVIII. NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF BIOLOGICAL STANDARDISATION AND QUALITY
CONTROL, NEW DELHI

18.1 For the year 1998-99, the institute has been given an allocation of Rs. 35 crores on
the Plan side. Elaborating on the need for such an institute, the Secretary stated that the
institute attends to the need of a high standard quality control of biologicals in the country.
The institute will also look into the areas of blood products etc. The Secretary informed that
the project is a tripartite project and is being funded by the US aid, OEC of Japan and the
Government of India. The Committee was also informed that as the Government will not be
able to give the kind of attention the project requires at présent it has been reviewed. by a

|. Governing Body consisting of eminent scientists. Since, the quality:is‘not be compromised,

the Department is taking the help of the Department of Biotechnology, major laboratories
and heads of various institutions. The Committee hopes that the Institute will be constituted/
constructed as per the schedule.

XIX. CENTRAL DRUGS STANDARD CONTROL ORGANISATION

19.1 Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation was provided Rs. 11.71 crores on the
Plan side in BE 1998-99 which was drastically reduced to Rs. 2.10 crores at the RE stage.
For the current year, there is a provision of Rs. 6.00 crores.

19.2 Justifying the decrease, the Department stated that under BE 1997-98, CDSCO
was given an allocation of Rs. 11.71 crores, of which Rs. 9.51 crores was provided as
external component for Capacity Building Project to be implemented both at the State and
Central Jevels with support from the World Bank. The Capacity Building Project, inter-alia,
seeks to strengthen the Drug Administration at the State and Central level with a view to
improve quality control. Since the Capacity Building Project, which was envisaged to
commence in 1997-98, did not materialise as scheduled, the entire external component of

~ Rs. 9.51 crores was reduced from the Budget allocation:

19.3 The Department further stated that in 1997-98, Rs. 2.20 crores was provided in the
general component for meeting the recurring cost on projects initiated in the Eighth Plan
The Ministry of Finance had advised that this component be continued during the Ninth
Plan as part of the Plan Component. Accordingly, in 1998-99 Rs. 6.00 crores have been
provided in the general component. Of this allocation, Rs. 2.30 crores will again be utilised
for meeting the recurring cost on the Eighth Plan component in the current financial year
while Rs. 0.70 crores has been provided for expansion of enforcement machinery of CDSCO
at the Head Quarters, Zone and Sub-Zone levels. For this purpose approval of EFC is
proposed to be sought. Based on the approval received, further requests for funds will be
sought if so required.

19.4 The Committee is of the opinion that the drug enforcement machinery both at the
Central and State level requires strengthening because of the large availability of spurious
drugs in the market. The Committee, therefore, feels that the EFC approval should be
sought early so that enforcement machinery could be strengthened.

XX. PRIMARY HEALTH CENTRES

20.1 The functioning of Primary Health Centres in the rural areas is a matter of grave
concern for the Committee. The Committee was given to understand that the Department
provides facilities to the PHCs initially after which it is the responsibility of the State
Government. The Committee feels that it,should not be the case. Responsibility of the
Department does nvt end with mere allocation of funds. The Department has to ensure that
PHCs in rural areas should also attend to the medical needs of public in real sense. The

Committee is happy to note that some concrete steps have been initiated by the Department
for monitoring of PHCs. The Committee finds that inspection of PHC is being carried out by
a team consisting of two officials from the Department, two individuals alongwith the. State
officials. The Committee desires that local MLAsMPs may also be associated with the
+ inspection team. The Committee feels that better assessment would be made if PHCs
showing both good and bad performance are inspected. A tribal area where the conditions
are worse should also be made a part of this inspection. The Committee is of the view that
the new methodology of joint inspection team would lead to better functioning of PHCs.
Taking into account the overall condition of PHCs, the Committee desires that a one-time
grant be given by the Government of India, for all PHCs to bring them into a working
condition. हु
XXI. COMMITTED LIABILITY

21.1 The Committee in its 60th Report had recommended that the Department should
make a thorough review of the schemes and identify the committed liability. In this matter,
the Committee considered the Report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance
Commission have ‘observed as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan scheme,
the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of Eighth Plan scheme
completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The
Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider
providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92.”

21.2 The Committee in this connection heard the views of the Secretary, Department of
Expenditure last year to clarify the position. He informed the Committee that even though
communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the
Committee expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under
Demand No. 31. The Secretary also assured that if required more funds for this purpose will
be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the Departments may approach the
Department of Expenditure for their share.

21.3 The Department has informed that it proposed to transfer Rs. 87.75 crores from
Plan to Non-Plan as committed expenditure. The information relating to the committed
expenditure was furnished to the Ministry of Finance and revised information was also
furnished by the Department thereafter. However, it had been made clear by the Ministry of
Finance that there was no case of either transfer of committed expenditure from Plan to
Non-Plan or for additional provision for committed expenditure in the Bydget Estimates
1997-98. The committed expenditure proposed to be provided is already built into the BE
1997-98 (Plan), it was 1010, Even the transfer of committed expenditure from Plan to Non-
Plan would lead to double counting of the estimates as the next year’s Plan allocations will
be based on the Budget Estimates for 1997-98 and not on the reduced figures for RE
1997-98. In view of this, the Ministry of Finance did not agree to provide any funds on
account of committed expenditure from Plan to Non-Plan under BE/RE 1997-98.

21.4 The Committee views with concern that the Finance Ministry has not honoured
such clear cut commitment made before the Parliamentary Committee. As the’
recommendations of the Tenth Finance Commission have been accepted by the
Government, it is the commitment of Government too. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department of Health should get the assurance implemented without
any: delay.

vulnerable segments of our society without whose upliftment real development cannot take place.

3. The Committee feels that gender inequality is one of the problems all over the world. Actual 
development cannot take place unless the Govt. takes initiative to remove this bias and guarantees 
equal status to women as enshrined in our Constitution. Committee is of the view that all out efforts 
should be made for greater involvement of women in the national development process by raising their 
status - social, economic, legal and political - at par with that of man. The Department of Women 
and Child Development has started a number of schemes for the development and welfare of women 
and children The Committee has deliberated only on some of the points relating to Demands for Grants 
(1994-95) which are enumerated in the following paragraphs along with the Committee's observations 
and recommendations. 
Women Welfare and Development 
(i) Rashtriya Mahila Kosh 
4. Rashtriya Mahila Kosh was set up in March, 1993 under the Registration of Societies Act, 
1869. With the main aim to help the poorest of the poor and assist women who are unable to utilize 
formal banking facilities but are in need of credit. For the purpose, a Corpus of Rs. 31 crores was 
sanctioned, to be utilised in a phased manner. 
5. The Committee observes that as against Rs. 31 crores sanctioned last year for this scheme, only 
a token amount of Rs. one lakh has been earmarked this year. It feels that unless 

schemes for the utilisation of sanctioned money are formulated well in time, setting up of such 
funds becomes infructuous. Therefore, it recommends that Department should, ensure that schemes 
are framed for prop er utilisation of the funds without delay. 
(ii) National Commission for Women and Commissioner for Women's Rights 
6. The Nation al Commission for Women was set up as a nodal agency to monitor the 
enforcement of lega l status of women, to review the existing legislation and suggest amendments 
and to liaise with the concerned Ministries, State Governments and NGOs, in order to create 
awareness and spread literacy. For this purpose, an amount of Rs. 1.75 crores in RE was 
provided in 1993-94, which has been increased to Rs. 2 crores in the Budget Estimates for 1994-
95. 
7. The Committee notes that there is substantial increase in the Budget provisions for the 
National Commission for Women for 1994-95, as compared to 1993-94. Govt. should ensur e full 
utilisation of the budg et of Rs. 2 crores by the Commission. 
8. The Committee recommends that Govt. should fulfil the assurance given to th e Parliament 
by creat ing the post of Commissioner for Women 's Rights and all consultations and other 
formalities be completed as early as possible. 
(iii) Hostels for working Women 
9. To protect young working women in urban areas from exposure to undesirable and anti­
social elements, financial assistance to the extent of 50% of the cost of land and 70% of the 
cost of building construct ion is provided to Voluntary Organisations. In 1993-94 Rs. 7.00 crores 
were provided which has bee n increased to Rs. 7.75 crores in the Budget for 1994-95. This 
year's target is to provide assistance to 60 hostles which would benefit about 3000 working 
women.

11. The Committe e is of the view that though there is acute shortage of working Women' s 
Hostels in the country, the Department could not achieve the physical targets during 1993-94, but

12. As frequent complaints are received about mismanagement of the hostels rece1vmg grants 
and assistance from the Government the Committee is of the view that there is need for evolving 
some system of monitoring so as to control any sort of irregularities in these hostels. For this 
purpose, the Committee recommends that a Government representative be included on the Board 
of Management of each of such hostels. 
13. The Committee eA.presses its concern over the inadequacy of hostels for working women 
and recommends that , taking into consideration the importance of these hostels, Government 
should encourage construction of more such hostels not only through grants but also by allotment 
of land where ever necessary. 

(iv) Education for prevention of atrocities against Women 
14. The programme was sta rted in 1982 with the aim of creating public opinion against exploita tion 
of women and atrocities against them. This objective is sought to be achieved mainly through 
programmes, publicity and research work , as well as holdin g meetings, conferences, seminars , 
exhibitions, etc. 
15. Financial assistance extended in 1993-94 for this purpose was Rs. 35.00 lakhs and the same 
amount has been allocated during 1994-95. 
16. The Committee expresses its concern over the increasing numbers of cases of atrocities against 
women an d recommends that Govt. should conduct some review of these publicity programmes to find 
out whet her these are sufficient to create a significant impact on the public mind. 
17. The Committee recommends that the amount sanctioned for the year 1993-94 for legal aid in 
cases of atrocities against women should be increased. 
18. The Committee was informed of training and other awareness generation programmes 
undertaken by the Department. Production of legal literacy manuals in regi ona l languages and gender 
sensitization are part of this programmes. The Committee feels that such programmes should be 
extended to the grass root level also. 
(v) Indira Mahila Y ojna 
19. Indira Mahila Yojna, as originally conceived in 1991 and included in the President's Address of 
the year, has four basic components: (i) Awareness generation (ii) Income generat ion (iii) Convergence 
of inter-sectoral services; and (iv) Integration of field cadres of all related departments in the country. 
20. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the fact that though the scheme was announced 
in the President's Address in 1991, till this date it has not been operationalised. 
21. The Committee was informed by the Department that the original draft scheme for Indira 
Mahila Yojna contained components of awareness generation, income generation, integr ated system of 
delivery, inter-sectoral services and integration of field cadres of concerned Departm en ts, with an 
allotment of Rs. 1785 crorcs for the Eighth Plan. The concerned Departments could not, however, 
come to a consensus on integration of cadres and transfer of schemes from one Ministry to the other. 
Subsequently, there was a revised scheme to cover 200 blocks, with income generation and awareness 
generation components (Rs. 78 crores for the remainder of the 8th Plan.) But this also is yet to be 
approved by the Planning Commission. The Provision of Rs. 8 crores in the 1994-95 Budget may go into 
the World Bank-aided ICDS project, if the approval does not come in time. 
The Committee feels that such a big scheme should be implemented only when proper assessment of 
financial and infrastructural implications is made. Duplication of efforts should be avoided. whether a 
single-window delivery system would benefit women, in immensely varied circumstances, has also to be 
assessed. 
(vi) Mahila Samridhi Yojna 
22. This is a new scheme launched on 2nd October, 1993 to promote thrift, self-relia nce and certain 
amount of economic independence among rural women. It is implemented by the Depar t· of Posts 
through the network of 1.32 lakh post offices in rural areas. An amount of Rs. 10.5 cror cs \',as initially 
sanctioned for the scheme which has been increased to Rs. 19.89 crores in the Budgetar y orovis ions for 
1994-95. 
23. The Committee notes that significant increase in allocations for Mahila Samridhi Yojna has been 
made this year. The Comm.ittee, however, recommends that there should be proper monitoring to see 
that these funds are properly utilised. 
24. The Committee is of the view that various programmes under the Mahila Samridhi Yojna are 
implemented keeping in view the welfare of rural women, whereas poor women in urban areas , who are 
also in need of assistance, are not covered under it. The Committee recommends that requiremen ts of 
needy urban women belonging to the weaker sections of society should also be kept in mind while framing 
and implementing schemes for women's welfare. 

25. Committee also feels that there is not sufficient awareness among the rural people regarding 
the benefits of Mahila Samridhi Yojna. Secondly, the postmasters in the villages are not fully info.-med 
and trained about the scheme, and there is also dearth of forms. The need is, therefore, to train 
postmasters about the functioning of the scheme and to make the forms available so as to avoid 
inconvenience to the needy. 
26. There should also be a monthly review of the progress made under the scheme so as to take 
corrective measures wherever necessary. 
Nutrition and Child Development 
27. The Committee expresses its concern over the sharp decli~e in the Plan Budget estimates 
under the Head 2235 for Child Welfare. As against. Rs. 43.35 crores in 1993-94, it has gone down to 
Rs. 20.17 crores in 1994-95 and recommends restoration of the last year allocations. 
(i) Integrated Child Development Services (/CDS) 
28. The main thrust of ICDS programme is on the provision of Anganwadis in every village and 
urban slum areas. Generally, there is one Anganwadi for a population of 1000 in rural areas and 
urban slum areas and of about 700 in tribal area~, which is run by an Anganwadi worker, a female 
voluntary worker and a helper. By the end of 1993, 3120 ICDS projects were sanctioned which 
benefited about 1.94 crorc children and women. For the year 1994-95 an outlay of Rs. 426.00 crores 
has been approved for the ICDS and 200 new projects are likely to start. 
The Committee feels that a large portion of the increased outlay is likely to be absorbed in the 
increased honorarium to Anganwadi workers. Therefore, the Committee feels that the amount available 
for the projected expansion of the scheme to cover new areas seems to be insufficient. Of 5239 blocks, 
2119 block remains to be covered. At the rate of 200 projects per year, it will take another 10 years for 
all blocks to be covered. Thus is too slow. To expedite the process, any shortfall in the projected 
expansion by the end of the 8th Plan should be properly estimated and additional allocations made. 
29. The relative success of the ICDS scheme in improving child health and lowering IMR is due 
to its decentralized and popular structure. probably because of this, ICDS is being increasingly seen 
as an umberlla organisation within which other schemes could be incorporated. Thus, early childhood 
education is now a part of ICDS_. There is a new scheme for adolescent girls, creches and day care 
centres arc sought to be made a part of ICDS. Indira Mahila Yojana, in its revised form, will become 
a component of ICDS. Separate allocations have been proposed for these schemes, but the National 
Creche Fund has only been notified. Allocation of Rs. 8 crores for Indira Mahila Yojna has not yet 
been approved. Therefore, the Committee recommends that until and unless spearate additional 
allocations are obtained for these additional components, ICDS should concentrate on strengthening 
and expansion of its own structure with whatever allocations it has. The proposal to entrust a 
percentage of !CDS schemes to NGOs should be properly assessed before it is implemented, because in 
the absence of community-based monitoring arrangements, it would be difficult to ensure accountability 
of these NGOs. 
30. With the usc of ICDS infrastructure, a special scheme for adolescent girls has been 
formulated, mainly for those who have been out of schools, to meet their nutritional, educational and 
recreational needs. 
31. Regarding education of adolescent girls, the Committee recommends that there should be a 
scheme to help meritorious girls enabling them to pursue their studies further. 
32. In order to meet the requirement of trained personnel for implementing the programmes for 
pre-school children, the Bal Scvika training programme was started in 1961-62. There are 25 Bal 
Scvika training Centres and each centre is provided with a sum of Rs. 1,74,750/- to train 50 Bal 
Sevikas each year. 
33. The Committee observes that out of the three components of ICDS, namely executive, workers 
and recipients, two do not appear to be happy with the service. Therefore, monitoring system should be 
strengthened to ensure proper functioning of the ICDS Scheme to the satisfaclion of all its components. 

of the population through ICDS, as well as nutritional education. In this context, the Committee 
recommends revival of the scheme of supply of milk to the under-nourished school Children. 
44. The Committee also feels that, year after year, the focus of attention of the Deptt. keeps on 
changing from one scheme to another and there seems to be no long-term perspective. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that instead of framing new schemes every year and letting the earlier ones to 
just continue, the Department should concentrate on some major schemes and work to achieve the 
targets fixed through suitable action plans. The Department was set up in 1985 but its strerigth has 
remained the same although many new schemes have been introduced during this period. The 
Committee feels that strengthening of Departmental infrastructure is necessary inorder to ensure the 
effectiveness of the schemes.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The National Health Policy of 1983 emphasised to initiate organised measures to
enable each of the systems of Indian Medicine to develop in accordance with its genius and
find an appropriate role and place for these different systems in the overall health care
delivery system for the benefit of the people. India has a large resource of ISM&H
practitioners of Homoeopathy whose services need to be fully utilised in the national health
care delivery system. For this purpose, a new Department of Indian Systems of Medicine
and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to promote and develop the Indian systems of
Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and drugless Therapies like Yoga and
Naturopathy).

1.2 The Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy have practically grown and
developed in the Indian society on the basis of learning through family traditions of Guru
Shishya Parampara, although a few colleges had come up in the late 19th century and the
earlier part of the 20th century. There was practically no Governmental support to this
system. There were no regulations either, regarding the practice and educational standard.
Patients used to approach these indigenous physicians on the basis of faith in their skill,
knowledge and integrity.

1.3 However, after Independence, institutions like Central Council of Indian Medicines
and Central Council for Homoeopathy were established to register practitioners in these
Systems and to lay down minimum standards for education. The Central Council: of
Research in Ayurveda and Siddha, the Central Council of Unani Medicine, the Central
Council of Research in Homoeopathy, the National Institute of Ayurveda at Jaipur and the
National Institute of Homoeopathy at Calcutta have been set up as apex bodies for research
and teaching. In order to formulate Standards for Drugs, Pharmacopoeia Committees for
each of these Systems were set up and supported by the Pharmacopoeia Laboratory for
Indian Medicine (PLIM) and the Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia Laboratory (HPL) both
located at Ghaziabad, U.P. The Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM) and the
Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH) are responsible for laying down and maintaining
uniform standards of education and regulate the professional practices of the practitioners in
the field of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy, respectively.

Il. EIGHTH FIVE YEAR PLAN

The Eighth Plan outlay for ISM&H was Rs. 88 crores. However, the annual allocations
made during the plan period come to Rs. 104.44 crores. The actual expenditure made by the
Department is only 92.07 crores. The Plan allocations made could not be utilised fully during
the 8th Plan period except in the first year i.e. 1992-93.

गा, BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

3.1 The total allocation, both Plan and Non-Plan taken together, provided to the
Department for the year 1997-98 was Rs. 56.80 crores in BE which was enhanced to 66.45
crores at RE stage. The allocation made for the year 1998-99 is Rs. 85.60 crores (Plan Rs.
49.00 and Non-Plan Rs. 36.60 crores). The Committee finds that the Plan allocation has
been increased only by Rs. 6.20 crores. The Committee is of the firm belief that ISM&H
facilities need to be developed at a faster pace. It, therefore, recommends that Plan
allocation should be increased at RE stage.

3.2 The Committee is happy to note that the Department has initiated some sort of

monitoring system and activities undertaken by Research Organisations, National Institutes,
achievement of tar; a The problems are being examined every month and corrective
measures are being takén. The flow of budget under various schemes is also being reviewed
quarterly. The Committeé\appreciates this and hope that effective monitoring will continue
in the coming years.

IV. NINTH FIVE YEAR

4.1 A Working Group was setup by the Planning Commission for the Development of
Indian Systems of Medicine and Ho) thy during the Ninth Plan Period. The Working
Group after detailed study and delibekations formulated proposals for Ninth Five Year Plan
suggesting an outlay of Rs. 1840.00 crares. Based on that, the Department formulated its
proposals for Ninth Five Year Plan for R$, 1997.87 crores with programme-wise and scheme-
wise break up and submitted the same Yo the Planning Commission for consideration.
However, the Deartment was asked by the Pianning Commission to slide down the proposed
outlay due to resource constraint. After re-pyioritising its schemes and programmes, the
Department, accordingly, submitted the reviséd proposal for Rs. 1436.00 crores to the
Planning Commission. On yet another request made by the Planning Commission to reduce
the proposed outlay the Department again re-considered its requirement and worked out the
minimum required domestic budgetary support for the Ninth Five Year Plan as Rs. 754.00
crores by phasing and deferring some of the schemes\and submitted the same to Planning
Commission. However, even this minimum requireméat has not been agreed to by the
Planning Commission an outlay of only Rs. 280.37 trores has been provided to the
Department. The Secretary clarified that as this outlay iy woefully inadequate there is a
genuine need for significant increase in Plan allocation for the ISM&H sector as it has
accumulated large deficiencies in almost all the vital areas)

4.2 The Committee is in agreement with the contention of\the Department with regard
to inadequacy of allocation. The Committee strongly feels that\this meagre allocation will
defeat the very purpose of setting up a separate Department of\ISM&H. Although there
might be some exaggeration in the proposal of Rs. 1998 crores for the Ninth Five Year Plan,
the Committee fails to understand on what basis Rs. 280 crores was allocated to the
Department, out of projections of Rs. 1997.87 crores which is just about 15% of its demand.
The Committee feels that since the existence of this Department is vital to the health care of
Indian masses, it is imperative that adequate funds will have to be mde available and if

ecessary, a re-appraisal of projections for the Ninth Plan in respect 4f ISM&H may be
_eomsidere

V. AYURVEDA

5.1 The allocation made for Ayurveda was Rs. 20.25 crores in BE last year which was
raised to Rs. 28.97 crores at RE stage. This has substantially been increased to Rs. 34.59
crores in 1998-99 (Plan 10.54 crores and Non-Plan 24.05 crores). Explaining the reason for
the increase in the allocation of Ayurveda, the Department submitted that it is mainly due
to the enhanced allocations for Central Council for Research in Ayurveda & Siddha
(CCRAS). Besides meeting the expenditure on implementation of Sth Pay Commission
recommendations and continuing research activities, the enhanced allocation will be utilised
for construction of buildings for various field units which could not be taken up earlier.

5.2 The Committee has observed that plan allocation to CCRAS has been increased
from Rs. 495 lakhs to Rs. 744 lakhs in the Annual plans of 1997-98 and 1998-99 respectively.
The Committee hopes that the increased allocation will be fully utilised in the developmental
activities of Ayurveda.

1484/RS/F—3-B



VI. UNANI

6.1. Under the allocation for the Unani system, Plan provision was enhanced from
Rs. 5.05 crores in BE 1997-98 to Rs. 5.40 crores in the RE and further a quantum jump to
the level of Rs. 8.55 crores has been effected in BE 1998-99. The Department informed that
in 1998-99, besides the research activities the additional funds will be utilised for
strengthening Central Research Institute of Unani Medicine, Hyderabad, construction of
buildings for RRIUM, Srinagar and Karimganj for which the land has already been provided
by the State Govts. and acquisition of land and construction of building for RRIUM, Delhi.
The Committee hopes that all activities as envisaged will be undertaken during the current year.

6.2 The Committee is perturbed to note that the construction work of the main building
of the National Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore has been delayed due to the decision
of the Governing Body to start only PG courses instead of UG and PG both. The
Committee recommends that this building plan be finalised expeditiously keeping in mind
the future development of Unani system of medicine.

Vil. HOMOEOPATHY

7.1 For Homoeopathy, the BE 1997-98 on the Plan side was Rs. 5.11 crores which was
increased to Rs. 6.94 crores at RE stage. In BE of 1998-99 it has been reduced to the level
of Rs. 6.77 crores. When the Department was asked to explain the reasons for these
variations, it was informed that in the RE 1997-98, a provision of Rs. 6.94 crores was made
primarily to meet the arrears and enhanced Pay and allowances on account of Sth Central
Pay Commission recommendations in NIH and CCRH where there are a number of Plan
posts. The liability of arrears to be paid to the employees during 1998-99 has become less
and hence provision has been reduced.

7.2 The Committee notes with serious concern that expansion of NIH Calcutta proposed
to be made during 1997-98 from 50 beds to 100 beds could not be taken up. The Committee
is dismayed to note that the expansion of bed capacity does not find a place in the Annual
Action Plan for this year too. The Committee is not aware, except one time payment of Rs.
88 lakhs made to West Bengal Govt., on what other activities the amount of Rs. 253 lakhs
released to NIH, Calcutta was utilised. The Committee would also like to suggest that
research on detoxication of arsenic poisoning being conducted by NIH, Calcutta should be
intensified as this problem has severely affected West Bengal. ©

शा. YOGA AND NATUROPATHY

8.1 For Yoga and Naturopathy, the BE for 1997-98 on the Plan side was Rs. 1.70
crores, which was reduced to Rs. 1.16 crores in the RE 1997-98. However, it has been
increased to Rs. 3.95 crores in the BE 1998-99. When asked how it proposed to utilise the
additional sum, the Department explained that due to non-finalisation of project report for
Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga (MDNIY) the funds provided for acquisition of
land and construction of building could not be utilised. Now an amount of Rs. 170 lakhs has
been provided in BE 1998-99 for MDNIY. During the current year, provision for MDNIY
has been considerably increased based on the decisions of the Department to set up and re-
activate MDNIY. Besides this, allocation for CCRYN has also been increased from Rs. 75
lakhs in BE 1997-98 to Rs. 130 lakhs in BE 1998-99 to meet the committed liabilities.

8.2 The Committee feels that Yoga be tought in the schools right from the Primary.
Level. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department may take up this issué
with the Department of Education.

8.3 Regarding national existence of National Institute of Naturopathy (NIN), Pune, the

=


Department submitted that comprehensive Project Report for the establishment has been
finalised and it will be shortly placed before the EFC. The Department further submitted
that a provision of Rs. 75 lakhs has been kept for the purpose and if required, it would seek
additional allocation at RE stage. The Committee would like to recommend that every effort
should be made for early implementation of the Project.

IX. MEDICAL EDUCATION

9.1 The Committee was informed that the standards of education in the ISM&H
Institutions are far from satisfactory. The facilities available are inadequate. They are no
where near the norms fixed by the Statutory -bodies. There is a mushroom growth of sub-
standard colleges. Though the norms for running the colleges and hospitals of ISM&H have
been laid down but these are not fulfilled even by the State Government colleges in all
respects. The shortcomings are mostly in non filling up of the posts of teachers, lack of
adequate space, college buildings, hospitals, hostel facilities, equipped laboratories, library,
medicjnal plant gardens etc. The Secretary informed that as a policy, Government does not
engourage setting up of néw sub-standard colleges. Various conferences have passed
resolutions that no new colleges be permitted during the 9th Five Year Plan period. This

Lm has been communicated to all State Governments so that attention is focussed on

n ening the already existing colleges.

नि The Committee was given to tnderstand that Government would notify the
guidelines to establish a new college and also to prescribe the minimum standard for the
existing colleges within 2 months after receiving the same from CCIM and CCH. Although
the Department has received the recommendations of CCIM about the norms for phased
manner development of new Ayurvedic colleges, the comment of the State Governments in
this regard, are yet to be received. The Department further informed that it is studying
amendments made in the Indian Medical Council Act about the sub-standard education and
the mushrooming growth of.sub-standard medical colleges and the same would be taken into
account before finalising the amendments. The Committee feels that speedy action is called
for ‘checking the growth of sub-standard colleges and also having minimum standard of
education in the existing infrastructure.

9.3 Another aspect on which the Committee is worried is that there are ISM&H
colleges where not even 20% of the students have passed. The results of such colleges range
between zero to five per cent and zero to ten per cent consecutively and they have not
shown any improvement whatsoever. The Committee feels that urgent steps needs 10 be
taken to arrest this trend. The Committee would like to have a detailed State-wise
information of such colleges.

9.4 As part of the continuing education and reorientation, training programmes for
teachers, physicians and para medics have been undertaken. The State Governments have
also been asked to take more interest in sponsoring teachers and physicians to these courses.
However, the benefit is yet to fully reach the physicians and para medics.

9.5 The Committee was also informed that the Department is yet to tackle the need for
para medic education in Pharmacy and Nursing. Though some isolated courses are being
conducted in Pharmacy and nursing, they do not have Government recognition. There are
no separate Statutory Councils for laying down the standards and norms for pharmacy and
nursing colleges of ISM&H, the Secretary admitted. Project Reports have been prepared for
Pharmacy colleges of Ayurveda, Unani and Homoeopathy. The Department is examining
the feasibility of setting up separate Councils for Pharmacy education in ISM&H. Another
area of teaching is in the field of Yoga and Naturopathy. There is no regulatory body for


5

regulating the education in Yoga and Naturopathy. Temporarily the Department has thought
of entrusting the work to the Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy. ~

9.6 The Committee recommends that action should be initiated without any further
delay for laying down the standards and norms for pharmacy and nursing colleges in
ISM&H. The issue of having a separate regulatory body for Yoga and Naturopathy should
be considered, keeping in view its vital role in the present day society.

9.7 The Committee was informed that CCIM visited 107 colleges during 1997-98, out of
which 16 colleges were debarred from making admissions. Other colleges were issued
instructions to rectify their shortcomings by January, 1998. The Committee would like to
know the latest position in this regard.

9.8 The Secretary informed the Committee that in order to check huge amounts of
donation £apitation fee being taken by some colleges under ISM&H, a fee structure to be
charged by private colleges as per guidelines of Supreme Court Orders is being finalised
actively. The Committee recommends that the Department should intensify its efforts in this
direction.

X. POOR QUALITY OF DRUGS

10.1 The Secretary informed the Committee that the pharmacopoeial Committees have
been reconstituted recently and a thrust is being given to a time bound programme to
complete the work of laying of standards for ISM&H by 9th Plan period. At present two
drug testing laboratories are providing the technical back up to these pharmacopoeiai
Committees. There is also a need for setting up of Regional Drug Testing Laboratories. In
order to accelerate the work of evolving of standards, 30 Research institutions’ laboratories
have been provided financial assistance for working on the standards for 10 drugs per year.

10.2 Although the pharmacopoeial Committees have been in operation for a long
period, fool-proof method of testing the quality of drugs has not been evolved so far. This is
one of the weak areas which needs specific attention. The Committee feels that. it is
necessary to prescribe standards for ensuring efficacy of ISM&H drugs, in view of the fact
that manufacturers of such drugs do not have sophisticated and latest technology for
ensuring meticulous standards required for preparation of these drugs.

XI. NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS

11.1 The Department informed the Committee that it has initiated various steps to
enhance the supplies of medicinal plants. These are conservation and preservation of
medicinal plants through in situ and ex situ cultivation, developing tissue culture, storage in
gene banks, developing large scale gardens of medicinal plants in coordination with
concerned Ministries/Departments. A special scheme to provide assistance to research
organisations for development of agro techniques has also been introduced. 26 such
organisations are participating in the scheme and 97 species of plants have been allotted to
them. A component of R&D has also been included under the scheme to achieve better
results. The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department and hopes that
desired results would be achieved in this regard.

11.2. The Committee feels that the Department may approach the States for exploring
the possibility of earmarking some portion of forest lands for Ayurvedic and Unani colleges
for development of medicinal plants.


XII. PATENT CELL

12.1 The Department informed the Committee that a major area of concern is the keen
interest taken by foreign countries in the development of herbal products and intellectual
property rights. Some of the well known medicinal plants of India have been patented
abroad. In order to put a stop to these attempts, a Patent Cell has been formed in the
Department.

12.2 The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the Patent Cell is functioning
with inadequate manpower and various posts are lying vacant. The Committee, therefore
strongly recommends that vacant posts should be filled up at the earliest. The Committee
feels that this is a genuine case for substantial enhanced allocation.

XII. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT

13.1 There are 4 apex research councils which are carrying out research activities like
clinical research, drug research, laboratory research, family welfare research, etc. The
Central Council of Research in Ayurveda and Siddha (CCRAS) is the largest council with
over 86 units spread all over the country. The Council has patented 18 ayurvedic and siddha
drugs. The Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine (CCRUM) is another major
research organisation having a network of 32 institutions/units functioning in different parts
of the country. This council has also developed some products and is in the process of
patenting them. The Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy (CCRH) has a network
of 50 institutions/units located all over the country. However the Central Council for
Research in Yoga and Naturopathy (CCRYN) has a very limited activity. It is providing
grant to voluntary yoga and nature-cure institutions for running training programme. The
Department also informed that the Research Councils have been advised to have time bound
research projects and to focus attention on National Health Programmes such as AIDS and
Family Welfare etc. A new orientation is being given to the research activities.

13.2 The Committee was given to understand that it is not possible for the Research
Councils to take up all the research work by itself. A Scheme of Extra Mural Research has
been introduced under which financial assistance is provided for special research projects
(slide) to accredited research organisations.

13.3 The Committee in its 61st Report had inter-alia observed that no research activity
worth the name is carried out by the Research Councils. The Committee still has the
impression that research activities have not picked up in these Councils in the desired”
measure inspite of increased allocation in the first two years of Ninth Plan. The Committee
recommends that effective monitoring of the research undertaken by these councils be made
regular and it must be ensured that the Councils do real work. The Committee desires that
the Department should make efforts to publish the research activities that has been carried
out so far by these Councils. a

XIV. PUBLICITY 2४

14.1 The Committee was informed that a number of measures have been taken by the
Department for giving wide publicity to merits of ISM&H Systems. NGOs have also been
involved in spreading the message. The Committee, however, feels that adequate attention
has not been paid to this aspect and there is a greater need to focus on the utility of ISMH
particularly in chronic diseases and even in those areas where allopathy has not succeeded so
far. There is thus an equal need for enhancing the allocation proportionately.

14.2 The Committee expressed its serious concern over the fact that a lot of misleading
advertisements appear in the newspapers and on radio and television on magic remedy


i

drugs. The Drug Controllers of the States have been advised to take stringent action against
such misleading advertisements, the Department informed.

XV. COMMITTED LIABILITY

15.1 The Committee in its 56th Report had recommended that the Department should
make a thorough review of the schemes and identify the committed liability. In this matter,
the Committee considered the Report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance
Commission have observed as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan
scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan
scheme completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The
Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider
providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92.”

15.2 The Committee in this connection heard the views of the Secretary, Department of
Expenditure last year to clarify the position. He informed the Committee that even though
communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the
committed expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under
Demand No. 31. The Secretary also assured that if required more funds for this purpose will
be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the Departments may approach the
Department of Expenditure for their share.

15.3 The Committee notes that the Budget proposals of the Department for Revised
Estimates 1996-97 and BEs 1997-98 both Plan & Non-Plan were framed in accordance with
the guidelines of the Planning Commission. The Budget proposals for 1997-98 (being first
year of the 9th Five Year Plan period) inter-alia included the committed liability of the order
of Rs. 11.19 crore as a result of completion of some schemes/creation of some posts during
8th Five Year Plan period, As the amount was not agreed to be allocated in 1997-98, the
matter was taken up demi-officially at Secretary and Minister level with Ministry of Finance
who somehow did not agree thereto.

15.4 The Committee views with concern that the Finance Ministry has not honoured
such clear cut commitment made before the Parliamentary Committee. As the
recommendations of the Tenth Finance Commission have been accepted by the
Government, it is the commitment of the Government too. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department of Education should get the assurance implemented
without any delay.

Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-first Report of the Committee on the

from the Department of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development and also
heard oral evidence of the Officials of that Department and also the officials of the state
Govts. of U.P., Bihar, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi on the subject and got the first hand
information during its visits.

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE) has been accepted as a
national goal since 1950. The Directive Principles of the Constitution of India envisage
provision of free and compulsory elementary education to all children until they complete
the age of 14 years. In pursuance of the constitutional Directive, the need for a literate
population and provision of elementary education as a crucial input for nation building,
the National Policy on Education, 1986 as revised in 1992, states that free and
compulsory education of satisfactory quality should be provided to all children upto 14
years of age before the commencement of 21st century. The targets for 8th Five Year
Plan were set in keeping with these policy objectives. Though considerable progress has
been made towards achieving the targets, yet more vigorous and sustained efforts are
required to be made to achieve UEE at least by the end of 9th Five Year Plan.

1.2 The Sub-Committee on the Problem of Drop-outs was initially constituted on
16th January 1997 for making an in-depth study on the Problem of Drop-outs.
Subsequently, the Sub-Committee was reconstituted on 6th August, 1997. The Sub-
Committee, thereafter, called for a detailed comprehensive background note on the
subject from the Department of Education. After receiving the status report, the Sub-
Committee heard the oral evidence of the representatives of the Department of
Education, National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) and
National Institute of Educational Planning and Administration. In addition, the Sub-
Committee also heard the views of the Education Secretaries of the Government of
States/UTs of U.P. and Delhi on 12th June, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and
Union Territory of Chandigarh on 13th June, Andhra Pradesh on 8th and Tamil Nadu on
9th July, Rajasthan on 13th October, Union Territory of Andaman & Nicobar Islands on
11th November, Orissa and West Bengal on 14th November, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh,
Meghalaya, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim, on 17th November, 1997
respectively.

1.3 The Sub-Committee on the Problem of Drop-Outs has endeavoured to fulfil, to
the best of its ability, the objectives of the terms of reference set before it. The Sub-
Committee tried to study a wide perspective, including all the aspects affecting the
retention and progression of the students in the schools all over the country.

1.4 Since this was the first investigation of its kind, the Sub-Committee has no model
or material to use as a framework of reference. As the assessment of the problem of
Drop-Out could not be possible without making field visits, the Sub-Committee visited
Hyderabad and Chennai from 7th to 11th July, Jaipur from 13th to 16th October and
Port Blair, Calcutta and Guwahati from 11th to 18th November, 1997 to get first hand
information on the subject. The Sub-Committee had planned to visit these States/UTs
keeping in mind the diversities and inequalities that are prevailing in the field of
education and also with a view to know the latest position of the drop-out rate, retention
rate and also the progression rates of the students from Classes I to VIII.

1.5 During its field visits, the Sub-Committee had exchanged views with Village
Education Committees, Parents Teachers Associations, Mothers’ Associations, Mahila
Samoohas and the Members of the Village Panchayats and tried to know the role being
played by them in the field of education. The Sub-Committee also tried to ascertain the
attitudes of the villagers towards education.

1.8 The Indian elementary education system has become one of the largest in the world.
At the primary stage 8.76 lakh habitations covering 94 percent of the Country’s rural
population now have schooling facilities within one km. distance. At the upper primary stage
also 7.26 lakh habitations covering 83.98 percent of the rural population have a school within
three km. distance. But the Committee is not of the same opinion after making field visits.

1.9 The 8th Five Year Plan envisaged UEE to mean universalising access, retention and
achievement. The plan goals were set as following:

(a) Universal enrolment of all children, including girls and children belonging to
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

(b) Provision of primary school within 1 km. of walking distance and facility of non-
formal education for school drop-outs, working children and girls who cannot attend
formal schools.

(c) Improvement of ratio of upper primary schools to primary schools from existing
1. : .4,to-1.: 2.

(d) reduction of drop-out rates between classes I to V and I to VIII from the existing
46% and 60% to 20% and 40% respectively.

(e) Achievement of minimum levels of learning by all children at the primary level and
introduction of this concept at the upper primary stage.

1.10 The studies have indicated that even after the end of the Eighth Five Year Plan,
6.3 crore children in the age group of 6—14 years are still out of school. The majority of out
of the school children are girls and children belonging to SCs and STs in rural areas. The
Sixth All India Educational Survey (1993) has shown that there are still 11,574 schoolless
tural habitations in the country.

1.11 Eighth Five Year Plan had envisaged that the ratio of upper primaty schoois to
primary schools will be improved from the existing 1 : 4 to 1 : 2, However, there has been
marginal improvement in the ratio. which was 1 : 3.4 in 1995-96.

1.12 In order to improve retention, it was targeted that drop out rates will be reduced
to 20% in case of primary classes and 40% in case of upper primary classes. However
though declining, the drop out rates are still high at 34.5% for primary classes and 51.6%
for upper primary classes in 1995-96.
