II. OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

I. Methods of computing drop-out rate:

1.1 Fhe Committee during its visit had held discussions with many NGOs and experts
working in the field of education and felt that there is a lot of ambiguity about the method
of computing the drop out rate. In view thereof the Committee wishes here to redefine the
definition of the popular methods which are used for computing drop-out rates. The three
methods for determining drop-out rates are as under:

(a) method based on grade-to-grade progression rates.

(b) method based on ratio of grade V enrolment to grade I enrolment of 5 years
before; and

(c) method based on individual students data on their year to year progress in schools.

The Committee recommends that the three above mentioned methods may be used as
parameters to locate drop-outs for which a Retention Register should be maintained.

Il. ENROLMENT RATIO

2.1 The Committee is of the opinion that enrolment ratio and drop-out rates are co-
related. Accurate drop-out rate can be arrived at only on the basis of actual enrolment ratio.
However, the Committee understands that this is not the position in most of the States. At
present, what is happening is that Headmaster of a, primary school simply shows all school-
going children in the village as enrolled in his school in Class I. No consideration is being
given to the percentage of children actually attending the school on a regular basis. Besides
that, problem of double enrolment was often found in evidence by the Committee during its
State visits. The Committee feels that accurate enrolment figures can be easily arrived at by
involving the Village Education Committees and local youth in this task. The Committee
also recommends that the admission age of the child in Class I should be strictly adhered to
in order to avoid the instances of fictitious enrolment.

Ill. MAINTENANCE OF ENROLMENT, PROGRESSION AND RETENTION REGISTERS

3.1 The Committee during its visits noticed that except the schools being run by the
Shiksha Karmi and Lok Jumbish Projects in Rajasthan, and in some parts of Assam no other
schools of the State Governments are maintaining the Enrolment, Retention and Progression


6

Registers to monitor the drop-outs rates in the primary and upper primary schools. The
Committee finds that no corrective action has been taken by the concerned State
Governments. The Committee expresses its serious concern over this State of affairs.

3.2 The Committee has noticed that in the past the emphasis has been only on
enrolment due to which large number of fictitious enrolment figures in Class I were noticed.
These fictitious figures of enrolment not only affect the policy making but also make it
extremely difficult to estimate the correct drop-out rates. The Committee has seen that the
data available in the official documents appears to have been given only as estimated data
because whatever data procured during the field level visits was found contrary to the data
available in the official documents.

3.3 The Committee feels that there is a need to convince the administrators and
teachers about the need for correct enrolment figures. Guidelines should be issued for
regular monitoring of absent students and planned efforts should be made to ensure
continued participation of every child in the schools to prevent drop-out. The Committee
recommends that the task of monitoring the Enrolment, Retention and Progression Registers
should be assigned to the Village Level Education Committees.

IV. OPENING OF MORE PRIMARY AND UPPER PRIMARY SCHOOLS

4.1 The scheme of ‘Operation Black Board’ was launched in 1987 with the objective to
bring about both qualitative and quantitative improvement in primary education. Central
Government has extended financial assistance to the extent of Rs. 1551.68 crores from 1987-
88 till 31st March, 1995. However till 31st March, 1995 only 81% of the total central funds
1.6. Rs. 1253.09 crores could be utilised by the States.

4.2 Even after a decade of the launching of ‘Operation Blackboard’ the Committee finds
that so far as basic infrastructure is concerned, it cannot be said that all the primary schools
all over the country are fully provided for. The Schools visited by the Committee during its
study tours were selected in advance by the State Governments. So, they cannot be said to
be true reflection of the physical state of primary schools. Even then the Committee is
constrained to state that these pre-arranged schools were also lacking in basic facilities. No
doubt, by and large school buildings were there and in some cases extensions were also
being carried on. But these were insufficient to the needs of school-going children. Drinking
water and toilet facilities were also inadequate. In some of the schools which the Committee
visited, the students were being made to sit on bare floors. The Committee also observed
that in majority of primary schools, two or three classes were being held in one room under
the supervision of only one teacher. The Committee feels that this state of affairs is
responsible to some extent in non-retention of children in schools. Urgent steps, therefore,
need to be taken for creating facilities so that every class has its separate room. The
Committee during its visits noticed that due to non-availability of infrastructure and lack of
schools very large number of children perhaps 20% do not have access to school. The
problem is particularly more grave at the upper primary stage from class VI to VIII specially
in the case of girls. On ascertaining the reasons for not opening new schools, the Committee
was informed that the rigid norms for opening new schools and increase in the population of
the States are the main barrier, resulting in. more out of school children.

4.3 The Committee recommends that the norms for opening new schools in remote,
hilly and desert areas should be relaxed and the Village Education Committees (VEC)
should be empowered to make survey of the existing situation, identificaiton of non-
schooling areas and preparation of plan for facilitating the State Governments to open good
quality non-formal education centres. Keeping in view the growth rate of population, the


a

Central Government should also make plans for creating extra upper primary schooling
facilities equal to the primary schools in the country.

4.4 The Committee hopes that a funding pattern under JRY worked out by the
Department of Education in consultation with the Ministry of Rural Development would
accelerate the pace of construction of school buildings.

V. JOYFUL LEARNING

5.1 The Committee during its visits has seen that the present system of imparting
education to the children is very traditional and rigid and is not based on scientific pattern.
The Committee is of the view that Text-books should be colourful and attractive from the
children point of view and oral joyful teaching learning mechanism should be introduced
atleast upto IIIrd standard as the Committee observed that the maximum rate of drop-out is
from Class I to Class III.

5.2 The Committee feels that school can be made an attractive place and learning a
joyful experience, if teaching is made child centred and activity oriented as has been done in
the ““Anandapath” schooling system adopted by the Government of West Bengal and also by
production. of colourful and attractive textbooks and low cost teaching aids. The creation of
these items would automatically result in improving the retention rate.

VI. MOTIVATION OF TEACHER

6.1 The Committee feels that lack of motivation on the part of a section of teachers is
indirectly responsible for dismal retention rate of students in the schools. Dedicated teachers
are required for making the stay of a child in school a joyful experience. However, at
present, this is not very much visible primarily in the Government set up of schools. The
Committee is of the considered view that inculcation of motivation can be successfully,
attempted by making it an essential component of teacher’s training programme.

6.2 The Committee finds that almost all the States have the required strength of
teachers. But mere filling up of the existing vacancies of teachers is not the end, but it is just
the beginning. The Committee feels that motivated, dedicated and fully trained teachers are
the need of the hour. The Committee finds that all the State Councils of Educational
Research and Training (SCERT) are not fully equipped to impart adequate training to the
teachers. Even many of the SCERTs Personnel require training by master trainers. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that NCERT should launch a pilot programme in close
collaboration with the SCERTs for the training of teachers. This becomes all the more
necessary as studies have pointed out that the utilisation of teaching learning material has
not been very satisfactory because of lack of training of teachers. The Committee is of the
considered view that if teachers are imparted training on how to use available equipment
effectively in a classroom teaching situation, it is bound to have a positive impact on
improvement in quality of teaching.

6.3 The Committee is in full agreement with the findings of evaluation of the ‘Operation
Blackboard’ that there is a need to:—

(i) Streamline the purchase procedures with inbuilt quality controls;
(ii) provide for greater involvment of teachers in selection of teaching aids;
(iii) develop better linkage between teaching aids and curriculum requirements; and

(iv) motivate teachers to improve teachers aids from inexpensive locally available
materials.


6.4 The Committee is of the considered view that the working environment and work -
load of teachers, particularly those working in rural primary schools are far from satisfactory
and contribute to a large extent, to lack of motivation on their part. Following factors can be
cited as responsible for this situation:—

(a) Schools without adequate buildings and devoid of essential facilities;

(b) Lack of teaching aids and libraries;

(c) Heavy curriculum and workload, particularly for rural primary teachers;
(d) Multi-grade teaching responsibilities without adequate supervisory support;
(e) Commuting from long distances;

(f) Lack of proper housing facilities; and

(g) Non-instructional and administrative duties such as supervising elections,
participating in census operations, conducting family planning activities etc.,
producing adverse impact on the main task of teaching.

6.5 The Committee feels that State Governments should initiate immediate action so as
to bring about over all improvement in the working conditions of teachers.

VII. Change in Examination System

7.1 The Committee finds that in many States, students even in primary classes are
promoted to the next class only on the result of the annual examination. This indirectly acts
as a demotivating factor so far as retention of children in schools is concerned. There are a
couple of States viz. Andhra. Pradesh and West Bengal where there is no examination system
upto the level of Classes V and VI. Students are being promoted only on the basis of
attendance.

7.2 The Committee, however, recommends that annual examination system as the
criteria for promotion to the next class should continue.

शा. IDENTIFICATION OF HIGH DROP-OUT RATE AREA

During the visit of the Committee to certain States, it observed that there were some
districts maintaining very high drop-out rates and among the low level drop-out districts,
there were some blocks having high drop-out rate. There are also some villages with high
drop-out rate in such districts. Thus, the drop-out problem is prevalent throughout the
country. The Committee feels that there is a need to locate the exact area of high drop-out
rates. In Shiksha Karmi and Lok Jumbish Projects, at the village level, the school mapping
system exercise has proved very fruitful in enrolling all out of school children in the age
group of 6—14 years. The Committee feels that this kind of school mapping exercise should
be undertaken in all the States in order to get the exact picture of the enrolled and drop-out
children. The Committee recommends that the local bodies/PRIs/PTAs should be involved
in this task.

IX. NON-FORMAL EDUCATION PROGRAMME/PREHAR PATHASHALA AS A BACK
UP_ METHOD
9.1 Out of school children are being taken care of under the Non-Formal Education
Scheme since 1979. Almost all the States are running NFE centres. NGOs are also

contributing a lot in this field. However, even after two decades, the NFE Scheme could not
achieve the desired target to bring back the Non-Formal students to the mainstream


9

education. There are a varied number of factors responsible for it. Poor infrastructure, lack
of motivated and trained instructors, very low honorarium for instructor, lack of community
participation, no linkage between Formal and Non-Formal System of education, NFE being
treated as second grade education can be cited as the major reasons for NFE Schemes’
failure.

9.2 The Committee is of the considered view that revamping of entire NFE Scheme with
special emphasis on the following points is urgently required:

(a) Creation of basic facilities at NFE Centres.
(b) Increase in honorarium for instructors.
(c) Involvement of community and PRIs.
(d) Training of Instructors.
(e) Mechanism for effective supervision and monitoring of NFE Scheme.
X. SETTING UP OF JUNIOR TECHNICAL/VOCATIONAL EDUCATION INSTITUTE

10.1 The Committee was given to understand during the field visits, by the State
Governments that the drop-out rates are very high in classes VII or VIII. The primary
reason for this situation is that there is a general feeling among parents/students that no
purpose would be served by continuing studies after class VIII. To check this high drop-out
rate, the Committee is of the opinion that some technical/vocational education institutes
should be set up for imparting two years certificate courses in the field of craft, carpentry,
mechanical, food processing and poultry farms etc. after VIIIth Standard. The Committee
feels that setting up of such institutes would not only give a pragmatic approach towards the
educational system but it will also help in earning their livelihood and for inculcating an
attitude towards vocationalisation.

10.2 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Education and the
Planning Commission should initiate action for setting up of technical/vocational education
institutes parallel to the secondary stage in some selected districts on an experimental basis
and make a budgetary provision accordingly in the Ninth Five Year Plan.

XI. ESTABLISHMENT OF RESIDENTIAL PRIMARY SCHOOLS FOR CHILDREN OF
CONSTRUCTION WORKERS AND MIGRATORY POPULATION

11.1 The Committee during its visits has observed that in many states large number of
Nomadic Tribe, Construction and agricultural workers move from one place to another due
to the very nature of their profession and also in search of work. Because of their frequent
mobilisation, their children suffer a lot in the field of education due to which they are either
not admitted in school or if in case, children are admitted in school, the drop-out rates are
very high amongst such children.

11.2 The Committee understands that a Scheme for Residential Upper Primary/
Secondary Schools in Rural Areas already exists. Govt. should take effective steps to
implement the same without further delay. Besides that, NGOs can be effectively involved
in the task of motivating migratory labour in sending their children to the nearby schools.

XII. MID-DAY MEAL SCHEME

12.1 The Mid-Day Meal Scheme was launched by the Central Government on 15th
August, 1995 to give a boost to the universalisation of Primary Education by impacting upon
enrolment, attendance, retention and the nutrition needs of children in Primary Classes. The


» 10

Committee has noticed that cooked meal is not being served in all the States and instead 3
kg. wheat/rice is being distributed to the children in many states without adhering to the
stipulated condition of 80% attendance, once in a month. The Committee was apprised that
the attendance rate on the day of distribution only remained very high.

12.2 The Committee feels that to have a direct impact of the Mid-day Meal Scheme on
the retention side, to check the problem of absenteeism and drop-out and also to provide
nutrition to the school going children instead of distributing 3 kg. wheat/rice, cooked meal
should be served.

12.3 During the study visits, the Committee also noticed that pilferages are taking place
and the distribution system of foodgrains has also not been developed systematically due to
which untimely and short supply are the frequent phenomena which could be judged from
the fact that in some of the States/UTs like Rajasthan, West Bengal and Andaman &
Nicobar Islands, foodgrains have not been distributed to the targetted group even once in
the academic session of the 1996-97.

12.4 The Committee makes the following recommendations to correct the above
mentioned situation:- fe

(1) Cooked meal should be served;

(2) Strict monitoring system delegating the power to Village Level Education
Committee or PTA should be evolved;

*(3) Co-ordination between the Civil Supply and Education Departments of State
Governments needs to be strengthened;

(4) Local youth may be involved for the preparation of the cooked food; and

(5) Mid-day Meal should be provided through a separate mechanism without disturbing
the normal academic work of Teachers.

The Noon Meal Programme of Tamil Nadu Government may be adopted as a model for
implementing Mid-Day Meal Scheme:

XIII. INCENTIVES TO SC/ST, OBC AND MINORITIES COMMUNITY

13.1 The Committee finds that all the States are providing special incentives to SC/ST/
OBC students of Government Schools so as to motivate them towards studies. As a result, ©
there has been gradual increase in the enrolment ratio and gradual decrease in the drop out
rates of these categories of children.

13.2 The Committee feels that the incentives being given to SC/ST/OBC students may
be extended to the children who belong to the weaker sections of the society so as to bring
them into the arena of education. There is a need to revise the present incentive scheme.
The Committee also feels that children from the Minority Community are not so interested
in education. Therefore to spread the light of education and to check the drop-out rate
among them, more madrasas should be set up and special incentives should be given to
them.

XIV. DISTRIBUTION OF FREE TEXT BOOKS

14.1 In most of the States, free text books are being distributed amongst the children
upto Class V but the Committee during its visits noticed that there are cases of late supply
of text books. Even in some places, it reaches at the fag end of the academic session. The
Committee recommends that strict monitoring system should be evolved to check this


11

problem. The Committee also feels that the contents of the text books should be at par with
the MLL.

XV. GIRLS EDUCATION/WOMEN’S DEVELOPMENT

15.1 The survey carried out in the field of education reveals that the education has been
an intervention for women’s equality and the time has now come that Government should
make its utmost efforts so that the existing gap between the girls and boys is bridged.
Unfortunately, in India girls’ education deprivation is the most glaring manifestation of
India’s educational backwardness and the educational indicators are very adverse in classes I
to V and I to VIII. The All India drop out rate for 1995-96 amongst the girls in classes I to
V is 38.35% and in classes I to VIII it is 52.77% which is very high. The main reason for
this large number of drop-out rate is that the girls are engaged in house hold work such as
fuel and fodder collection, fetching of water and care of siblings etc.

15.2 The Committee recommends for giving suitable incentives to girl child, like
providing free uniform, free teaching/learning materials and construction of toilet and
providing drinking water facilities particularly in the girls schools/Co-education schools. The
Committee also recommends that a Special Management structure should be set-up wherein
women should be placed in the key position and at the micro level women’s groups should
be engaged for the development of the girl child.

15.3 As women have traditionally played a subordinate role in sotiety, so they have
been conditioned into thinking of themselves as inferior to men, to be tolerated only if they
toil, fetch, carry and procreate. Financial burden is only a hurdle in the education of boys
but it becomes an insurmountable barrier when the question of education of girls arises.
Sending her to school would also mean an additional loss of income because the mother will
have to stay away from work to look after the younger ones and to do the household chores.
But education can be an enduring and strong factor in women’s empowerment.

15.4 The Committee feels that unless a systematic effort is made to improve women’s
access to education it will not be possible to achieve the objective of education for all by the
year 2000. Experience has shown that the rural women have not kept pace with the
‘Sathin’s’ progress. It is now a recognised fact that instead of focussing on just one women,
‘Sathin’ village level activity should be central around a Group of women. The Committee is
of the view that this collective, the Samooh, after adequate orientation and training would
enable the village women to take an interest and play an effective role in community
activities especially related to Education.

XVI. CONTINUATION OF PLAN PROJECTS

16.1 The Committee was given to understand by Secretaries of the State Governments
during the discussions that many schemes which were introduced during the plan period
were not continued in the next Plan due to which the State Governments had to face a lot of
problems to continue that project because of non-availability of funds. The State
Governments were of the opinion that ‘before discontinuing any schemes in the next Plan
period the viability of the existing schemes should be reviewed and they should be carried
forward on merit basis. The Committee recommends that view-point of the State
Governments may be examined by the Centre.

XVII. COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT

17.1 The Committee during its field visit observed that local people are little bit
indifferent to the present system of education due to lack of people’s mobilisation, school


12

community interaction, centralisation and also due to concentration of management powers
in the hand of the bureaucracy. To correct the present system, the Committee feels that
there is a need for creation for mechanism of community involvement, decentralisation of
powers and reimposing faith in grass root-level people. The Committee also interacted with
the management body of the Lok Jumbish and Shiksha Karmi Projects at Rajasthan. The
Committee has seen that people’s movement activities for the development of education are
really getting their root of Rajasthan. The Committee was also very impressed by the
activities of Village Education Committee functioning in the villages of Andhra Pradesh.

17.2 The Committee feels that there is a need for formation of Village Core Teams to
mobilise the people which will ultimately form the Village Education Committee. The
Committee understands that Panchayati Raj Institutions have been given sufficient powers
by 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments to have an effective say in the functioning of
schools in their area. But so far, this has been only on paper. State Government have still to
show their willingness to implement these constitutional amendments by handing over all the
powers and required funds as envisaged. In West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh, the
Committee during its visit noticed that these Panchayati Raj Institutions are discharging a
pivotal role in the rural economy and also in spreading education. The Committee hopes
that in the very near future, scenario in the field of elementary education would definitely
change in the light of all the constitutional amendments made. The Committee, however,
urges upon the Department of Education to call a meeting of the Education Ministers of all
the State Governments to work out modalities to provide a legal status to the Panchayati
Raj Institutions in this regard.

REPORT

INTRODUTION

1. Development of a nation in every sphere depends largely on the attitude, values,
knowledge and skills of its people which are in accordance with the modern-day life. The
only way this can be accomplished is through education and literacy is the first step towards
education. The National Literacy Mission was set up in 1988 with the goal of making 80
million persons in the age-group of 15-35 years functionally literate by the year 1995. NLM
is now committed to make 100 million people literate by 1998-99 and to bring about total
literacy by 2005.

2) The Sub-Committee on Adult Education, initially constituted on 16th Jan. 1997 was
reconstituted on 6th August, 1997. The Sub-Committee heard the views of representatives of
the Deptt. of Education, Education Secretaries of State Govts. of Kerala and Orissa and
also UT of Delhi. As the assessment of overall impact of Total Literacy Campaigns launched
in different parts of the country could not be possible without. making on the spot study
visits, the Sub-Committee visited Trivandrum and Bhubaneswar from 22nd te 28th
September, 1997. During its field visits, the Sub-Committee visited a number of Adult
Education centres and also interected with various authorities involved in literacy campaigns
and also learners.

3. The Background Note furnished by the Deptt. of Education states that ‘the Total
Literacy Campaign (TLC) is the principal strategy of the NLM for eradication of illiteracy in
the country. TLCs are delivered through voluntarism and implemented by Zilla Saksharta
Samities (ZSS) or Distrsict Literacy Committees usually headed by District Collectors
Literacy campaigns are implemented by ‘funding ZSS through the Central and State
Governments'in the ratio of 2:1. However, for distrsicts under Tribal Sub Plan their ratie is
4:1

4. The compaigns are initiated with appropriate environment-building activity coupled
with a door-to-door literacy survey during which potential learners and volunters are
identified, Suitable primers are developed and primer-specific training is provided'to the
trainers. The environment-building activity as well as the monitoring and supervision are
continued throughout the teaching/learning process which accounts for a total of 200 heurs
spread over a period of 6’months. Concurrent, mid-course and external evaluations are
conducted by evaluation agencies identified for the State Directorate of Adult Education and
NLM.

5. After completion of the TLC, Post Literacy Campaign (PLC) is launched to reach
out to remaining illiterates to consolidate the gains acquired during TLC, and also to enable
the neo-literates to develop self-learning-skills.

6. The Department informed the Committee that an Expert Group was constituted in
April, 1993 under the Chairmanship of Prof. Arun Ghosh to undertake a status-cum-impact
evaluation of literacy campaigns launched in different parts of the country. Some ef the
important findings of the Report are as under:—

Overwhelming impact on women;
Positive impact on caste and communal relations;
Demand generated for primary education;

d:

ee an 2


2

Literacy placed on the national agenda;

Quality suffered in some places because of pre-occupation with total literacy;
Bureaucratization—in some cases;

Need for quick follow-up post literacy campaigns in order to consolidate fragile literacy
skills;

Some campaigns launched without adequate preparations.

The Committee was given to understand that in view of the way the Mission has moved
and findings of the Prof. Arun Ghosh Committee, the Government have evolved the
following new strategies:

— Preparation of time-bound action plans for TLC coverage of uncovered districts in the
States of Bihar, U.P., Rajasthan and Maharashtra.
—Non-cash incentives for motivating volunteers.

— Establishment of strong linkages between literacy campaigns and Panchayati Raj
Institutions.

— Decentralisation and delegation of authority for implementation of literacy programme to
State Government by establishment of State Literacy Mission Authorities (SLMAS).

7. In the light of findings and recommendations of the Expert Group and having regard
to the emerging literacy scenario, the Scheme of Continuning Education of neo-literates was
launched in December, 1995 to replace the earlier scheme of Post Literacy and Continuing
Education and the Jan Shikshan Nilayams (JSNs) under the pre-revised scheme was ceased
with effect from 1st April, 1996. However, in the districts which have not so far been
covered under TLC/PLC, JSNs established under the earlier scheme will remain the

——~principal mechanism to fulfil Post Literacy and Continuing Education needs of. the local
population. The existing JSNs will, therefore, be continued in the non-TLC districts until
such districts are also taken up for TLC

OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

8.1 National Literacy Mission is committed to make 100 million people literate by 1998-
99 and to bring about total literacy by 2005. The Committee notes that 442 districts i.e
majority of the districts in the country have been covered under TLC so far. However, the
Committee finds that the number of persons made literate is very less if details are gone
into. The compaigns have covered an estimated 147 million persons among whom 120.34 -
million learners were identified through surveys. Out of these, only 90.55 million persons
could be enrolled and only 64.34 million persons have been made literate so far. The
Committee fails to understand as to how the proposed target of making 100 million people
literate by 1998-99 can be achieved. The Committee feels that whereas coverage of districts
under TLC has been impressive, it seems to be only on paper. Although identification of
illiterate persons through surveys is being done, the follow-up action for enrolling such
illiterate persons and making them literate is not being taken up with the same spirit. The
Committee apprehends that until some radical measures are taken, the target date may again
have to be extended. There is a strong need of working out a mechanism of enrolment of
adults, their retention and their continuing education. It must be ensured that any adult
enroled is helped to reach the final stage of permanent functional literacy. Therefore, tracer
study approach will have to be adopted.

8.2 The Committee would also like to point out that against the total allocation of
Rs. 1400 crores for Adult Education during the 8th Plan, actual expenditure was only Rs.
718.14 crores. Similarly, for 1997-98 although there was an allocation of Rs. 129.81 crores,


|

3

expenditure was only Rs. 84.48 crores. The Committee expresses its deep concern over
under-utilisation of funds. It is true that in some of the educationally backward States like
Bihar, U.P., Rajasthan and MP, campaigns have lagged behind leading to under-utilisation
of funds. The Committee strongly feels that merely requesting such State Govts. to draw up
a time-bound action plan for bringing uncovered districts under Tot~'” ost Literacy
Campaigns will not serve the purpose. What is required is a result-oriented co-ordination
between the Centre and States. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Deptt.
should impress upon the States for effective implementation of Adult Education Programme.
The role of bureaucracy should recede and involvement of people should increase to the
ownership level of the programme. Strategy for this will have to be worked out.

POST LITERACY CAMPAIGNS

9.1 The Committee was informed that after completion of TLC, Post Literacy Campaign
(PLC) is launched to mop up the left over illiterates and to consolidate the gains of literacy
acquired during TLC and to enable the new-literates to develop abilities for self-learning and
help upgradation of skills for their economic betterment. The Committee, however, is -
constrained to note that PLCs have not taken off in the country in the real sense. Whereas
442 districts have been covered under TLC, Post Literacy Campaigns have been launched in
only 229 districts so far. Figures relating to educationally backward States are self-
explanatory.

State TLCs launched PLCs launched
Bihar 40 distts. 11 distts.
MP 45 distts. 19 distts.
Orissa 24 distts. i 12 distts.
Rajasthan 31 distts. 18 distts.

UP 68 distts. 11 distts.

9.2 The Committee also finds that there is a gap of 2 to 3 years in the launching of TLC
and PLC in all the districts. Thus the basic objective of PLC to provide opportunities of
continuing education to neo-literates so as to facilitate retention of their literacy skills and to
enable the learners to continue their learning beyond elementary literacy stands defeated.
The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should impress upon all the
States specially the educationally backward States to launch PLCs in the remaining districts
so as to ensure that benefits of literacy are sustained by the neo-literates.
OPERATION RESTORATION है eo

%

10. The Committee was informed that ‘Operation: Restoration’ for TLC Projects in the
districts which for various unavoidable reasons have stagnated or have not taken off is being
taken up during the Ninth Plan. 25 districts in six States of Bihar, Haryana, Karnataka,
Orissa, Rajasthan and UP have been identified. The Committee finds that districts identified
are those which had taken up the Campaign Programme without adequate preparation, the
project had dragged behind for ‘two to three years and are stagnating after an initially
successful Total Literacy phase. However, mere identification of districts and allocation of
funds would not achieve the desired results. Concerted efforts by the Central Govt. are
required so that State Govts. are impressed upon to take corrective measures


4

BROAD-BASING THE COURSE CONTENT

_11. Persons in the age-group of 15-35 years are to be made functionally literate under
Adult Education Programme. The Committee feels that traditional literacy courses will not
prove to be attractive for this particular age-group. Hence, special area-specific approach
needs to be kept in mind while formulating primers for learners. Element of folk lore/folk
songs/dramas can also be inducted so as to draw larger number of adult population towards
this programme. The Committee also recommends that steps should be taken for introducing
some vocational courses based on local needs which can become source of income for the
participants.

WOMEN MAJOR BENEFICIARIES

12.1 The Committee is happy to note that women constitute 62% of total beneficiaries
under the Adult Education Programme. Involvement of women at such a large scale has led
to several wholesome social spin-offs reported from various districts such as:

— improvement in enrolment of children at primary level.
— women becoming more confident and forward-looking.
— immunisation improved to record levels.

— small family norm getting increasingly accepted.

The Committee is of the view that successful implementation of Adult Education
Programme would also indirectly result’ in a positive impact on various Govt.-run Family
Welfare Programmes.

12.2 The Committee feels that Anganwadis can also be used as Adult Education
Centres for women. The Committee would also like to point out that besides normal
education courses, traditional rural art/vocation/skills can be imparted in an organised way
to women at these centres. The Govt. should also work out a via media whereby a
commercial outlet is provided for such products made by women through co-operative
movements.

CLIENTELE OF ADULT EDUCATION PROGRAMME

13.1 The Committee was informed that the initial objective of NLM was to make 80
million persons in the age-group of 15-35 years literate by the year 1995. However,
subsequently, this was revised to include children in the age-group of 9-14 years also in areas
where Non-Formal Education Programme was not in operation.

13.2 The Committee had noticed children in the age-group of 9-14 years in Adult
Education Centres during its field visits in Delhi. This may be the position in other areas
also. The Committee is very much disturbed by the fact that children in the age-group of 9-
14 years are also being handled by Adult Education Centres. The Committee feels that this
is not a healthy trend. Adult Education Centres are located in the villages/localities where
already Normal School/NFE facilities exist for children in the age-group of 9-14 years. Steps
are also being taken by both Govt. and voluntary agencies to motivate out of school children
to attend schools/NFE Centres. The Committee, therefore, fails to understand the rationale
behind inclusion of children in the age-group of 9-14 years under the Adult Education
Programme. The Committee is of the firm view that Adult Education Programme should
strictly adhere to the age-group of 15-35 years.

SHRAMIK VIDYAPEETH

14. The programme, with specially designed courses, addresses the needs of the socially
and economically deprived sections of workers communities. The Committee notes that


during the year 1996-97, 4,86,556 persons out of whom 35.20% were males and 64.80%
females benefited from 11,663 programmes conducted by SVPs. The Committee was given
to understand that the Scheme of SVPs which was hitherto restricted to urban/semi-urban
industrial areas will now be expanded to all districts. It is proposed to sanction at least one
SVP to each district in the country. The Committee, however, feels that Govt. proposal to
sanction at least one SVP to each district would not have the desired results. There might be
many districts where there is no industry at all. What is required is to make, in the first
instance, the existing 58 SVPs more purposeful, based on the area-specific needs of the
working class. Evaluation of SVP Scheme, if not already done, may be initiated by the
Deptt. before further expansion of this Scheme.

ADULT EDUCATION CENTRES

_ 15, The Committee would like to point out that location and timing of Adult Education
Centres is very important for achieving the set goals under Adult Education Programme.
Centres should be as near to general masses as is possible. Infrastructure available at schools
and even the services of school teachers can be used by Centres after school hours. Keeping
in view the social background of women, there should be exclusive centres being run by
women volunteers (Preraks) and during the timings convenient to women at large.

SELECTION OF VOLUNTEERS (PRERAKS)

16, The Committee feels that the village education committee/ocal community should
be involved in the selection of volunteers for running of Adult Education Centres in order to
ensure the acceptability of Preraks in the community. Local students from higher classes may
also be involved in this task.

VOLUNTARY AGENCIES

17.1 The Committee finds that Voluntary Agencies are playing a big role in the Adult
Education Programme. The Committee was given to understand that upto March, 1996, 158
TLC Projects have been sanctioned to 148VAs for making a total of about 23 lakh persons
literate. The Committee, however, finds that non-constitution of Screening Committees for
identification of VAs at State and district level, adverse reports from certain State Govts,
regarding performance of VAs and non-submission of audited accounts and proper Project
Reports by VAs are some of the main hurdles which are coming in the way of effective
involvement of VAs in Adult Education Programme, The Committee feels that services of
VAs can be more gainfully employed if identification of really motivated VAs is got done by
State Governments.

17.2 During the course of interaction with State Govt. officials as well as NGOs in
Orissa, the Committee came to know that the literacy rate in the tribal areas was very low.
It seems that Total Literacy Campaigns have not reached the remote tribal areas of Orissa.
The Committee was given to understand that in Orissa, TLC has not become a mass
movement as yet as it is still in the hands of State’ authorities. The Committee is of the firm
view that in such a situation, Voluntary Agencies can play a vital role. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Deptt. should impress upon the State Govts. to take steps to
involve the VAs having a good track-record in reaching out to illiterate population in tribal
areas.

ROLE OF MEDIA

18.1 The Committee was informed that as part of media support to literacy campaigns
some of the: main activities undertaken are as follows:—

1. Production of video films in various languages.
2. Half-an-hour chunk for literacy on DD-1 on every Friday.


6

3. Attractive spots highlighting benefits of literacy telecast through Doordarshan and
closed circuit TVs at selected railway station/ airports.

4. Special Ads. designed and released through DAVP in National Dailies of different
languages in connection with International Literacy Day.

5. Literacy Messages printed on postal stationery and computerised railway tickets of
Northern Railway.

18.2 Mass awareness is an integral part of Adult Education Programme. This
programme can be successfully implemented only if a message reaches to the general masses
that without literacy, a person cannot be successful in, life. The Committee, however, feels
that effective use of media is not being made in the implementation of Adult Education
Programme. The Committee is of the view that steps like advertisements in Hindi on TV,
literacy messages printed on postal stationery and computerised railway tickets of Northern
Railway etc. would not serve the purpose. The Committee therefore recommends that Govt.
should plan its media campaign keeping in view the region-specific demands of areas where
Adult Education Programme is yet to take its roots. Advertisements/Posters in the language
of the area and according to the specific social background would result in higher
participation in this programme.

LIBRARIES

19. The Cornmittee feels that libraries are a must for neo-literates if their interest in
education is to be, sustained. The Committee finds that libraries have played a very
important role in spreading literacy in Kerala. Similar efforts are required in other parts of
the country. Community libraries can be made use of in generating interest in reading
among the neo-literates.

ROLE OF PANCHAYATI RAJ INSTITUTIONS

20.1 The Committee was informed that the 73rd and 74th Amendments to the
Constitution have assigned the responsibility of implementation of Adult Education
Programmes to Panchayats. This is being ensured wherever Panchayat Bodies are active by
involving their representatives in the Executive Bodies of the Zilla Saksharta Samities. The
areas where it is proposed to involve them actively are generation of environment and
creation of motivation among learners and volunteers, in securing cooperation and mass
participation of people and in monitoring and evaluation of literacy programmes. However,
as gathered during interaction with public, the Committee feels that the Panchayats have
their own preferences such as economic activities, construction, development and literacy is
accorded the least priority. The“Committee, therefore, recommends that steps should be
taken to ensure that Adult Education programme is taken up on a priority basis by
Panchayats. There is a specific responsibility of making the district fully literate as per
functional norms set by the NLM which may be given to Zilla Panchayats with total
planning, implementation and monitoring. The funds for this as per requirements of the
Zilla Panchayat should ‘be provided by the Central Government from the Centrally
sponsored schemes. [t must be made clear that this fund is in addition to the fund allocated
by the State Finance Commission. The achievement of the target set by the Zilla Panchayat
should be externally evaluated and responsibility for any shortfall should be fixed on the
concerned agency. This will ensure the responsibility and accountability coupled with
decentralisation of power and implementation.


7

20.2 The Committee was also given to understand that there is a proposal to shift
Collector Centric model to alternative second-line of command to implement the campaigns,
through involvement of more and more non-officials and voluntary agencies. The Committee
in this connection would like to suggest that the Kerala model may be experimented by
making District Panchayat President as the Chairman and District Collector as coordinator.
EVALUATION

21.1 The Committee was informed that the NLM has introduced more meaningful and
rigorous evaluation system and each literacy campaign is now required to take up concurrent
evaluation of the ongoing programme through an outside agency nominated by the State
Directorates of Adult Education. The State Directorates have been asked to empanel
agencies for undertaking concurrent evaluation. Concurrent evaluation aims at quick mid-
term appraisal of a project to assess the strengths and weaknesses of an ongoing programme
and to identify correctives for improvement of the programme. Besides concurrent
evaluation, each literacy campaign district is now subject to final evaluation towards the end
of the project through an independent external evaluation agency nominated by the NLM.

21.2 While appreciating the monitaring mechanism for Adult Education, the Committee
feels that involvement of local MPs/MLAs in this task will prove to be more effective.

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-third Report of the Committee on
Dreaded Diseases.

2. The Committee in this connection appointed a Sub-Committee under the convenor-
ship of Dr. Shrikant Ramachandra Jickhar, in its meeting held on 16th January, 1997 to look
into the various aspects of Dreaded Diseases for making an in-depth study on the subject
and to present a report thereon to the Committee at an early date.

3. The Sub-Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received
from the Department of Health, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also heard oral
evidence of the Officials of that Department on the subject. The Sub-Committee also heard
the views of various experts in the field and got valuable and detailed information on the
subject particularly on AIDS and Hapatitis-B.

4. The Draft Report submitted by the Sub-Committee was cansidered and adopted on

9th October, 1998. The Committee at its meeting held on 19th November, 1998 decided to
present the Report in the House during the Winter Session of Parliament.

New DELHI; S.B. CHAVAN,
Chairman,

aera Department-Related Parliamentary
Asvina 17, 1920 (Saka) Standing Committee on Human

Resource Development.

4310/RS/F—3-A (श)


REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 According to the Oxford Dictionary, ‘Dreaded’ means a thing or a disease which is
greatly feared or one from which one shrinks or looks forward with great apprehension.

1.2 Generally three considerations are taken before terming a disease as dreaded
(i) morbidity, (ii) mortality, and (iii) social stigma attached to the disease.

1.3 Accordingly, the following diseases may be classified as dreaded (i) AIDS,
(ii) Cancer, (iii) major heart diseases or Internal diseases which damage the Kidneys or
other Important organs, (iv) major neurological or nephrological Problems, (v) Hepatitis-B,
and (vi) Hepatitis-C.

1.4 Of the above diseases the Committee has taken up AIDS and Hepatitis-B to make a
detailed study about the impact of these diseases in the country.

II. AIDS
2.1 The first case of AIDS in India was noticed in Tamil Nadu in 1986 when some sex-
workers were detected HIV Positive. The main problem during that time was poor

monitoring of the disease. Despite the Central Government spending a lot of money, there
was no feedback about AIDS from the States.

2.2 According to a WHO source, there are about 27.5 million people who have been
infected with HIV in the world, and out of this, there are 21.5 million people’ living with
HIV Positive. As far as the sex distribution between the male and female, the ratio is 50 : 50
and it is around 20 per cent in children.

2.3 The position in India as on date is, 8.13 million cases Positive and out of this 4,725
have developed into full fledged AIDS cases. In 4,725 cases, 4% children are infected by
HIV virus. There is a chance of even all the 65,200 may finally emerge as AIDS cases, but
the time period to mature into a full fledged AIDS case varies. Internationally the average
period to develop into a full fledged AIDS case is 7 years whereas in India it ranges from 5
to 8 years.

2.4 Considering the prevailing situation, the Government of India launched a Centrally
sponsored scheme, in the National AIDS Project in 1992. This project is being implemented
with committed IDA Credit of US$ 84 million with the objective to slow the spread of HIV
in India so as to reduce the future morbidity, mortality and impact of AIDS. It attempts to
achieve the following:—

(a) involving all States/UTs in developing HIV/AIDS preventive activities with a

special focus on the major epicentres of the epidemics;

(b) to attain a satisfactory level of public awareness on HIV transmission and

prevention; zh

(c) developing health promotion interventions among risk behaviour group;

(d) to screen the majority of blood units collected for blood transfusions;

(e) decreasing the practice of professional blood donations;

(0 developing skills in clinical management, health education and counselling, and

psycho-social support to HIV sero-positive persons, AIDS patients and their
associates:


Zz

(g) to initiate steps to strengthen STD control; and
(h) to monitor the development of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the country.

2.5 Deposing before the Committee, the project Director NACO stated that as far as
the policy of the Government is concerned the objective is to slow down the spread of HIV/
AIDS infection through creation of awareness and aiming at behavioural change. He also
stated that earlier the emphasis of the Government was confined to the high risk groups i.e.
commercial sex workers and intravenous drug users and now the strategy of the Government
is to expand and spread across the country about AIDS through the State Governments and
district administration. In this situation, the role of State Governments in the programme is
very crucial, he added. The Government has also directed its efforts towards strengthening
the hands of the State AIDS Control Organisation in turn they will be able to spread the
message right up to the district level. The Committee was also informed that actually in rural
areas HIV is still less than 0.4 per cent and the response is good in rural areas to the
programme when compared to towns and urban areas.

2.6 Further elaborating about the project to the Committee, he informed that the
Government is adopting a very comprehensive strategy aimed at addressing all the aspects of
the disease which includes AIDS prevention, strengthening the programme management
capacity at national and State level including surveillance and clinical management and to
provide necessary infrastructure to start a counselling service in the States.

2.7 The Committee. was also informed that the programme was subject to a mid-term
review by the World Bank Mission and Inter-alia recommended discontinuance of credit to
the slow performing States until they utilise their unspent balances. It was also stated that
the Review Mission expressed its pleasure on the action taken by the Ministry and overall
improvement of the programmes at the Centre and several States.

2.8 The Committee heard the views of the Experts on 8th September, 1997. Experts
who appeared before the Committee apprised that the standard for confirming HIV
diagnosis is the culture of the virus which is very difficult and not possible. It was informed
that whenever diagnosing takes place, diagnosing does not takes place based only on
laboratory tests and it was added that more specific tests are required to confirm HIV virus
and specificity is most important in the third test. Further, they informed that the equipment
and the machinery required for testing is highly expensive and it would not be possible to
have these at all the labs. The Committee was further informed that there is a need for
identifying some laboratories which aré involved in conducting the third test.

2.9 The Experts further informed the Committee that for proper implementation of the
programme there is a need for uniform testing system in the entire country and it means that
the entire programme should be decentralised and every State should have a reference
centre.

2.10 The Committee was further informed by the Experts that there is a need for
developing our own kits for testing. They felt it necessary because the import of kits is very
costly and another thing is that kit should be developed based on the virus that is affecting
the particular area. It was also informed that whereas the western kits are based on’ virus
sub-type B, the viruses that are affecting our country is either sub-type A or C, and in some
areas it is sub-type B. So, the experts stressed that there is a need for developing our own
kit, which is best suited to our needs.

2.11 Elaborating on the progress made in the context of developing a kit suiting our
needs, it was informed by one of the experts that NIC has developed a synthetic base kit.
Another kit has been developed by Delhi University and Cancer Institute, Mumbai has


3

developed a kit for HIV-1 and HIV-2. These locally developed kits were evaluated by
NICD, New Delhi and a lot of Pitfalls were found, and suggestions to rectify the same were
given and they are still working on it, it was informed.

2.12 The Committee was informed by the experts that blood screening is one area
where all our efforts should be directed, It was also informed that the most distressing
problem is blood transfusion. It was due to the yawning gap between the demand and supply
of blood and also because of the fact that majority of the blood is being donated by
professional donors and they have a very objectionable kind of life-style. Under normal
medical regulation, one is not supposed to donate blood more than once every three
months. Professionals keep on donating once in 15 days and once they get money they
immediately go to a red-light area. It was also informed that dependence on voluntary blood
donation is not adequate.

2.13 The Committee was also informed that in the case of HIV testing there is a need
for training of the technicians and doctors, because they never had any training of this kind.
So when the concept of quality assurance and quality control is introduced,, they virtually |
had no idea, It was further informed that whenever training programmes are conducted,
such people are being trained who had never seen any HIV case, this infact results in
training going waste. It was stressed that people at the grass root level should be trained, so
that the benefits of the training can be reaped.

2.14 The Committee was also informed by the experts that the customs duty for

Ill. OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

3.1 The Committee is constrained to note that funds granted to the States are not
utilised fully. The matter of low utilisation of funds has been of grave concern at all levels.
The main problem is that State Aids Promotion Organisations (SAPO) face a number of
difficulties in receiving and utilising funds due to the current financial system at the State
level. The major hindrance is that they do not have the direct power to spend the money
and yet are accountable for it under the project. This is peculiar system and needs to be
changed immediately. The country is facing such a gigantic task of dealing with the problem
of AIDS and frivolous matters such as delayed release of funds etc. should not hinder the
implementation of the project. The Committee strongly recommends that the Centre in
coordination with the States should take all required steps to see that funds flow smoothly to
the grass root level for successful implementation of the programme. The Committee was
given to understand that the funds were released by State Finance Department at the last
moment or sometimes at the end of the current financial year. The Committee feels that this
kind of situation should not prevail any more. The funds should be released in advance,
atleast six months before, and on receiving the expenditure certificate, the next instalment
may be released immediately.

3.2 The Committee is pained to note that a number of states have not filled in the
sanctioned posts. The reason given that this has been done in view of the fact that the
National Aids Control Programme is a time bound project, is not convincing to the
Committee. The Committee feels that this aspect could have been tackled by the Centre in a
better manner by convincing the States about the importance of the programme and the
necessity of creation of the posts and a via-media for the continuance of the posts created
could have been found out. It is surprising for the Committee that the Department has not
done anything in this regard till now. This aspect needs to be considered immediately and all
the States should be asked to create the number of posts as are required.

3.3 The Committee was given to understand that IMA and NACO are making a
combined effort to train general medical practitioners for clinical management of AIDS and
HIV infected persons. The training given is too less to cover a chunk of general physicians in
the country, particularly in the States where AIDS and HIV are rampant. A large scale
training to the physicians and nurses is required so that they may be able to effectively
tackle the patient. The Committee is also given to understand that many physicians and
nurses do not turn up or attend to the HIV and AIDS patients mainly because of the lack of
general awareness and the skills to treat and tackle them. Therefore, the Department should
chalk out a massive scheme to cover, atleast once, for some period for training most of the
general physicians in the major cities of the country. Nurses training is also not very
satisfactory. They need to be given specialised skill training.

3.4 The Committee understands that blood banks are the area which needs to be
strengthened and modernised for securing safe blood supply. Blood banks are the places
from where infected blood is donated and transfused. The Committee is, however,
constrained to note that many blood banks in the public sector are yet to be taken up for
modernisation to achieve the goal of securing safe blood supply. All the blood banks, atleast


7

in the public sector, should be immediately covered to ensure supply of safe blood. The
Committee also feels the necessity of a regular monitoring on the public sector blood banks
on any possible violation of norms. Similarly, the Committee is equally concerned about the
blood banks in the private sector. There is hardly any monitoring over the activities of the
private blood banks. Efforts are also required to modernise Government Blood Banks and
provide necessary facilities for testing AIDS/HIV etc. Similarly, Government should also see
to it that the recently amended Drugs and Cosmetics Rule which provide that no blood bank
shall collect blood from professional donors, is strictly adhered to by all the blood banks.

3.5 The Committee is aware that there is no cure for AIDS. Prevention is the only
aspect which has to be strengthened. For prevention a large scale public awareness is
required. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the awareness programme
has not picked up in India. Even though the problem of AIDS is enveloping the whole
country, the Committee has come to note that the literature prepared and the programmes
initiated are either not related to the local needs of the people or the local dialects. Half of
India’s population are illiterate. One aspect on which one can feel happy is that the AIDS
syndrome has not yet touched, in a bigger way, the horizons of the rural areas. This is,
therefore, the area which is to be protected with very well chalked out programmes. The
programmes to be launched should take into view the local people’s conditions, their culturql
behaviour and the language. Unless the message transmitted is not properly received the
whole effort will go waste. The Committee strongly recommends the department to give a
serious consideration on this. The Committee is of the view that in the awareness
programme participation of NGOs, students, local bodies etc. should be given preference to
the maximum extent because these are the groups which can effectively transmit the
messages through the language understandable to the local community.

3.6 The Committee was given to understand that the IECs material for strengthening
awareness programme was reviewed and revised material have been finalised. The
Committee desires that a local scrutiny should be kept on the IECs materials being used and
whenever any review is made the State Government concerned should also be consulted.
There is also a necessity of training the people who handle the IECs material and also those
involved in making the audio and video programmes. Specialised skills are required for this
and Government should consider strengthening the training programme for every group
including NGOs.

3.7 The Committee is given to understand that care, support and medicines for people
living with HIV/AIDS is very inadequate. This is particularly in view of the social stigma
attached with this infection and the affected persons being treated as social outcast by the
community as a whole. Infected persons are also required to be counselled to ensure that
they take all precautions to avoid any further infection to others. For this, the Committee
feels, highly skilled and efficient counselling and education are required. The Committee has
the evidence to note that very few counselling centres are existing in the country. This
counselling should have been started much earlier and the Committee is pained to note that
much effort has not been done in this direction. Therefore, much more emphasis should be
laid on this aspect and also on educating the general populace about their behavioural
pattern with the infected people. Similarly, as already recommended earlier, medicines to
the infected people should be regularly ensured and Government should provide sufficient
budget for this purpose and assistance from foreign agencies may be obtained, if need be.

3.8 The Committee is of the firm view that much emphasis under the AIDS Control
Programme has not been so far laid on the high risk behaviour groups like sex workers and
frequently travelling males and drug users. These are main groups which are highly

vulnerable to HIV/AIDS infection. Awareness and counselling are much more required on
these people than on the other groups of the society. They should be made to understand
the danger of the STDs/HIV/AIDS and the risk factor involved in not using condoms and
taking other precautions. Special awareness programme should be taken up particularly for
sex workers and frequently travelling males.

3.9 NGOs have a very vital role in: AIDS Control Programme. They are the groups
which can work in close proximity to the people particularly the high risk behavioural
groups. The Committee, however, is constrained to note that the Central Government which
sanction funds to the NGOs and the Central Government does not have even the list of
NGOs working under the programme in various States. But the Committee feels that Centre
should take initiative in bringing the NGOs forward under the implementation of the
programme.

3.10 The Committee has learnt that various international agencies are implementing
various programmes in different parts of the country for tackling the problem of HIV/AIDS.
In this connection the Committee is constrained to note that NACO is not involved in the
implementation of all the projects in all parts of the country. For example, even though
many pilot programmes are being implemented in Tamil Nadu, NACO is involved with the
implementation of only USAID Project. The Committee recommends that NACO should be
involved in the implementation of all pilot projects in all parts of the country so that it has
complete information about the implementation of all the projects.

3.11 The Committee is constrained to note that many States were performing very slow
and the World Bank Mission in its mid-term review in 1995 recommended discontinuance of
credit to such states. The Committee was given to understand that the reasons for slow
performance were non-adherence to action plans, non-availability of infrastructure, political
and social problems. It also appears that many States do not perceive the AIDS Control
Programme as their own concern. The Empowered Committees of the States have also not
been effective and have little control over initiating activities. The Committee perceives that
there is still lack of awareness and enthusiasm in the States. If the State Government do not
rise to the occasion and pool in all the sources and energies available with them, it would be
difficult to tackle the problem of AIDS/HIV either by the Central Government or any
International Agency. It is the State Governments which are nearer to the people and which
implement the programme. They should therefore, be more concerned about the problem.
The Central Government should therefore, seriously consider this aspect.

3.12 The Committee was informed that efforts were being made to introduce AIDS
education in the Schools. It is true that young people in India are equally vulnerable to HIV
infection and they are also required to be educated in a proper atmosphere. Inclusion of
AIDS education as a part of the curriculum is of course one of the best alternatives to
increase awareness about it. The Committee desires that it should be finalised as early as
possible and it should be introduced from the academic year 1998-99 onwards.

3.13 The fact that there being no cure for AIDS is agitating the minds of scientific
communities the world over. Whatever medicines that are available are only to give
temporary relief. Even those medicines are not available to a large number of infected
population because of the high cost. The Committee is pained to learn from the
representative of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare that there is no company which
is importing the drugs. Even if the Government does not want to introduce the drug for
treatment, efforts should at least be made to ensure the availability of the drug in the
market. The Committee recommends that the Government should consider this and see that

medicines which are available in other parts of the world are brought/made available in
India at a cheaper cost. The Committee was also given to understand that the Indian systems
of medicines such as Ayurveda and Homoeopathy claim to have got medicines for curing
AIDS. Government should seriously examine and have research done on the efficacy of all
those medicines as early as possible. This is all the more necessary because if indigenous
medicines are found to be efficacious these could be made available at a cheaper cost.

3.14 The main concern facing the world community now is non-development of any
vaccine for HIV/AIDS so far. Many countries are still in the process of research on this.
However, the Committee is constrained to note that no research on development of vaccine
for this has been initiated in India so far. The Committee desires that our country also

may ultimately lead to success.

IV. HEPATITIS-B

4.1 Hepatitis is an acute infection of the liver caused by hepatitis virus. To date, several
hepatitis viruses have been documented and designated. At present, there are six types of:
hepatitis virus i.e. from A to G. Out of them, hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a major cause of
morbidity and mortality world-wide and it is therefore a serious global health hazard.

4.2 The Committee heard the views of the experts who are working on Hepatitis-B on
8th September, 1997. The Committee was informed by the experts that acute Hepatitis-B is
a serious disease. This is because it is most infectious and hundred times more infectious
than HIV. A tip of a needle which has been injected is sufficient to cause a disease as the
blood needed to transmit Hepatitis-B from an infected individual to a healthy person is very
small being only 0.00004 ml.

4.3 According to the experts who appeared before the Committee, India, with a
population close to 930 million, has approximately 40 million HBV carriers contributing an
astonishing 10% of the world estimated total of 400 million carriers. The number of cases
and deaths due to hepatitis as reported by the state health authorities to the Central Bureau
of Health Intelligence (CBHI) in the last five years is as given below:

Year Cases Deaths
1992 98047 1268
1993 117789 1267
1994 98880 1183
1995 98940 943
1996 116031 799

4.4 It was also pointed out to the Committee that data regarding this disease is not
based on all India’s figures as it has been observed that no information about North-eastern
and Central part and hilly areas is available. Based on the limited data available on
prevalence of Hepatitis-B in the country, it is estimated that the carrier rate of Hepatitis-B
virus ranges. from 3—5%, with an average estimated rate of 4% among the general
population. However, most of the carrier rates relate to the urban areas as extremely small
amount of data is available from rural areas. Not only this, there is a difference in carrier
rate in rural and urban areas. Use of unsterilised needles by Registered Medical
Practitioners (RMP) were to a large extent responsible for the higher carrier rate prevalent
in rural areas.


10

4.5 The Committee was also informed by one of the experts that as far as children
below six years are concerned, the carrier rate happens to be very high partly because they
acquire this carrier status from their infected parents and also from their community.
Between the age of 16 to 18 years it sets about 4 to 4.5 per cent and is the same both in
rural and urban child population. However, in the case of children coming from high
economic strata, the carrier rate is less as compared to the corporation school going
children, because of their background and living conditions, it was informed.

4.6 The Committee notes that evidence of higher positivity rates among orphans as
compared to normal children leads to the conclusion that low economic status, poor hygenic
conditions are indirectly responsible for transmission of this disease. A positivity rate of
14.7% has been observed in children where as the positivity rate among healthy adult
populations ranges between 10—38%.

4.7 According to the data available on Pregnant women, 3.7 to 4 per cent is the carrier
rate. At least 25 per cent of Hepatitis impregnancy is caused by Hepatitis-B. Twelve per
cent or One eighth of maternal mortality is contributed by Hepatitis-B. Out of this 12 per
cent, at least 20 per cent are highly infective as they will transmit the disease to the new
born during the immediate post delivery period. It was pointed out that 90 per cent of the
new born who get this virus, develop chronic liver disease.

4.8 The Common mode of transmission is the transfusion of blood. This was due to the
fact that most of the blood banks, in the country use unstandardised kits. However, this ca:
be effectively checked by making the screening method for Hepatitis-B standardised and
adhering to all the Government rules.

4.9 The medical and paramedical staff are also a high risk group for HBV infection due
to repeated contact with infected individuals and waste with blood and body fluids. Among
the medical and paramedical staff, it is the dentists who are the most vulnerable.

4.10 The Department apprised the Committee that the Hepatitis-B virus spreads mainly
through contaminated blood and blood products, contaminated (unsterilised) syringes and
needles, unsafe sex and from mother (if she is a carrier) to the unborn child. As far as other
hepatitis are concerned, Hepatitis C, D and G are spread by the same route as Hepatitis-B
virus. Hepatitis A and E viruses are water-borne and spread through contaminated water.

4.11 The experts explained to the Committee that the transmission of Hepatitis-B virus
takes place in five ways namely, transplacental, horizontal, parenteral, sexual and vector-
mediated. Elaborating the peculiar mode of transmission in the country, one of the Experts
clarified that below 1rd of them get from mother at birth and the rest 2rd are infected by
horizontal mode that is from one person to other person. Of these 22rd, about 14rd are
infected during their pre-school age i.e. from 1 year to 5 years.

4.12 Some of the experts were of the opinion that revamping the existing screening
method in the various blood banks and laboratories was very essential so as to prevent the
Hepatitis-B cases. In order to assess the situation, cases of acute viral Hepatitis-B and also
liver chronic diseases were taken up for study. It was found that 62 per cent of blood
transfusion cases suffered from Hepatitis-B infection. In other words, proper screening has
not been done in such cases unstandardised type of kits also seemed to a large extent
responsible for this situation, The experts, therefore, emphasised that the screening method
for Hepatitis-B must be properly standardised and all Government rules must be adhered to.
Studies have revealed that at least three out of hundred infected with this virus would
develop chronic liver disease or liver failure. This may eventually lead to liver cancer

for prevention of this disease are required.

4.13 It has come to the notice of the Committee that at present there are two types of
vaccine which are safe and effective (a) Plasma Derived Vaccine (b) Recombinant DNA
Vaccine. It was pointed out that the raw material for Plasma Derived Vaccine is the human
blood and for Recombinant hepatitis it is yeast cell line and cloned into Elcoli Bacterial

Plasma Derived Vaccine is cheaper in comparison to Recombinant DNA Vaccine.

4.14 The Department informed the Committee that the total requirement of vaccines for
the country cannot be met. At the current population of 943 million, with the birth rate of
28.3 per thousand and 3 doses per child, 80 million doses are required annually. However,
there was no single unit in India which can today sell even 20 million doses. Production
capacity all over the world is very limited. Foreign firms would invest in infrastructure if
specific requirements are made to them.

4.15 To the question as to what action has been taken by the department to reduce the
risks of Hepatitis-B infection, the Department submitted that guidelines have been issued for
mandatory testing of blood in all blood banks; promotion of safe sex under the National
AIDS Control Programme; health awareness campaigns regarding the dangers of using
unsterilised syringes and needles under the National AIDS Control Programme. Guidelines
have also been issued to the state health authorities for the use of a separate sterile syringe
and needles for each injection.
