4.6.4. The Committee views with serious concern that in view of the post-Pokhran developments,
fundings for Phase III of both the Programmes which were to start from 1st July, 1998 has been
withdrawn by Swedish International Development Authority (SIDA). As a result, against an
allocation of Rs.37.50 crores and 16.17 crores for LJP and SKP respectively in 1998-99, to only
Rs.4.5 crores and 5.2 crores could be utilised. The Committee was informed that UK’s Department
for International Development (DFID) has come forward provide alternate funds for Phase III of
both these programmes. The Committee hopes that enhanced allocation proposed for SKP and LJP
in 1999-2000 in anticipation of DFID Funding would be fully utilised and the work accomplished so
far under these two projects would not suffer a further setback.
7. Mid-day Meal Scheme
4.7.1. Mid-day Meal Scheme launched in August, 1995 covers all the children studying in primary classes
in all Govt., local body and Govt.-aided schools in the country. As per the 1998-99 figures, 9.75 crore
children in about 6.88 lakh schools were beneficiaries of this Scheme. The State Govts are to supplement
the Central efforts by providing the conversion costs for serving cooked meals for which financial
assistance is available to them under the JRY/EAS funds. However, the Committee was informed that only
5 states and 1 UT, i.e. Gujarat, Kerala, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh (in 174 Tribal blocks only)
and Pondicherry serve cooked meals. What is more surprising is that two states, Haryana and J&K which
used to, had to revert to the distribution of the food-grains in 1996-97 due to resource constraints,
inadequate cooking arrangements and resentment among teachers. Non-serving of cooked meals defeats
the very objective of the Scheme. The Committee views with serious concern the total lack of state
initiative in the implementation of a scheme designed to give a boost to the universalisation of
primary education. The Committee strongly feels that successful implementation of Mid-day Meal
Scheme by 5 states and 1 UT can well be followed by the remaining states of the country. The
Committee is of the view that there should be supply of food grains to the States only on the
condition of serving of cooked meals to the children.
4.7.2. The Committee was informed that the Mid day Meal Scheme was facing a severe resource crunch.
During 1998-99, there has been disruption in supply of foodgrains due to paucity of funds and non-
reconciliation of lifting figures between states and FCI. As a result, lifting of foodgrains during the current
year has been lower than the average of 70-75% allocation during the last three years. The Committee was
given to understand that allocations for 1997-98 and 1998-99 were much below the requirements under
this scheme. The proposed allocation of Rs. 1031.10 crore for 1999-2000 would be too meagre to meet the
requirement of approximately Rs. 3000 crores to continue coverage of all the children of primary classes in
the country. Consequently, FCI may again resort to suspension of supply of foodgrains. This is an
alarming position which warrants urgent action on the part of the Govt. for augmentation of allocation of
funds under this scheme.
4.7.3. The Committee views with serious concern the proposed move of the Govt. to restrict the Mid
day Meal Scheme to Girls, SCs/STs only. Instead of restricting this scheme to a limited category, the
Department should explore all the possibilities for removing the bottlenecks – both physical and
financial – in close coordination with state govts. and implementing agencies. The Committee hopes
that findings of the evaluation study of Mid day Meal Scheme presently being conducted by the
Operation Research Group in 10 states would prove to be useful in taking a decision in the right
direction.

4.8 Non-Formal Education
4.8.1. The implementing agencies for this Programme are both State Govts. and NGOs. During 1997-98,
the number of NFE Centres being run in the State Sector was 2.41 lakh which remained the same in 1998-
99 too. However, there was increase in the number of centres being run by NGOs. Against 49,000 centres
run by 740 NGOs in 1997-98, there were 58,000 centres managed by 825 NGOs during 1998-99.
However, enhanced provision ;of Rs. 309.21 crores in BE 1998-99, in view of the revision of NFE Scheme
with enhanced cost parameters had to be reduced to Rs. 160 crores at the RE stage. The Committee has
been given to understand that unspent balance of Rs. 61.88 crore lying with State Govts and delay in the
finalisation of revised NFE Scheme were the two factors responsible for drastic reduction at the RE stage.
However, the Committee finds that even this reduced allocation is not likely to be utilised fully as there
has been an expenditure of only Rs. 108.61 crores upto 26.2.99.
4.8.2. The Committee views with serious concern the conclusion arrived at by the evaluation study
conducted in 6 states by the Planning Commission that NFE Programme has not made any notable
contribution. Some of its major findings as detailed below are very disturbing :-
o        erratic and much less than required flow of funds to NFE centres in the State
Sector.
o        Acute shortage of teaching /learning material in NFE Centres;
o        Attendance and enrolment in girl centres are low. Large number of girl centres
have male instructors;
o        Lack of coordination between State Govts and NGOs; and
o        Very weak supervision and monitoring of NFE Programme.
4.8.3. The Committee has been informed that proposed revision of the NFE Scheme incorporating the
modifications as suggested by the Planning Commission, views of experts and NFE practitioners and State
Govts.is at an advanced stage of preparation for consideration by EFC. The Committee strongly feels
that Department should make concerted efforts for finalisation of revised NFE Scheme without any
further delay and full and judicious utilisation of enhanced allocation of Rs. 350.00 crores proposed
in BE 1999-2000.
4. The NFE Programme initiated way back in 1979 on an experimental basis, was scaled up
in 1987 into a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for educationally backward States and was
further expanded during the 8th Plan period. It took 20 years to arrive at the conclusion
that NFE Programme has been perceived as a low cost, inferior and ineffective alternative
for full-time school meant for the poor people. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the revised NFE Programme should have an effective in-built
mechanism for monitoring with full coordination between implementing agencies
i.e.. State Govt/NGOs and the Central Government.

released to voluntary agencies and Resource Centres (State and Regional). The Committee finds that the
major portion of assistance is being given to State Resource Centres. The Committee would like to have an
idea about the composition of these resource centres and their functionings.

coming years because of universalisation of elementary education causing a greater transition to secondary

and from the details of expenditure upto 26.2.99 made available, it is evident that there are little

VII Higher Education
7.1 University Grants Commission
UGC provides financial assistance to 16 Central Universities both for maintenance and development
purpose, development grants to 107 State Universities and development or maintenance grants, as the case
may be, to the eligible Deemed Universities. UGC also provides development grants to 4815 eligible
colleges. The Committee was informed that 8th Plan allocation for UGC was only 8% of the budget of the
Department of Education as against 16% in the 7th Plan, which was already down from the previous Plans
averaging 22 to 25%. The Committee notes that an allocation of RS. 1002.62 crores against the 8th Plan
proposal for Rs.1767.70 crores based on actual requirement not only resulted in an estimated unpaid
liability of Rs.400 crores but also led to freezing of several schemes, including the prestigious ones.

was forced to prepare its 9th Plan outlay at Rs.2500 crores. However, an allocation of only Rs. 2050 crores

Fellowships, Special Assistance Programme etc. would be severely affected. What is more worrying is that
some research related schemes would have to be closed down.

same. The Committee is in agreement with UGC’s argument that things could be managed somehow
as most of the new schemes were in the finalisation process during the first two years of 9th Plan.
However, an allocation of Rs.418 crores against an projected requirement of Rs.658.59 crore for
1999-2000 would worsen the situation further.

implemented, many of them achieving their targets in a time bound manner so as to enable the
disadvantaged groups, i.e. women/children belonging to SC/ST/minority/belonging to economical weaker

rd Amendment) Bill 1993 for making the right to free and
compulsory education for children of 6-14 years age a Fundamental Right was presented to both the
Houses of Parliament on 24th November, 1997. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the

fails to understand the need for initiating a wider public debate on the issue.
8.3 Educational development in the N-E Region
The Committee notes that a number of interventions are being made by the Department in the North-
Eastern region so as to bring the people of this remote region of the country to the mainstream. In view of
high percentage (35%) of untrained teachers in N-E region, a special programme called ‘Diploma in
Primary Education’ has been launched there jointly by IGNOUand NCERT. In the realm of higher and
technical education, 26.37% of total budget allocation for the Central Universities during 9
th Plan, has
been allocated to NEHU, Nagaland, Assam and Tejpur Universities. Setting up of 6 engineering colleges,
19 polytechnics, 6 MBA and 2 MCA level colleges have been sanctioned by AICTE during the last year
for NE region. The Committee is happy to note that special emphasis is being laid on
initiation/implementation of various centrally sponsored schemes for the NE region.
8.4 New Initiatives

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
8.4.1. The Committee observes that three new schemes were proposed to be initiated during 1998-99.
o        ‘Free Education For Girls’, a new scheme, for which an amount of Rs.100.00
crores was earmarked, was proposed to be launched in 1998-99 for providing
free education for girls upto college level including professional courses.
However, the Committee finds that EFC Memorandum is still being
finalised.
o        it was proposed to either upgrade or set up 20 sports schools by suitably
adapting the Navodaya Vidyalaya Scheme in different States. An amount of Rs.
20 crore was earmarked in 1998-99 for the purpose. The Committee notes that
the proposal is still at the consideration stage.
o        A new Centrally sponsored scheme of strengthening of Statistical Machinery in
States was to be launched in 1998-99 to strengthen the educational database and
to meet the international requirements of the educational statistics. A notional
provision of Rs.1 crore was provided in 1998-99. The Committee finds that
EFC Memo of the Scheme has been prepared.
8.4.2. The Committee views with serious concern the general tendency of announcing a new scheme
and earmarking of Funds for the purpose even without undertaking preliminary exercise of scrutiny
by the administrative Ministry or by Ministry of Finance or sometimes by both the Ministries. The
Committee feels that it is a very unhealthy practice. Once the proposals have been approved by the
Parliament, efforts should be made to initiate the scheme without any procedural delay.
8.4.3. The Committee observes that a new scheme ‘Education Guarantee Scheme’ has been announced by
the Finance Minister in his Budget Speech this year Provision of an elementary school in every habitation
not having one within a radius of 1km has been cited as the objective of the proposed scheme. The
Committee would like to point out that according to the Fifth All India Education Survey, 95% of the
country’s rural population is already served by a primary school within a distance of 1 km. The Committee
has its own doubts about the veracity of the data given in the Fifth All India Education Survey report. The
Committee feels that the need of the hour is the proper implementation of the already ongoing identical
schemes instead of launching a new one.
IX. Committed Liability
9.1. While examining the Demands for Grants 1997-98 of the Departments under its purview, the
Committee noted that the committed liability of the Plan Schemes has not been reflected in the
budgetary allocations.
9.2. The Committee, in this, connection considered the report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The
Tenth Finance Commission have observed in this regard as under:-
"Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of
reference in deciding the cut off date for transfer of committed liability on
account of plan scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-
98 on account of 8
th Plan scheme completed in the next two financial years
would have to be provided for. The Commission are, therefore, of the view
that the Planning Commission may consider providing for the maintenance
of such scheme till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was done for the schemes

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92".
9.3. The Committee also sought clarifications from the then Secretary (Expenditure). He informed
the Committee that even though communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries
could not identify the committed expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been
provided under Demand No. 31. The Secretary also assured that if required, more funds for this
purpose will be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the Departments may approach the
Department of Expenditure for their share.
9.4. The Committee, accordingly, directed the Department to approach the Ministry of Finance in
this regard. However, while considering the Demands for Grants 1998-1999, the Committee noticed
that no progress in this regard seemed to have taken place. The Committee, therefore, reiterated its
stand. In spite of the Departments initiating some exercise, the matter could not be sorted out. The
Committee, therefore, heard the Secretary (Expenditure) on 27
th March, 1999.
9.5. The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee, submitted that at the end of the 8th Five
Year Plan the Planning Commission issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the committed
expenditure from plan to the non plan side. The Ministry of Finance (Budget Division) also issued a
letter to all the Financial Advisors of the Department requesting them to indicate the amount to be
included from plan to non plan.
9.6. The Secretary submitted that as on 10
th February, 1997, 24 Ministries/Departments responded
indicating a figure of Rs.450.28 crore. However, some Ministries/Departments like Education,
Culture, Women and Child Development did not respond. Accordingly a lumpsum provision of Rs.500
crores in the Ministry of Finance Budget was provided for this purpose. As a result of this exercise, a
sum of Rs.150 crores was indeed transferred from plan to non plan for the various Ministries as
committed expenditure during the year, on the basis of scrutiny with reference to the Planning
Commission’s guidelines. The rest of the amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found
acceptable.
9.7. The Secretary agreed in principle that whatever is the committed expenditure, it should be
transferred from plan to non plan. Otherwise the plan has no meaning.
9.8. The Secretary assured that the proposals pertaining to UGC (Rs.27 crores) and Department of
Education (Rs. 80 crores) which were under consideration would be cleared. Moreover, the Tenth Finance
Commission Report has given a breathing time till 1999-2000 for this transition. The Committee would
like to impress that the real picture should be projected before Parliament.
9.9. The Secretary also apprised the Committee that another Sub Committee has been appointed by
the NDC, consisting of representatives from seven states and Ministry of Finance. This Sub-
Committee will look into the structural distortions which have entered into the finances of the states
on account of 5
th Pay Commission and to suggest a suitable package linked to fiscal reforms.
9.10. The Committee observes that a similar problem exists in the case of Central Ministries also.
The Committee, therefore, desires that a similar exercise be carried out in the case of Central
Ministries also.

I. INTRODUCTION  
1.1. The main responsibility of the Department is to ensure qualitative and quantitative 
improvements in Youth Programmes and also on broad basing and bringing about awareness of 
sports and physical fitness amongst school children and youth. The Programmes undertaken 
by the Department are mainly Sports and Games and Youth Programmes.  
1.2. The Department finances various youth welfare programmes which ranges from 
personality development to vocational training. Most of these programmes are implemented 
by reputed institutions, non-governmental organisations as well as State Governments 
whereby financial assistance is provided by the Department as per the stipulated norms. The 
major schemes for youth development are National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra 
Sangathan, National Integration Programmes, Youth Hostels and National Service 
Volunteers Scheme,etc.  
3. The Department also finances a number of programmes which aim at promotion 
of sports, including creation of sports infrastructure in all parts of the country, 
grants for laying of synthetic surfaces, spotting and nurturing of talents through 
the schemes of Sports Authority of India, grants to National Sports Federations, 
National Championships, organisation of tournaments for rural youth, women in 
the North-Eastern Region.  
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
1. The total outlay, both Plan and Non-Plan taken together, provided to the 
Department for the year 1998-99 was Rs. 214.76 crores in BE which was reduced 
to Rs. 200.00 crores at RE stage. The allocation made for the year 1999-2000 is 
Rs. 230.09 crores (Plan Rs. 190.00 crores and Non-Plan Rs. 40.09 crores). When 
asked about the reaction to the marginal increase, the Department submitted that 
for the year 1999-2000, it has projected a demand of Rs. 282.09 crore (Rs. 230.00 
crores under Plan and Rs. 52.09 crores under Non-plan) and the marginal increase 
of Rs. 16 crores will be only sufficient to take care of inflationary impact. Scale 
of operation of various scheme would remain as same as of the previous year. It 
was also informed that the Department had requested for an enhanced allocation 
of Rs. 51 crores under Plan over the BE of 1998-99, out of which Rs. 33 crores 
are required for Sports Authority of India, for upgradation and maintenance of 
existing infrastructure as well as for creating new facilities, particularly in view of 
Afro-Asian games to be held in 2001.  
2. The Committee is of the view that in fact there is no real increase in the 
allocation of the Department for 1999-2000 and if there is no substantial 
Page 4 of 18REPORT
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/83rsport.html

allocation, various youth and sports activities being undertaken by the 
Department may be adversely affected. The Committee, therefore, finds 
enough justification for higher allocation in the RE.  
3. The Committee has also noted in this connection, that a tendency to keep 
higher allocation in the BE and then reducing it in the RE has developed. 
The Committee does not approve this. It is of the considered view that once 
an allocation is made and the same is approved by Parliament no one has the 
privilege to curtail it subsequently. In this regard, Parliament’s authority is 
supreme.  
III. APPROACH TO THE NINTH FIVE YEAR PLAN  
3.1 The Committee has taken note of the approach on Youth Affairs and Sports during the 
Ninth Plan period. The contents of the relevant paras from the Approach Paper to the Ninth 
Five Year Plan are reproduced below:-  
"The thrust in Youth Affairs will be to consolidate and expand 
youth activities by involving youth in the entire gamut of the 
developmental process as the youth are a major resource in the 
task of nation building. Youth activities will focus on 
environmental and health programmes such as greening of 
wastelands, solid waste management, anti-smoking compaign, 
prevention of drug abuse, health education with emphasis on 
reproductive health and prevention of AIDS, population control as 
well as various adventure activities. Greater access will be given 
to the rural and marginalised youth in the vocational training 
programmes of Nehru Yuva Kendras by involving the NGOs, 
self-help groups and community polytechnics in the task.  
The thrust in sports will be on providing greater access to sport 
facilities through substantial investments in physical education, 
infrastructure development including centres of sports physiology 
and sports medicine and in creating widespread awareness for 
physical fitness through nutrition, health education and yoga with 
special focus on school children. Area specific sports programmes 
recognising the traditional sports skills of the inhabitants, 
specially tribal population, will receive priority consideration. 
Rural sports programmes will be revamped in order to tap vast 
talents available in the rural areas. Special attention will be given 
for the promotion of sports and games among the disabled. The 
need for a holistic approach that will integrate youth and sports 
activities and programmes within the context of education is well 
recognised and will guide all action". 
3.2 The Committee feels that the objectives are laudable. However, unless dedicated 
and sincere effort are made to achieve these objectives, they will remain on paper only.

The Committee hopes that earnest efforts would be made in the right perspective for 
translating the objectives into action for better delivery of services to the target groups. 
IV. NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN  
1. Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS), an autonomous organisation under the 
Department, has about 500 district level offices throughout the country. It is the 
largest grass-root level organisation in the Asia and Pacific region catering to the 
needs of more than 6.4 million non-student rural youth in the age group of 15-35 
years enrolled through 1.79 lakh village-based youth clubs covering education, 
training, employment promotion, income generation, self-employment, Health 
awareness etc. The strength of NYKS is its vast network of youth clubs at grass-
root level. Allocation to Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan on plan side has been 
enhanced from Rs.17.35 crores in BE 1998-99 and Rs.19.30 crores in RE 1998-
99 to Rs.19.85 crores in BE 1999-2000. Explaining the enhancement of fund 
allocation under plan as well as Non-Plan, the Department informed that it was to 
take care of increased expenditure on salaries of Nehru Yuva Kendras Sangathan 
employees on account of granting benefits of Fifth Central Pay Commission. In 
Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan there are 196 Kendras under Plan and 304 
Kendras under Non-Plan.
  
4.2 The Committee was also informed that there are 500 functional District Nehru Yuva 
Kendras in the country and each District Nehru Yuva Kendra should have a District 
Advisory Committee on Youth Programme (DACYP). However, out of 500 District Nehru 
Yuva Kendras, the DACYP is functional in only 436 Kendras. According to the Department, 
the reason for non-functioning of DACYP in remaining 64 districts is primarily because of 
holding of additional charge by other Districts Youth Coordinators. The Committee in this 
connection would like to impress upon that District Youth Coordinators should be 
relieved of their additional charge as this additional charge may be affecting the 
activities of their District Yuva Kendra and DACYP in the remaining 64 districts 
should be formed without further delay.  
3. Regarding representation of women in the DACYP, the Committee was informed 
that as far as possible, 30 percent of the total membership of DACYP would go to 
women and this could be assessed after receiving the information from District 
Nehru Yuva Kendras. The Committee would like that sincere effort would be 
made to give due representation to women and the information in this 
regard would be shared with the Committee.

V. ASSISTANCE TO YOUTH CLUBS AND SPORTS CLUBS

7.3. Explaining the reasons for allocation of Rs.18 crore in BE 1999-2000 compared to the

REPORT 
I INTRODUCTION  
1.1 The Department of Culture plays a vital role in the promotion and dissemination of art and 
culture. The aim of the Department is to develop ways and means for instilling basic values and 
perceptions in the minds of the people, particularly the young. The Department also undertakes 
the prgoramme of preservation, encouragement and dissemination of various manifestations of 
creative activity, both past and present. The Department is engaged in excavation, conservation 
and promotion of ancient monuments and historic sites; administration of libraries, museums and 
institutions of anthropology; collection, preservation and ethnology of national character; catering 
to institutions and organisations in the areas of Buddhist and Tibetan Studies; promoting literary, 
visual and performing arts; observing centenaries and anniversaries of important personalities 
and entering into cultural agreements with foreign countries. The Department carries out its 
various programmes through two attached offices, six subordinate offices and 26 autonomous 
organisations.  
1.2 During the Ninth Five Year Plan period, the Department proposes to focus on a 
comprehensive plan for preservation of the archeological heritage and development of the 
monumental complexes in the country. Efforts would also be directed towards the preservation of 
archival heritage and the promotion of classical, folk and tribal art and crafts and oral traditions 
which are threatened with extinction.  
IIBUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
2.1 The Committee finds that the total allocation of the Department for the year 1999-2000 is Rs. 
376.21 crores which includes Rs. 165.00 crores under Plan and Rs. 211.21 crores under Non-Plan. 
The Department had initially proposed a Plan outlay of Rs. 201.22 crores to the Planning 
Commission. But the finally agreed amount is Rs. 165 crores. Similarly, the original proposal for 
Non-Plan was for Rs. 268.57 crores and the allocation finally agreed to by the Ministry of Finance 
is Rs. 211.21 crores. The Ninth Five Year Plan outlay has been kept at Rs. 920.41 crores against 
the proposed requirement of Rs. 1124.40 crores . According to the Department, the reduction of 
Rs. 203.99 crores in the Ninth Plan allocation which in almost 18 percent of its modest proposal 
would result in substantial cut in the promotional and support activities in the area of promotion 
and dissemination of arts and culture, Archaeological Survey of India, Libraries and other 
expenditure sector.  
2.2 The Committee feels that the Department of Culture has been entrusted with certain 
important activities and responsibilities and it is necessary that it carries on its activities smoothly. 
The Committee would therefore, urge upon the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance to 
consider grant of enhanced allocation to the Department so that its main activities are not 
adversely affected.  
III NATIONAL CULTURE FUND  
3.1 The Committee in its 67th Report had noted that the incentives for contributions to National 
Culture Fund (NCF) were inadequate and felt that a total Income Tax exemption for the 
contribution made to NCF would prove to be a much desired incentive for the possible donors. It, 
Page 4 of 12REPORT
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/84repcul.html

therefore, recommended that the contribution to the NCF be fully exempted under section 80 G 
(2) of the Income Tax Act.  
2. The Committee is happy to note that the Govt. of India vide the Finance Act, 1998 
notified on 1st August, 1998 have provided that the donations to the NCF would be 
eligible for tax benefits under section 80 G(2) of the Income Tax Act. It also feels that 
adequate publicity needs to be given about NCF and the incentive to the donors, so 
that more donors could contribute to this Fund.  
3. The Secretary explained that under NCF it has been decided to select and execute a 
few selected projects of modest scale with participation of local community or 
corporate entities. So far, two projects, namely Shaniwarwada Project, Pune for 
restoration of the ancestral palace of Peshwas and the Project for renovation of Water 
Works of the Humayun’s Tomb, New Delhi have been selected. In addition, expansion 
of Prince of Wales Museum, Mumbai is also under consideration.  
4. The Committee has also been apprised of certain constraints in this regard such as 
rigidities and red-tapism, inflexibility in the operation and use of Funds of NCF. The 
Committee expects that the Department would do something concrete to avoid these 
apprehensions in the minds of the people and see that the NCF is able to achieve the 
objectives for which it has been set up. For this, complete transparency is must.  
IV ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA (ASI)  
1. Against a projected requirement of Rs. 37.75 crore for 1998-99, only Rs. 20.00 crore 
were allocated to ASI. Only a limited number of monuments Taj Mahal, Khajuraho, 
Ajanta, Ellora, Konark, Bodhgaya, Nalanda, Vaishali, Sarnath and Hampi were to be 
brought up to world standards during 1998-99. However, the Department has 
informed that due to financial constraints, this task could not be accomplished. The 
Committee, however, finds that out of the allocation of Rs. 20.00 crore, enhanced to 
Rs. 22.00 crore at the RE stage, only Rs. 12.48 crore have been utilised upto 28th 
February, 1999. Allocation for 1999-2000 has been enhanced to Rs. 28.00 crores. The 
Committee strongly feels that the Department should make concerted efforts for 
maximum utilisation of the funds. Priority should be given to such monuments which 
need urgent attention.  
4.2 The Committee has been informed that Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation, 
Govt. of Maharashtra has been requested to explore the feasibility for organising Sound and Light 
Programme at Ajanta and Ellora. Their response is awaited. The Committee is of the opinion that 
the matter needs to be pursued vigorously by the Department with the Govt. of Maharashtra. As 
these caves attract a large number of foreign tourists also, the Committee feels that there is a need 
for the Department also to take some initiative in this matter.  
4.3 With regard to the preservation of monuments, the Committee has been informed that there 
are 3598 centrally protected monuments in the country and if the total number of individual 
structures is taken into consideration, this figure exceeds 5000. These monuments are in the care 
of just 3443 Monument Attendants. As per the Action taken note of the Department, the Planning 
Commission has rejected the Department’s proposal for creation of 5000 posts of Monument 
Attendants for protecting these monuments. The Planning Commission has instead suggested that 
Archaeological Survey of India should go in for other solutions of engaging/hiring private agencies 
wherever they are available instead of adopting a mass employment strategy. The Committee has 
been further informed that the matter has been taken up afresh with the Planning Commission for 
reconsideration primarily on grounds that the Monument Attendants do a multifarious job which 
private security agencies cannot perform, apart from being expensive. The Committee is of the 
Page 5 of 12REPORT
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/84repcul.html

considered opinion that on an average provision of only one Monument Attendant per monument 
would not be adequate enough, in view of the increasing trend in the cases of theft and vandalism. 
Even this provision is not being fully met at present. The Committee, therefore feels that where 
there are no Monument Attendants at present, engaging/hiring/private agencies may be 
undertaken. However, this can be done as a temporary measure till the time a viable solution is 
worked out.  
4. The Committee does not wish to go at length with regard to the preservation of 
monuments, in view of the fact that the Sub-Committee on Preservation of monuments 
is already looking into the various aspects relating to the preservation of monuments. 
However, the Committee is of the view that certain aspects like maintenance of 
monuments, provision of public conveniences at monumental sites, encroachment in 
and around the monuments, progress/policies for attracting tourists – both domestic 
and foreign to our cultural sites and monuments etc. need to be given greater 
attention. The Committee is in no doubt about the practical difficulties and problems 
which are facing the ASI in this regard. Nevertheless, the Committee would be happy 
if the ASI is able to overcome the inherent difficulties/constraints to the maximum 
extent and fulfil its responsibilities and obligations which have been entrusted to it.  
V. MUSEUMS  
1. The Secretary informed the Committee that during the year 1998-99, the scheme for 
promotion and strengthening of regional and local museums was revamped with the 
objective of promoting in a professional manner the setting up and modernisation of 
museums at the regional, state and local level. As per the new strategy, regional 
responsibility has now been placed on certain nodal museums, viz, Indian Museum, 
Calcutta for East and North-East, Salarjung Musuem, Hyderabad for South, National 
Museum, New Delhi for North, Allahabad Musuem for Central and Prince of Wales 
Museum, Mumbai for Western India. Besides this, action has also been initiated to 
prepare a computerised National Register for Antiquities in the Central and State 
Museums in the country by the end of the year 2000. In due course, the Register would 
be extended to cover all districts and local museums.  
2. Upgradation of conservation facilities is another activity which has been given the 
highest priority and a high level Scientific Advisory Committee has been constituted 
with experts drawn from all fields of conservation and from Science and Technology, 
the Committee was informed.  
3. On a specific query as to whether there was any proposal to exhibit the Nizam’s 
Jewellery for public, it was informed that plans were there to exhibit the same on I5th 
August, 1999. It was further explained that National Museum is the only Museum 
where with some modifications the Nizam’s Jewellery can be displayed for public 
viewing. In the meanwhile, a request has been received from the Chief Minister of 
Andhra Pradesh stating that the Nizam’s Jewellery being historically connected with 
Hyderabad, it should be kept there only. The matter is, at present, under submission 
to PMO.  
4. The Committee appreciates all the new initiatives taken by the Department during 
1998-99. The Committee hopes that decision on exhibition of the Nizam’s Jewellery 
would be taken at the earliest.

VI ARCHIVES  
6.1 It has been reported that there are estimated three crore Manuscripts in several languages 
which are languishing with individuals and institutions in several parts of the Country. For 
protection of this endangered intellectual property, a National Mission for Manuscripts is 
proposed to be launched in 1999-2000. The first phase will comprise compilation and publication 
of a Directory of Institutions/ Individuals possessing these manuscripts and collecting data on 
their historical importance and physical state of these manuscripts and the preservation facilities 
available.  
6.2 The Committee welcomes the new initiative. The Committee hopes that this mission would be 
accomplished under a time-bound action plan so that these age-old Manuscripts enshrining the 
ideas and thought processes of our ancestors are protected.  
6.3. Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the steady increase in the number of archival 
records in the possession of the National Archives of India. Due to the gradual increase in the

therefore to work in close, active and willing cooperation with State Governments and

movement in the country with special emphasis upon inculcating the reading habit 
among the rural masses. This objective is very laudable and in order to achieve this 
objective the Foundation has framed equally laudable schemes like "Scheme of Book 
Assistance’ and "Books for the millions at their doorsteps"etc. The Committee is not 
very sure as to what extent the Department has been able to achieve this lofty 
objective, in view of the fact that the National average literacy rate is around 62 per 
cent. In this connection the Committee also notes the rejection of the Department’s 
proposal for setting up of Rural Libraries at the Panchayat level by the Planning 
Commission and instead suggesting the urgent need for developing Community 
Information System which would encompass the Rural Library System and 
Continuing Education under National Literacy Mission. The Committee is of the 
considered view that as the concept of Public/Rural Library is linked to the literacy of 
the masses throughout the country; a holistic and integrated approach would have to 
be taken in consultation with all the concerned agencies of the Department such as 
Department of Education, Planning Commission, Ministry of Finance and States and

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Department of Women and Child Development is engaged in the giving the much needed impetus
to the holistic development of women and children. The Department, as the national machinery for the
advancement of women and children, formulates plans, policies and programmes; enacts/amends
legislation; guides and coordinates the efforts of both Governmental and non-governmental organisations
working in the field of Women and Child Development. The Department also implements certain
innovative programmes for women and children covering welfare and support services, training for
employment and income generation, awareness generation and gender sensitisation. They play a
supplementary and complementary role to the other general developmental programmes in the sectors of
health, education, rural development etc. For the holistic development of the child, the Department
implements the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) providing a package of services

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
comprising supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-up and referral services, pre-school and
non-formal education and health and nutrition education.
1.2. The other major schemes implemented by the Department include funding of Hostels for working
women, Support, Training and Employment Programme, Scheme of Training-cum-Employment-cum
Production Centres (NORAD), Socio-Economic Programme, the Programme of Condensed Courses of
Education and Vocational Training etc. Most of the programmes of the Department are run through non-
Governmental organisations.
II OBJECTIVES AND APPROACH OF THE NINTH PLAN
2.1 The Approach Paper to 9
th Five Year Plan, while laying emphasis on empowering women, under
scored harmonization of various efforts on different fronts, i.e., social, economic, legal and political. The
Approach Paper also emphasises the need to make reservation of seats for women in the Parliament and
State Legislatures, to fulfil the goal of education for women equality, to adopt a life cycle approach to
women’s health. As regards child development, the Approach paper proposes to take the convention of
child’s rights ratified in 1992 as the guiding principle and would like to review the national policy for
children. In order to promote a community based approach, action will be initiated to decentralise women
and child programme involving Panchayati Raj Institutions and local women’s self-help groups.
2.2 The Department informed that it is continuously making efforts for better delivery of services to the
targeted groups under the various schemes. As was emphasised in the approach paper, the Department is
already striving for the social, economic, legal and political empowerment of women. The Department is
also trying to get 33% reservation of seats for women in Parliament and in State legislatures. Department is
taking various steps to speed up the implementation of the Schemes for empowerment of women which
includes (I) computerisation of administration of NORAD and to some extent STEP and Working Women
Hostel Scheme; (ii) monitoring and implementation of projects under various schemes (iii) Nutrition
Education of the community in rural, urban and tribal areas through the field infrastructure of Food and
Nutrition Board; (iv) organisation of demonstration programmes/orientation training courses/integrated
nutrition education camps; and (v) involvement of Panchayti Raj Institutions and women co-operative
societies in the implementation of ICDS Scheme.
2.3. While welcoming the initiatives taken by the Department, the Committee would
also like to emphasise that sustained, dedicated and sincere efforts are the pre-requisite
to fulfil the commitments and for this purpose, cooperation of other concerned
Governmental bodies whether it be in Centre or State as well as non-Governmental
organisations is a must.
III. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
3.1. The Department’s annual plan outlay for 1998-99 was Rs.1274.23 crores (Rs.1225.95 crores Plan and
Rs.48.28 crores Non-Plan) which was reduced to the level of Rs.1179.93 crores (Rs.1134.48 crores Plan +
Rs.45.45 crores Non-Plan) at the RE stage. The Committee was informed that during 1997-98 against
plan allocation of Rs.900 crores enhanced to Rs.1025.95 crore at the RE stage, only Rs.894.76 crores
could be utilised. The Committee notes that during 1998-99 too, there has been an expenditure of
only Rs. 978.90 crore upto February, 1999. The Committee apprehends that under utilisation of
funds will occur this year too.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
3.2. With regard to the Budgetary provision made for the year 1999-2000, the Department has been
provided with Rs.1371.83 crores (Rs.1320.00 crores under Plan and Rs.51.83 crores under Non-Plan).
When compared to the BE of last year there is an increase of Rs.97.60 crores i.e.7.6%. The Committee was
given to understand that this increase does not match the projected demand sought by the Department
which was Rs.1696.29 crores (Rs.1639.11 crores under Plan and Rs.57.18 crores under Non-Plan) for
example, in the field of Central Schemes concerning welfare and development of women, allocation of
funds is less by more than Rs.100 crore, i.e. allocation of Rs.143.67 crore against projected requirement of
Rs.252.01 crore. Higher outlays were proposed to take care of upward revision of norms under various
schemes such as ICDS (General), ICDS Training, Short Stay Homes and also to augment the Corpus of
Rashtriya Mahila Kosh and National Creche Fund. The Department further submitted that on account of
less provision than the projected requirement, the Department had to prune down the size of a number of
schemes.
3.3. The Committee is constrained to note that during the last 2-3 years, although allocation to the
Department has been invariably less than the projected requirements, the trend of under-utlisation
of funds is continuing. The Committee is, therefore, of the considered opinion that concerted efforts
should be made by the Department for maximum utilisation of allocated funds.
IV INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS) SCHEME
4.1. The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme aims to improve the nutritional and
health status of vulnerable groups including pre-school children, pregnant women and nursing mothers
through providing a package of services including Supplementary Nutrition, Pre-School Education,
Immunisation, Health Check-up, Referral Services and Nutrition and Health Education. In addition, the
Scheme envisages effective convergence of inter-sectoral services in the Anganwadi Centres.
4.2. The allocation made for ICDS during 1998-99 was Rs.603.4 crores which was enhanced to Rs.768.41
crores at RE stage. The Committee has noted that the actual expenditure under this scheme upto February,
1999 has been Rs. 767.14 crores. For the year 1999-2000, against the projected requirement of funds at the
level of Rs.1059.43 crores, a provision of Rs. 855.76 crores has been made. This provision is also meant to
cover expenses arising due to higher rate of honorarium payable to Anganwadi Workers and Helpers and
also increased project cost.
4.3. The Committee has been informed that in pursuance of its recommendation regarding according top
priority to the coverage and outreach of ICDS projects in the country, the Department has been included
for the implementation of Special Action Plan proposed by the Planning Commission. An additional
amount of Rs.450 crores has been allocated by the Planning Commission for the remaining 3 years of
Ninth Five Year Plan for ICDS. The Committee appreciates the decision taken by the Planning
Commission. However, the Committee finds that this has not been reflected in the budget allocation
for 1999-2000, as it is much below the projected requirements.
4.4. The Committee has been given to understand that the most important impact of the scheme is clearly
reflected in significant decline in the levels of severely and moderately malnourished children in the
country as also in significant decline in IMR. The percentage of children suffering from severe
malnutrition has significantly declined from 15.3% during 1976-78 to 8.7% during 1989-90. The IMR has
significantly declined from 80 per 1000 live births in 1991 to 71 during 1997.
4.5. While not disputing the decline in the average level of malnutrition in children, the Committee would

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
like to emphasise that in the tribal areas of the country, situation is very bad. The Committee would like
to draw attention to the Bastar region in M.P. where every year 1000 children are reported to die
due to malnutrition and other related problems like non-availability of potable water. Such cases are
bound to be there in other areas specially in Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh too. The Committee
is of the opinion that the Department’s work does not end with decline in the average figures of
malnutrition deaths in children. What is required is identification of vulnerable areas particularly in
remote tribal areas and facilitating the reach of ICDS activities there with full vigour.
4.6. The Committee’s attention has been drawn to the element of discontent being observed in Anganwadi
Workers due to unsatisfactory benefits/facilities available to them. The Committee notes that AWW, a
community based voluntary frontline worker of the ICDS Programme, is the central figure in helping the
community identify and meet the needs of their children and women. The Committee finds that in addition
to the job responsibilities of AWW originally envisaged, their services are also vital in the implementation
of RCH (Reproductive Child Health) Programme and National AIDS Control Programme. The
Committee strongly feels that noticeable improvement in the service conditions of AWWs is called
for if ICDS Programme is to be made a total success.
4.7. The Committee is happy to note that a national Committee has been recently set up to take stock of the
service conditions and duties of AWWs and Helpers and to identify Ministries/Departments/States etc.
which can provide additional remuneration to these ICDS functionaries. The Committee hopes that this
Committee would come out with its recommendations at the earliest.
4.8. The Committee notes that the ICDS programme is characterised by a built in monitoring system for
promoting assessment, analysis and action at different levels. There is a regular flow of information and
feedback between each Anganwadi and the project, between the ICDS project and the State Government
and between the State Government and Government of India. Quarterly status reports and performance
reports are sent to the State’s nodal departments in taking necessary corrective action. The Committee
hopes that the existence of an effective monitoring system for ICDS would lead to better
achievement of physical targets.
4.9. The Committee is happy to note that some activities as enumerated below have been initiated by the
Department for integration of
 
Ayurveda in ICDS Scheme:-
a. Ayurveda Doctors to regularly visit AWCs in rural and remote areas;
b. List of simple home remedies/Ayurvedic medicines for inclusion in the medicine lists
being procured ; and
c. Development of a training module for AWWs in Ayurveda and Ayurvedic concept of life
style.
The Department of ISMH has also been requested to forward a proposal with area-specific intensive
intervention for meeting full integration of Ayurveda and ICDS scheme.
Appreciating the initiative, the Committee hopes that gradually other Indian Systems of Medicine as
well as Homoeopathy would also be considered for inclusion.
4.10. The World Bank assisted ICDS projects are extending certain additional services like income
generation activities for women, interventions for adolescent girls, nutritional rehabilitation of the severely
malnourished in pre-dominantly tribal and backward areas in a number of States.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
4.11 The Committee last year took a serious view of the ban on further operationalisation of ICDS
Projects beyond the 461 Projects. The Department has now submitted that it is pursuing with the
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for expansion of this scheme in a phase manner during the
Ninth Five Year Plan.
4.12 The Committee observes that during 1997-98 and 1998-99, the funds allocated for World Bank
assisted ICDS projects could not be fully utilised as detailed below:-
(Rs. in crores)
BE RE Actuals
1997-98 214.50 214.50 153.27
1998-99 331.95 140.00 100.97(Upto Feb.1999)
The Committee is constrained to note that it has not been even possible to utilise the reduced
allocation during 1998-99. The prime reason cited for such a situation prevailing is non-availability
of necessary approval of the competent authority on World Bank assisted ICDS – Andhra Pradesh
Economic Restructuring (APER) Project in Andhra Pradesh and ICDS – III Project in the States of
Kerala, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh. As per the ATR, the Department
has successfully negotiated with IDA enhanced commitment of US $ 300 million for ICDS III Project
in May, 1998. The project was approved by the World Bank on 29
th June, 1998. Approval of the
competent authority is awaited in respect of this Project and also for ICDS Project in Andhra

4.13 The Committee views with serious concern the procedural delays in the final approval of these
two World Bank assisted ICDS Projects. The Committee would like to emphasise that the element of
delay continuing for such a long time would result in negative achievements. The Committee,
therefore, reiterates that concerted efforts should be made by the Department to expedite the
necessary approval so that there is utilisation of Rs.231.00 crores allocated in 1999-2000.
V. Training Programme Under ICDS
5.1. The effective delivery package of services envisaged in the ICDS Scheme depends upon proper
training and orientation at all levels. There is a network of training centres for imparting training to ICDS
functionaries. For the grassroot level worker of ICDS Scheme, i.e AWWs, there are 392 Anganwadi
Workers Training Centres (AWTCs) in the country. It has been observed that during 8
th Plan, there has
been a shortfall in achievement of physical and financial targets to train Anganwadi Workers. Non-
recruitment and non-deputation of trainees by the State Governments has been cited as the main factor
responsible for this shortfall.
5.2. The Committee observes that this trend seems to be continuing during 9th Plan also. The
Committee finds that funds allocated for Training Programme under ICDS have not been fully
utilised –

crores)

Not only this, during 1998-99 against a target of training of 35,000 AWWs, only 15,000 AWWs have been
trained upto November, 1998.
5.3. The Committee understands that for improving the reporting of AWWs to the training centres,
financial norms for conducting ICDS training are being revised which inter-alia provide for
incentive of one month’s honorarium to AWWs. In addition, the rate of boarding and lodging is also
proposed to be revised. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that this exercise has been
going on for a considerable time. Latest position is that the proposal for upward revision of financial
norms is awaiting final formal clearance of the competent authority which is expected shortly. The
Committee notes that during the last two years, i.e. 1997-98 and 1998-99, enhanced provision for
training programme under ICDS was made in anticipation of Govt.’s approval for enhancement of
financial norms. However, approval could not materialise during this period. For 1999-2000,
allocation has been further hiked to Rs. 60 crores. The Committee apprehends that the same fate
may befall this year too. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to expedite the
matter without any delay.
5.4. On a specific query regarding the names of the States where the achievement level of physical targets
had been lower, it was informed that physical performance in the States/UTs of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar,
Goa, HP, J&K, Maharashtra, Nagaland, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Delhi and A&N Islands
is low compared to other States/UTs. In order to coordinate, monitor and implement ICDS Training
Programme, nodal officers in all these States with the exception of Bihar, Goa, Sikkim and Delhi have
been appointed. The Committee hopes that this exercise will result in better performance. The
Committee, however, fails to understand the rationale behind opening of new Training Centres in
some of the States (Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Maharashtra, Nagaland,
Tripura and Adaman&Nicobar Islands) where services of already established training centres are
not being utilised fully.
5.5. The Committee appreciates that a comprehensive review of the ICDS training programme has
been carried out by the Department. As a result, a new programme called project ‘UDISHA’,
approved by EFC, is awaiting approval of the Government. The Committee recommends that
approval of the competent authority should be expedited for launching of this new training
programme.
VI BALWADI NUTRITION PROGRAMME
6.1. The Balwadi Nutrition Programme aspires to meet the very basic nutritional requirement of a child in
the age group of 3-5 years by ensuring that she/he is provided with 300 calories and 12-15 gms of protein
every day. Apart from nutrition supplement, the Balwadis offer a healthy environment, looking after the
social and emotional needs of the children. Since 1997-98, this scheme is being implemented only in non-
ICDS areas. 6.2. The allocation for Balwadi Nutrition Programme in BE 1998-99 was Rs. 6.17 crores
(Rs.3.00 crores under Plan and Rs.3.17) crores under Non-Plan), which was reduced to just Rs. 3.00 crores

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
only under Plan side. Explaining the reasons, the Department informed that in view of the fact that during
the year 1997-98, the entire plan provision remained unutilised, it was decided to utilise the plan provision
first and only thereafter, the funds under non-plan were to be utilised. However, on reviewing the position
at RE stage, it was observed that the funds under Plan head would be sufficient keeping in view the
expenditure in first six months and also non-expanding nature of the scheme. The Committee is,
however, constrained to observe that expenditure made upto February. 1999 is only Rs. 0.69 crores
against an allocation of Rs. 3.00 crores. Chances of expecting satisfactory expenditure at this stage
are very dim. This is not a happy situation keeping in mind that the proposal to phase out Balwadi
Centres w.e.f. 1.4.1998 has been deferred as the universalisation of ICDS programme in 1414 blocks
has also been deferred.
6.3. The Committee has also noted that the Planning Commission had agreed to the continuation of the
Balwadi Nutrition Programme in non-ICDS areas during the Ninth Plan period with the provision that the
scheme would be continued upto 31
st March, 2001 only. Only spill over liabilities will be settled during
the terminal year of the Ninth Plan.
6.4. On a specific query regarding what alternative options were there in case of universalisation of ICDS
not being achieved, the Department stated that a review of the BNP would be done to see whether it would
be worthwhile to continue the Scheme with reduced number of BNP centres till the end of the Ninth Plan
period and the question of alternative options will also be examined. The Committee feels that as things
stand, the ad hoc approach of the Department is likely to create similar position as evident in the
case of other schemes. Finalisation of any scheme requires so many procedural formalities/approvals
which take their own time as is being noticed in finalisation of World Bank assisted ICDS
Programmes.The Committee, therefore, recommends that all appropriate and necessary steps
should be taken to ensure that children covered under this scheme are not affected on account of any
delay in implementation of any alternative scheme.
VII Crèches/Day Care Centres
7.1. Children in the vulnerable age group of 0-5 and whose parent’s total monthly income is not more than
Rs. 1800/- p.m. are given essential day care services under the Creche Scheme started in 1975 and the
National Creche Fund set up in 1994. While the Creche Scheme is being implemented through three major
organisations, i.e. (i) Central Social Welfare Board (ii) Bharatiya Adimjati Sevak Sangh (iii) Indian
Council for Child Welfare, the National Creche Fund provides assistance to registered NGOs and Mahila
Mandals throughout the country to run crèches.
7.2. The Committee last year had observed that there was a greater need for extending the network of
Creches and Day Care Centres. The Department vide its Action Taken Report has clarified that the Creche
Scheme is non-expanding and efforts are underway to increase the corpus of the National Creche Fund so
that more creches can be set up.
7.3. The National Creche Fund set up in 1993-94 with a corpus of Rs. 19.90 crores, covers 1856 General
Creches and 599 Anganwadi-cum-Creches. The Committee is, however, perturbed to note that a
proposal to increase the corpus amount has not yet been approved and a provision of Rs. 1 crore
made in 1998-99 had to be reduced to Rs.1 lakh. Similar token provision has been made in 1999-
2000 also. The Committee notes that against an estimated requirement of 8 lakh creches for children
in the country, only 14,925 creches have been set up under these two schemes so far, leaving an

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
enormous gap which needs to be filled up at the earliest.
7.4. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the matter of unspent balances and lack of
information about expenditure should be taken up with the concerned States so as to ensure
maximum utilisation of funds under the Creche Scheme. The Committee also emphasises that
concerted efforts should be made to finalise the proposal regarding enhancement of corpus amount
under the National Creche Fund.
VIII. Hostels for Working Women
8.1. This scheme aims to provide suitable, safe and inexpensive accommodation to single working women
in lower income group. This scheme is implemented though voluntary organisations, women’s
development corporations, universities, schools/colleges of social work and local bodies etc. Allocation for
this scheme has been constant at Rs.7.75 crores at BE and RE 1997-98, 1998-88 and also BE 1999-2000.
The Committee, however, observes that against a target of 25 Hostels to be sanctioned during 1998-99,
only 5 could be sanctioned. During 1998-99, expenditure upto Feb., 99 has been only Rs. 4.68 crores.
8.2 The Department informed the Committee that since 1997, only 819 hostels have been sanctioned so
far. During the period 1994-97, 106 hostels were sanctioned out of which 16 were completed within the
stipulated time period. In view of the pace of construction of Hostels, the Committee is of the view that
there is a need to step up efforts.
8.3. The Committee feels that this scheme should not be restricted to working women only.
Wherever vacancies are available, girls pursuing higher studies/training programme can be
accommodated in working women hostels.
IX. INDIRA MAHILA YOJANA
9.1. Indira Mahila Yojana was launched initially on pilot basis in 200 blocks. Indira Mahila Yojana is a
strategy to create an organisational base in all parts of the country for women to come together and analyse
their needs and understand the processes of fulfilling the needs through existing developmental
programmes of the State and Central Governments. As per the information available from the states, more
than 38,000 women’s groups have been formed under this scheme.
9.2. The Department has informed that on account of very high operational cost of implementing Mahila
Samriddhi Yojana, it was not found feasible to continue the scheme after March, 1998. Amount yet to be
paid to the Department of Posts is Rs. 313 crores. As a result of this, it has been decided to merge erstwhile
MSY with IMY. However, in view of non finalisation of this proposal, an amount of Rs. 10 crore provided
in 1998-99 had to be reduced to Rs. 0.01 crore at the RE stage. The Committee observes that an allocation
of Rs. 10 crore has been made for IMY in 1999-2000. As per the latest information made available to the
Committee, the draft proposal for merger of these two schemes and strengthening the IMY is under
circulation to various departments. The EFC is likely to consider the proposal once the views of the
departments are available.
9.3. The Committee has noted that a rapid evaluation study of IMY by the Planning Commission and
Department of WCD, while appreciating the work done in some of the states, has made the following
observations :-

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/85repwcd.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:18]
lack of manpower at every level,
training was a missing component,
various committees set up under the scheme not regularly meeting,
resources material development not being given priority.
9.4. The Committee is happy to note that IMY is being recast incorporating the provisions for
removing the shortcomings pointed out in the evaluation study.
9.5. The Committee has been given to understand that the Planning Commission has approved the
expansion of IMY blocks to be taken up after approval of EFC during 1999-2000. The Committee
desires that a decision on this issue should be taken at an early date and if need be, enhanced
allocation may be provided for the purpose.
X SHORT STAY HOMES
10.1. Under this scheme, grants-in-aid are given to voluntary organisations for establishing and running
Short Stay Homes for rehabilitating women and girls, facing social and moral danger due to family
problems, mental strain, exploitation etc. The Committee has observed that against a plan provision of
Rs.10 crores in BE 1998-99 reduced to Rs.4.00 crore at RE stage, expenditure figures stand at Rs.2.50
crore upto February, 1999.
10.2. The Committee has been informed that since the inception of the scheme in 1969, 361 Short Stay
Homes have been established so far. Inspection of approximately 185 Homes has been organised during
the last two years. 83 Homes were, thereafter issued show cause notices, 13 Homes were closed down and
10 NGOs. were blacklisted. As a result of this exercise, the number of existing Homes was brought down
to 272.
10.3. The Committee hopes that inspections of remaining homes would also be carried out by the
Department as early as possible. The Committee welcomes the decision of the Department to
transfer the implementation of this scheme to Central Social Welfare Board from next year. The
Committee, however, has a word of caution. Alongwith the system of routine inspection, there is a
need for carrying out surprise inspections for better and real assessment of functioning of Short Stay
Homes. This becomes all the more necessary in view of the fact that assistance to a Short Stay Home
has been increased from Rs.1.87 lakhs to Rs.4.01 lakhs per annum with effect from 1
st April, 1999.
10.4. The Committee is shocked to note that as a result of a sample study of 37 Homes undertaken by the
Planning Commission, 6 Homes were found to be non-existing/non-functional. Major drawbacks as
enumerated below have been pointed out in this evaluation study :-
expenditure on establishing appeared to be on a higher side;
very little linkage with the local Government;
Greater publicity of the scheme is necessary to create public awareness;
State Government’s involvement in monitoring and implementation of the scheme should be
introduced.
10.5. The Committee would like to suggest that attempts should also be made to rehabilitate the
inmates of Short Stay Homes on a regular basis.
XI. RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH

11.1. The Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK) has been given one time corpus of Rs.31.00 crores which is
being used as a revolving fund to provide loans to poor women mainly through NGOs well versed in credit
management. It also channelises loan through women development corporations and Cooperative
Societies. Since its inception upto 31.3.1998, RMK has been able to sanction credit limits of Rs.47.85
crore through 256 NGOs to benefit 2,50,312 women.
11.2. It has come to the notice of the Committee that recently RMK commissioned impact studies on
its performance through seven reputed organisations including five universities which recommended
that RMK should be given at least another Rs.250 crores and it should have regional offices for easy
access to the applicant NGOs. It was also stated that the evaluation study has given certain
suggestions such as clear targeting of poor women, changing the profile of Governing Board of
RMK, induction of more professionals of RMK etc. A revised proposal is likely to be submitted for
consideration of EFC in the first quarter of the current financial year.
XII. Women’s Economic Programme – Phase II and ‘Support to Training and
Employment Programme for Women (STEP)’
12.1. The Committee observes that there are two Programmes with the objective of making women self-
dependent. Both the programmes are meant to promote women’s development through provision of
sustained employment both in traditional as well as non-traditional areas. Target group in both the
programmes are poor and needy women in urban slums and rural areas. Implementing Agencies include

13.1. The Socio-Economic Programme provides economic rehabilitation to the poor or disabled women by

XIII. ATROCITIES ON WOMEN
 
  
  
 
14.1. The Committee has noted that the National Commission for Women has been continuing its
work relating to review of laws, intervention in specific individual complaints of atrocities and
sexual harassment of women and remedial action for safeguarding their interest.
14.2. Attention of the Committee has been continuously drawn to reported sale of girls in different
parts of the country. Reports from Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh are the most recent one. When
asked in this matter, the Department informed that direct intervention has been made by the Andhra
Pradesh Government. So far as Rajasthan is concerned, it was informed that a report has been
received from the district authorities in this regard. A project on the lines of the scheme taken up by
Maharashtra Government in rehabilitation of Devdasis for such victims is being taken up there.

14.3. The Committee views with serious concern that in 6 metropolitan cities, about 30% of
the sex workers are reported to be below the age of 20 years. The Committee has been
informed that a Plan of Action to combat trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation of
women and children has been formulated by the Department and all the State Governments
and UT Administrations have been requested in February, 1998 to implement the same.
Proposals are also reported to have been received from a number of NGOs in this regard.
14.4. The Committee, while appreciating the steps taken in this regard, would like to impress
that the Plan of Action should be constantly monitored at all levels so as to ensure timely
feedback and remedial measures.
XIV. GENERAL
15.1. Allocation of an amount for a specific programme at the beginning of a financial year, its
subsequent reduction at RE stage, failure in expenditure of the same for want of approval from the
competent authority is a trend which is being noticed in a number of cases so far as launching of a
new scheme/revision of a scheme is concerned. The Committee would like to point out that there is
an urgent need for streamlining the entire procedure. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the
Department to give serious consideration to this aspect.
15.2. The Committee finds that most of the projects are being implemented through NGOs, some of
the NGOs are doing good work. However, the Committee views with serious concern that there are
reports also about a number of NGOs involved in financial irregularities. Committee’s attention has
been drawn to CAG Report (1 of 1998) wherein it has been observed that 6321 utilisation certificates
relating to Rs. 725.76 crore in respect of grants released upto September, 1995 by the Department
were outstanding at the end of March, 1997.
15.3. The Committee notes that a ‘National Evaluation and Monitoring Agency’ is proposed to be
launched during 1999-2000 for proper identification of NGOs involved in various schemes of women
and child development and also for evaluating and monitoring the implementation of various
schemes. The need for launching such an Agency is proof enough that the various schemes being
implemented were either not having an inbuilt mechanism for monitoring or the same was not
effective enough. The Committee hopes that there would be no delay in the launching of the National
Evaluation and Monitoring Agency.
XVI. Committed Liability
16.1. While examining the Demands for Grants 1997-98 of the Departments under its purview, the
Committee noted that the committed liability of the Plan Schemes has not been reflected in the
budgetary allocations.
16.2. The Committee, in this, connection considered the report of the Tenth Finance Commission.
The Tenth Finance Commission have observed in this regard as under:-
"Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of
reference in deciding the cut off date for transfer of committed liability on
account of plan scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-
98 on account of 8

16.3. The Committee also sought clarifications from the then Secretary (Expenditure). He informed

16.4. The Committee, accordingly, directed the Department to approach the Ministry of Finance in

Committee, therefore, heard the Secretary (Expenditure) on 27
th March, 1999.
16.5. The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee, submitted that at the end of the 8th Five
Year Plan the Planning Commission issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the committed
expenditure from plan to the non plan side. The Ministry of Finance (Budget Division) also issued a

16.6. The Secretary submitted that as on 10
th February, 1997, 24 Ministries/Departments responded
indicating a figure of Rs.450.28 crore. However, some Ministries/Departments like Education,

16.7. The Secretary agreed in principle that whatever is the committed expenditure, it should be

16.8. The Secretary assured that the proposals pertaining to UGC (Rs.27 crores) and Department of

Finance Commission Report has given a breathing time till 1999-2000 for this transition.
16.9. The Committee would like to impress that the real picture should be projected before
Parliament.
16.10. The Secretary also apprised the Committee that another Sub Committee has been appointed
by the NDC, consisting of representatives from seven states and Ministry of Finance. This Sub-
Committee will look into the structural distortions which have entered into the finances of the states
on account of 5
th Pay Commission and to suggest a suitable package linked to fiscal reforms.

INTRODUCTION
1. Main objectives of the Department of Health are:-
i. to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention,
control and eradication of communicable diseases;
ii. to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the
medical colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas;
iii. to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs;

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
2.1. The Department of Health has been allocated Rs.1160 crores on the Plan side and Rs.830.28 crores on
the Non-Plan side, for the year 1999-2000. The percentage increase in the approved outlay for 1999-2000
over 1998-99 works out to a meagre 1.29%.
2.2. On a specific query as to the projected requirements of the Department for 1999-2000, the Department
submitted that it had proposed an outlay of Rs.1269.11 crores for 1999-2000 to the Planning Commission
mainly on account of enhanced outlays to be provided for disease control programmes like Blindness,
AIDS, Disease Surveillance and Response System, Central Hospitals and premier institutions engaged in
medical education and research including construction of Delhi Nurses Colony. However, the Department
has been allocated only Rs.1160.00 crores which is less by Rs.109.11 crores vis-à-vis the projected
demand. As a result, not only there would be no enhanced outlays as planned for the programmes/schemes
mentioned above but also the overall programmes would be adversely affected. The programmes/schemes
adversely affected to a significant extent are National TB Control Programme and National Blindness
Control Programme while Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi, Lady Hardinge Medical College, Delhi and PGI,
Chandigarh will be affected marginally, it was clarified.
2.3 The Committee feels that the allocation made is not in consonance with the genuine needs of the
Department. The Committee was given to understand that there has been no substantial increase in
the total investment on Health and Family Welfare Sector over the last few years. As per the WHO
recommentation, if equity and universal coverage is to be realised, at least 5 percent of GDP is to be
made for Public Health Care. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance should give a careful thought to the above recommendation of

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/86repoh.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:35]
WHO, before finalising the budgetary allocations of the Department.
2.4. At the same time, the Committee has a word of caution for the Department. The Committee has
observed that during the last three years, although allocations made have been less as compared to
the projected requirements, trend of under-utilisation is very much evident:-

Expenditure Rs.1030.43 crores

2.5. The Committee has been given to understand that the position remains unchanged in 1998-99
too. The Committee is concerned to note that the main factors responsible for this situation, as come
out from the details furnished by the Department, are unspent balances lying with the State
Governments, non receipt of utilisation certificates, non-filling of vacant posts, procedural delays in
procurement of medicines and equipments. As admitted by the Department, there are all kinds of
delays which are not satisfactorily resolved. The Committee is fully aware that for providing health
care, both Central and State Governments have a role to play. The Committee, however, strongly
feels that in view of the scale of expenditure during the last three years, the Department of Health,
being the nodal agency has to take remedial steps so as to make basic health care within the reach of
common man a reality.
2.6. The Committee has been given to understand that sometimes delays are caused because the
administrative Ministry does not observe all the procedures in getting the expenditure finally
sanctioned. The Committee feels that the system needs to be modified so as to prevent these
procedural delays. Even in the case of new proposals, administrative Ministry should do away with
the element of adhocism and adopt a systematic approach.
7. A number of National Health Programmes are being run by the Central Government in
collaboration with the State Governments. The main objective of these programmes is to
bring down the rate of incidence of a particular disease. The Committee feels that these
programmes although evolved at a national level also need to have an element of local
input. What is required is a definite preventive scheme for every State according to the
prevalence of the disease there. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the
Department may initiate an exercise of review of all its National Health Programmes in a
phased manner.

XIII. NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME
