Central Health Services  are not of a satisfactory level.   The Committee hopes that after the  ongoing exercise of cadre
review is over,  things would improve for the better.   The Committee  is of the view that there is also a need for
evolving some system of co-ordination among the concerned authorities, i.e. UPSC, Directorate of Health Services/
Directorate of Medical Education and the concerned college.
XXII    JOINT CONSULTATIVE MACHINERY
22.1     The Committee is deeply disturbed by frequent incidents of doctors/teachers, para-medical staff, ancillary staff
etc. of medical institutions and attached hospitals all over the country resorting  to strikes on trivial matters and thus
putting public at large to great inconvenience.   The Committee strongly feels that a co-ordination mechanism needs to
be  evolved whereby all categories of employees – be it, faculty members, doctors, students, technicians -  get common
platform to air their problems and find a solution agreeable to all concerned.   The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Department should pursue the setting up of such a mechanism with all the State Govts/management of both
national level and private institutions.
22.2     The Committee is also of the view that a cell for receiving complaints and inviting suggestions from general
public and affected persons should be set up in the MCI to work as a watch-guard and also facilitate the functioning of
MCI.
XXIII   PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY STUDENT COMMUNITY
23.1     The Committee had very fruitful discussions with representatives of student community of all the medical
colleges visited by it.   Various suggestions for improvement of medical education based on their experience were put
forth before the Committee which are reflected in the Report.  Besides that, the students also drew the attention of the
Committee to a number of problems being faced by them which are enumerated below :-
a)
                  Due to a prolonged admission procedure for MBBS, session for 1st year generally starts very late.
b)                  Maximum publicity needs to be  given to the rules/regulations and conditions with respect to admission
procedure for the convenience of students.
c)                  Hostel accommodation satisfying the needs of entire student community not there.   Majority of the students
have to travel a long distance daily for attending their classes.
d)
                  Lack of  hospital accommodation has resulted in tendency of students not attending their classes regularly.   In
the process, there were frequent instances of shortage of attendance.
e)
                  Another peculiar development is students opting for private tuition.
f)                    Students of private medical colleges/younger institution not having adequate library facilities.
g)                  Very low rates of stipend being paid to trainee doctors.    Amount of stipend also varies from State to State,
institution to institution.
h)
                  Foreign textbooks  not fulfilling the requirements of students.
i)                    Complaints of biased attitude of external examiners  conducting practical exams were also there.
23.2     The Committee understands that a specific  time schedule for admission  to MBBS has been laid down by MCI.  
The Committee finds that due to  delay in the admission procedure, training schedule gets disturbed and as a result,
instances are there that results are delayed.  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that MCI should strictly monitor
the adherence of  time schedule by medical  colleges all over the country. 
23.3     Lack of required hospital accommodation has become a big problem for students.   The Committee recommends
that MCI should take up this issue with the concerned State Govts./Private college managements so that students’
problems are minimized.   The Committee is of the view that the   development of coaching classes in some states in
addition to the normal colleges cannot be considered to be a healthy sign.   MCI should, therefore, undertake a review of
this development in concerned states and pursue the State Govts. to take required steps for  putting a check  to this
unhealthy practice.    The Committee feels that possibility of students of private medical colleges/younger institutions
utilizing the library facility available in Govt. medical colleges strictly on merit and without disturbing  students  of such
colleges may be explored in the larger interests of medical education.   The Committee is also of the view that a
mechanism needs to be evolved  for periodic review  of stipend payable to students and bringing about uniformity to the

extent possible.   The Committee would also like to point out that there is a need for standardization  of medical
textbooks having a balanced mixture of foreign and national components.
XXIV     TEACHER-STUDENT RELATIONSHIP
24.1     There has been gradual erosion in the traditional relations between students and teachers in medical education.   
Over the years, what has happened is that  with the increase in the intake capacity in medical colleges all over the
country,  faculty strength with a few exceptions has continued to be the same.    The MCI ratio 10:1 for  student teacher 
is nowhere to be seen.   The Committee has been given to understand that in the majority of the medical colleges small
group teaching was being practiced only during tutorials, clinical teaching and  field visits.   The Committee feels that
the situation should be  such that the teachers are able to share their experiences with the students.   Teachers also  get
an opportunity to evaluate the students better in such an environment.   The Committee finds that  availability of video
cassettes and internet access has vastly improved interactive learning wherever available.   The Committee is of the
view that steps should be taken for compulsory introduction of such hi-tech facilities in all medical colleges  in the
country.
XXV    MEDICAL RESEARCH
25.1     The Committee visited the ICMR     to apprise itself about the medical research being carried out in the
country.   Even though ICMR is doing pioneer work in the field of medical research, the Committee notes that the
students in general are not pursuing research in their field of study for want of proper incentives and conducive
environment in the   country.   It has also been observed that the students are not  taking full benefit out of the research
projects undertaken by the ICMR, like short-term summer studentship programme, course on research methodology
etc.   The Committee is of the considered view that steps should be taken  to step up research activities in the   Health
sector, with the active involvement of both public and private sector.
 OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
OVERVIEW
            The Committee observes that the amendments made in the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 in 1993 by laying
down very stringent norms for establishment of new medical college, increase in the intake capacity and introduction of
a new or higher course of study  has  checked  the mushroom growth of  medical colleges in the country to some
extent.   However, these norms need to be enforced uniformly  and  with an objective approach.   Sporadic proposals for
starting a very large number of medical colleges at a stroke  still continue to be noticed. (Para 2.1)
Private medical colleges, in the initial period, barely reach the standards and  norms set up by MCI  with regard
to infrastructure, manpower etc.   Similarly, in the Govt. medical  colleges set up in different parts of the country, with
the passage of time there has been a steady deterioration in the infrastructure because of   inability of State Govts  to
provide any assistance  whatsoever due to their very poor financial position.   Other major   constraints noticed in the
smooth functioning of Govt. medical colleges are control of too many authorities, lack of accountability, prolonged
procedure of recruitment  and promotion of teachers.   Inadequate  staff, unwarranted interference by management and
manipulation in the admission of students can be said to be major drawbacks of private medical colleges.    The
Committee also noticed that access to clinical facilities having large patient attendance was there in Govt. medical
colleges.   In contrast in private medical colleges, in spite of having impressive      hospital  buildings, required clinical
material  was lacking. (Para 2.2)
MEDICAL COUNCIL OF INDIA (MCI)
The Committee observes that the  present composition of  MCI cannot be said  to be of an All India  character.  
This is all the more evident as only  fifteen members form the quorum  of the Council and all the acts of the Council
are   decided by a majority of the members present and voting. (Para 3.3)
            The Committee notes that out of 36 vacancies in the  113-member Council, 21 are in the seats reserved for
Universities.  Reason for vacancies in this category, as intimated by    the Department is non-constitution/non-
reconstitution  of Senate or Court of the Universities or  meetings of the Senate/Court not being held for a long time.   
What is a cause of  serious concern  is that Universities are simply not responding to the reminders  sent by the Council
and the Central Govt. from time to time and vacancies are continuing in some cases for the last 10-15 years. (Para 3.4)
Thus, as many as 21 Universities over and above 56 eligible Universities are not represented in the Council.

Health Universities   having a  large number of medical colleges under their   jurisdiction, specially  in southern  and
western states have no say in the decision-making apex body on medical education. (Para 3.5)
            The Committee is constrained to observe that in spite of funds towards expenses for conducting the  election
being provided by the Council, the Returning Officers  are simply not responding to the reminders of the  Council. (Para
3.6)
The Committee feels that chances of election process being completed in the near future seem to be very dim.
(Para 3.7)
            The Committee is of the strong opinion that procedure for election of different categories of  posts to the Council
is too rigid.   There is an urgent need for streamlining  the election procedure, more so, if the representative composition
of the Council as envisaged in the IMC Act, 1956 is sought to be maintained.   The Committee has been given to
understand that a proposal of the Council for bringing out amendment in the relevant provisions of the Indian Medical
Council Rules, 1957 for expediting election of members from Medical Faculty of Universities is pending with the
Central Govt.  since 15 th February, 1999.    The Committee recommends that the Central Govt. should take immediate
steps in the matter.    The Committee would also urge upon the Central Govt. to take up the issue of non-completion of
election process for other categories of seats with the concerned State Govts and impress upon them  to expedite the
same.   The Committee recommends that the Central Govt. should review the various provisions for constituting the
Council laid down in the Act and the Regulations made thereunder for removing the anomalies therein. (Para 3.8)
            The Committee is not inclined to agree with the viewpoint  of the Council.  In its all the study visits  and
interactions with the various   functionaries comprising the entire medical education   spectrum, one view  that has been
consistently put across before the Committee, was that with the increase  in the number of medical colleges over the
years, it is practically not possible for a centralized body like MCI to constantly monitor the standard of medical
education.    The Committee observes that there is no regional council of the MCI.   The State  Medical Councils are
autonomous bodies established by State Govts that too not by all the State Govts.    These  State Medical Councils have
no   authority in the maintenance of standards of medical education.   In such a  scenario with 183   medical colleges
spread across the country with chances  of future expansion, the Committee strongly feels that regional  councils  with
MCI continuing as the apex body need to be set up in the country.   The Committee is of the view that both the Central
Govt. and MCI should explore the possibility of setting up four regional councils  in  Southern, Northern, Eastern and
Western parts of the country.   This would ultimately lead to better monitoring of the standard of medical  education as
laid down in the IMC Act, 1956  and Regulations made thereunder.     The Committee also desires that the Department
may take up the matter of establishing  State Medical Council in the States where they are not existing.   Role of State
Medical Council may also be reviewed so as to involve them in the exercise of maintaining the standards of Medical
Education in the States under the guidance of MCI. (Para 3.11)
PROCEDURE/NORMS PRESCRIBED FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF A MEDICAL COLLEGE, STARTING A NEW 
OR HIGHER COURSE OF STUDY OR TRAINING AND INCREASING THE ADMISSION CAPACITY
The Committee recommends that  the MCI should undertake an exercise for reviewing the various norms so as
to  examine their viability in the present scenario and bringing  about necessary modifications therein without
compromising the quality. (Para 4.2)
However,  the Committee observes that there are certain practical problems also which go against the student
interest.   There are instances where medical college once started is not able to  fulfill the commitments made at the
initial stage, thereby losing recognition and thus playing with the future of students enrolled in that college.   The
Committee is of the view that there is a need for building up a mechanism whereby maximum standards are to be met at
the very beginning.   Reports are there  where college is started on the basis of Essentiality Certificate and conditional
approval.   However, in the very second year, conditions are not met.    In such a scenario, either the college is allowed
to function so as to safeguard the interest of students or students are shifted to a recognized medical college.   Both the
situations cannot  be considered to be desirable and this should not be allowed to happen. (Para 4.4)
            The Committee is, therefore, of the view that both the Central Govt. and MCI should have a more cautious
approach while giving approval for a new medical college.   There is a need for assessing  the background of a  trust,
specially its involvement in medical field and non-commercial approach before grant of any permission.   The
Committee, therefore, recommends that definition of the term ‘trust’ should be incorporated in the relevant provisions of
the IMC Act, 1956.        (Para 4.5)

            The Committee is not inclined to agree with the view of the Department that although it is necessary to have an
All India assessment of medical manpower requirement, it cannot be made a  pre-condition for starting a new college.  
The Committee strongly feels that the responsibility of the Central Govt does not end with the production of Essentiality
Certificate by State Govt.   The  Committee would like to refer to Sub-Section (7) of Section 10A of the IMC Act, 1956
which deals with recommendation of the Council and approval/disapproval by Central  Govt. for opening of a new
college.   One of the factors to be considered as enumerated in clause (f) is the requirement of manpower in the field of
practice of medicine.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that both Central and the State Govts should specifically
ensure whether there is a requirement in the  real sense for establishing a medical college in a particular area before
giving its approval for the same. (Para 4.7)
INSPECTION
The Committee notes that a number of steps  have been taken by MCI to make the procedure of inspection
foolproof.   For example, the medical colleges are now supposed to maintain a list of teachers on their strength 
alongwith their photographs  duly verified by the Dean of the College.    The Committee, however, is of the view that
there is a need for  streamlining the inspection procedure so as to make it more stringent and effective.  The Committee
understands that so far inspections are being carried out only  after giving prior  notice.   The Committee is of the view
that MCI should initiate measures  so as to build up  a  mechanism for carrying out surprise inspections and inspections
at a very short notice.   This would indirectly lead to a  situation where medical college authorities would work towards
having a proper set up as per the prescribed norms.   The Committee is also of  the view that rate  of fees charged  for
different  categories of inspection should be reviewed.   Specially, in spite of   the so-called annual inspections being 
carried out only once in five years,  annual fee of Rs. 30,000 is prescribed  which  seems to be on the high side. (Para
5.4)
            The Committee is surprised to note that this elaborate procedure does not   seem to be serving the required 
purpose.   The Committee would like to quote one example in this regard.   The General Body of the Council at its
meeting held on 17
th March, 1998 had recommended to the Central Govt. de-recognition of BRD Medical College,
Gorakhpur, UP.   It is  pertinent to point out that inspection of this college was carried out in 1995.   It took more than
three years for the Council to arrive at a decision which was communicated to the Central Govt. on 6
th July, 1998.   
Since then there have been correspondence between the Central Govt., State Govt. and MCI and the matter hangs    
there.   The Committee takes a very serious view of this situation.   Nobody  seems to have any concern-neither the
college nor the State Govt./University/Central Govt.    No doubt, students’ interest is safeguarded as de-recognition if
approved by the Central Govt. would be made effective from prospective date.    The Committee is of the view that in
the name of safeguarding the interest of students, interest of college authorities is being secured.   The Committee feels
that such developments defeat the very purpose of carrying out an inspection.   The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that a time-bound and result-oriented inspection procedure is required to be built up if the standard of
medical education is to be maintained.   (Para 5.6)
POOR CONDITION OF GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES
            The Committee is inclined to agree with this view-point.   The Committee  is of the view that there is an urgent
need for undertaking a review of  infrastructure status of all state-run medical  colleges in the country.   Non-existent
required facilities tend to create an atmosphere which  has a demotivating effect on the teachers/doctors/students.    The
Committee understands that Central Govt. has  already launched a pilot project for providing financial assistance to
some State Govt.  medical colleges/hospitals.   The Committee feels that a time-bound action plan for revamping the
infrastructure facilities should be drawn by the Central Govt. which could be implemented by State Govts in active co-
ordination with Central Govt. and MCI.  (Para 6.2)
The Committee is of the view  that against the backdrop of technological development, basic qualifications
required for technical staff need to be reviewed.   Besides that, regular in-service training, workshops and Continuing
Medical Education (CMEs) for technical staff should be made a regular feature.   The Committee also feels that
feasibility of having Medical Learning Technique (MLT) colleges imparting diploma/B.Sc degrees being attached to
medical colleges can be explored. (Para 6.3)
The Committee also observes  that NE region of the country  is virtually starved of spread of  medical education
as very few medical  colleges  have been established  there so farThe Committee is, however, of the view that Central
Govt. initiative is very much required for setting up medical colleges in NE states.   The Committee hopes that the

Central Govt. would initiate immediate action in this direction. (Para 6.4)
ADMISSION PROCEDURE
 
The Committee feels that a  uniform entrance test covering all the medical colleges – both Govt. and private
would be the ideal position.   The Committee, however, is of the opinion that in view of the different patterns of
secondary level education  in different states, uniform admission procedure would not prove to be feasible.   The
Committee  feels that this issue needs to be debated by the medical fraternity, its pros and cons thoroughly established
and evaluated first.  The Committee is of the view that Central Govt./MCI  should take the initiative to examine this
issue in detail so that number of entrance tests is minimized to the extent possible  thus lessening the burden of
students.  (Para 7.2)
The Committee notes that the students admitted against the 15% seats in medical colleges  filled by the
management have to fulfill the minimum eligibility criteria namely, obtaining the qualification equivalent to the pre-
eligibility qualifications prescribed  for Indian students for admission to medical courses prescribed by the MCI.
   However, the Committee has been given to understand that in view  of the different backgrounds they come from, it is
for the management concerned to judge the merit of these candidates, having regard to all relevant factors.   The 
Committee has its reservations on such a procedure.   The Committee strongly feels that there has to be a mechanism for
judging the basic knowledge and aptitude for medical profession even for NRI students.   The Committee,  therefore,  is
of the view that a separate entrance test should be prescribed for NRI students so as to somewhat  eliminate the element
of commercialization in admission through this category.  The Committee  has no hesitation in saying that track record
of such students will justify such an initiative. (Para 7.3)
The Committee, therefore, is of the view that entrance test for admission to MBBS should also include a
mechanism like aptitude test  for assessing the prospective student’s  inclination for medical profession. (Para 7.4)
NRI QUOTA IN GOVT. MEDICAL COLLEGES
The Committee understands that in some of the States, this practice has been started which is likely to be
followed in other States also.   The Committee has its own reservations about this Central Govt. directive.   While
noting that contribution of seats towards the All India Entrance Examination Quota by the State Govt. medical  colleges
will not be affected by this move, the Committee apprehends that requirements of local students are bound to be hit
hard.   The Committee wonders as to how the interest of local students will be taken care  of with the  total number of
seats remaining the same.   The Committee is of the view  that relaxation should only be resorted to if equal number of
seats are increased.   In that event also, availability of additional required infrastructure will also have to be ensured.   
The Committee also feels that there are little chances of funds thus generated being utilized for the development of a
particular institution.  Instances  have already  come to the notice  of the Committee where initial understanding with
State Govt. was  that money generated from NRI admissions was to be deposited with college and a special committee
was to be authorized to utilize these funds.   However, subsequently, State Govt directions were given  that such funds
are to be deposited with the State Exchequer to be allotted  afterwards to the college. (Para 8.1)
The  Committee, therefore, feels that alongwith entrance test, feasibility of having  individual cumulative
performance at the first, second and third MBBS examination and also aptitude of the students being  made the criteria
for admission to Postgraduate courses may be explored. (Para 8.3)
EXAMINATION PROCEDURE
            The Committee is of the view that MCI norms are not being strictly adhered to by many of the medical
colleges.   Had it been so, there would not have been such reservations and also variations in examination patterns being
followed by different institutions/universities.  The Committee would also like to point out that uniformity of
examination pattern to the maximum extent possible can only be   achieved if the teaching facilities and  courses are
also uniform.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that steps need to be initiated for evolving a forum for
interaction amongst medical faculties of different universities on this aspect of medical education. (Para 9.3)
CURRICULUM
The Committee notes that these amendments are at present under discussion between  Central Govt., DGHS and
MCI.  The Committee notes that no time-frame has been specified for upgrading  and updating the  curriculum.    The

TEACHERS
            The Committee finds that in states like Maharashtra and Gujarat, shortage of faculty strength in Govt. medical
college has been addressed to some extent by having two types of teachers -  Full-time and Honorary teachers. 
Although divergent views were given with regard to honorary teachers, the Committee had a feeling that both the
categories of teachers  were playing a complimentary role.   The Committee observes that in spite of there being a
provision for only full-time teachers in MCI Regulations, on the request of some State Govts., system of honorary
teachers has been further extended by the Central Govt.  upto 30
th June, 2002.   The  Committee is of the view that
Central Govt./MCI should undertake a detailed review of Honorary System of teachers in the concerned States.   The
Committee is of the view that after removal of all the  loopholes in this system and also safeguarding the interest of Full
time teachers, other State Govts. can be approached to take benefit of Honorary System of teachers to the extent
possible. (Para 11.4)
            The Committee finds that the UGC guidelines regarding extension of retired medical teachers of all medical
colleges/institutions on yearly basis upto the age of 65 years have been agreed to by the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare in 1997.   The Committee feels that this directive should be given wide publicity  so that the Govt. medical
colleges may take benefit of the same.  Besides that, possibility of hiring the services of  medical professionals –
Visiting Professors and practicing doctors without compromising the standard of medical education can also be
explored. (Para 11.5)
            The Committee observes  that MCI has not made any Regulations regarding separation of teaching and non-
teaching cadres.   The Council Regulations only provide for a required number of teachers and other non-teaching staff
required for each department in the medical college and attached  hospital  according to the seat intake capacity in
MBBS course.   The Committee is of the view that practice of inter-change between teaching and non-teaching cadres is
indeed creating problems for medical faculty in some of the states.   The Committee,  therefore, recommends that the

MCI should examine this practice and make specific provision in the best interest of medical teachers in its Regulations.
(Para 11.6)
            The Committee observes that the duties and responsibilities of medical teachers are different, immediate and
exacting in nature when compared with other categories  of professions/Govt. employees.    The Committee would like
to emphasise that there is an urgent need for providing the  best possible service conditions to the medical teachers.

            The Committee is not convinced by the stand of the Central Govt. that in the absence of central funding, it is in

feels that uniform pay scales  in accordance with the manifold duties performed by medical teachers across the country
would be the ideal  condition.   In order to maintain the standard of medical education, there is imperative need for

the proposal for having a  Central agency on the  pattern of UGC and AICTE was initially discussed in a meeting taken
by the Member, Planning Commission and the broad guidelines for establishment of such a Commission  were also 
worked out.   However,  subsequently in 1997 with the approval of the then Health Minister  it was decided to keep the
proposal in abeyance.   The Committee is of the view that a Medical Grants Commission  is required  to be set up
without any further delay.  The Committee is happy to note that draft National Health Policy, 2001 at present under
circulation to all concerned for their comments envisages the setting up of Medical Grants Commission for funding new
Govt. medical colleges and upgradation of the existing Govt. medical colleges.     The service conditions of medical
teachers should also be covered under the mandate of Medical  Grants Commission. (Para 11.9)
TRAINING
The Committee strongly feels that training in educational technology should be made the eligibility criteria for
appointment of a medical teacher.   If that is not considered feasible, extensive training programme of short duration
should be mandatory before   the prospective teachers join their duties. (Para 12.1) 
The Committee is, however, constrained to note that these directives are not being adhered to as only about 50-
60 medical colleges in the country  have established such units so far.   The Committee is of the opinion that fulfillment
of this condition should be pursued with all medical colleges both Govt. and private.  (Para 12.2)
            The Committee would also like to point out that there is also a need for encouraging the participation of more
and more medical teachers in CME Programmes, workshops, conferences, seminars etc. by making available the
required funds for this purpose.   MCI/Central Govt. should pursue this aspect also with the concerned authorities in the 
states. (Para 12.3)
The Committee finds that at present no incentive schemes are there to attract bright students towards teaching
and there is no such proposal also being contemplated by MCI.   In view of medical practice being more income
generating, the Committee is of the view that a  system of identifying and providing incentives  like earmarking funds
for research projects and job guarantee to students interested in teaching needs to be evolved on the pattern of various
schemes being implemented by the Govt. /AICTE/UGC for attracting young talent towards teaching.   The Committee
strongly feels that this is specially required for students of non-clinical and para-clinical subjects. (Para 12.4)
ASSESSMENT OF TEACHERS
The Committee is of the opinion that a scientific and professional mechanism for conducting such an assessment
in a fair/transparent and equitable manner needs to be evolved before taking any initiative in this direction. (Para 13.1)
PRIVATE PRACTICE
The Committee strongly feels that the teaching institutions should have non-practicing staff.   Private practice
wherever in vogue is largely affecting the quality of functioning of the Institute as well as proper patient care  because
teachers are more interested in private practice rather than in imparting teaching and research.   Keeping these factors  in
view, the  Committee emphasizes that it is very essential that the teachers are  well paid so as to compensate them for
their extra time and dedication to their profession.   The Committee has been given to understand that the varying rates
of NPA are prevalent in different State Govt. medical colleges which are less than Central Govt. rates.  The Committee
is of the firm view that  there should be a clear policy regarding private practice and non practicing allowance
throughout the country.   MCI/Central Govt. should take the initiative in this direction without any further delay. (Para
14.3)

PROBLEM OF SHORTAGE OF DOCTORS IN RURAL AREAS – REMEDIES THEREFOR
However, the Committee is not inclined to agree with this view mainly  because equal standards are required to
be maintained for both rural and urban areas.   One must not forget the fact that rural masses although generally illiterate
are gradually realizing the harm caused by unregistered doctors  practising in rural areas.   The Committee strongly feels
that creation of a class within a class will not be appropriate.  Such a distinction would be detrimental to the entire
medical profession. (Para 15.2)
The Committee is of the view that compulsion alone will not have the desired results.   The Committee,
therefore, recommends that alongwith compulsory rural service for a limited specified time, incentives like special
allowance, better housing and other allied facilities and special relaxation for admission to postgraduate courses are also
necessary for attracting young doctors towards rural areas. (Para 15.4)
The Committee would also like to emphasise that during internship period, PHC posting should be strictly
adhered to and monitored as it would motivate them towards rural service later on.  The Committee also feels that  there
should an orientation programme before doctors posted in rural areas join their duties. (Para 15.5)
There was also a need for developing proper infrastructure in PHCs.   The Committee is of the view that the
Department should pursue this issue with the State Govts.  The Committee understands the limitations of the Centre,
health being a state subject.   However, PHCs are being maintained through Central Grants.  Hence, the need for Central
monitoring about upkeep of PHCs is also there. (Para 15.6)
BRAIN DRAIN
   The Committee observes that there is another aspect of this problem.   Young pass-outs do not get to know all
the opportunities  which are available in the country.   There is a need for evolving a facility  on the pattern of
Recruitment agencies coming to the campuses of premier technical institutions for placements.   The Committee is of
the firm view that  remedial steps need to be taken for creating best job opportunities  thereby retaining our young talent
in the country.  The Committee also feels that if necessary, students may be asked to pay back in early installments,
wherever Government  funding is there.    Modalities in this regarding may be explored. (Para 16.1)
MUSHROOMING OF LABS/DIAGNOSTIC CENTRES
The Committee  however, observes that too much dependence of present-day doctors on technical know-how
has indirectly led to a  mushroom growth of Labs/Diagnostic Centres  conducting CT Scan and MRI and other
sophisticated tests all over the country.   The Committee has been given to understand that such centres are not generally
manned by qualified medical    personnel.   The doctors treat their patients on the basis of reports given by such centres
which sometimes give out incorrect interpretation of patient’s state of health.   The Committee strongly feels that there
is an urgent need for bringing out a comprehensive legislation to check  the mushroom growth of  such centres. (Para
17.1)
The Committee hopes that the procedural  formalities are completed at the earliest so that the proposed
legislation comes into force without any further delay. (Para 17.2)
INDIAN MEDICAL SERVICE
The Committee observes that although it is a welcome idea, there are some inherent problems which may arise
later on.   First is the difference between  the nature of jobs.   Medical Service is mostly research-oriented, teaching job
whereas IAS/IPS   is administration based service.   Secondly, it may not be  feasible as regional interest are not likely
to be served.   The Committee  would also like to point out that there were strong reservations about  transfer policy
being followed in the States.   Feedback which  the Committee received during its study-visits was that teachers, by and
large were not in favour of being transferred even within a  State.   Not only this,  Health being a State subject, it will be
very difficult to create such a cadre and its implementation would, therefore, be difficult for obvious reasons.   The
Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that this issue needs to be subjected to wide-scale discussions in the medical
fraternity before taking any decision. (Para 18.2)
THINK TANK
            The Committee is aware about the mandate of MCI and also the over-all involvement of the Central Govt. in

112th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/112threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:22]
regulating the standard of medical education in the country.   The Committee, however, is given to understand that the
required academic input for strengthening the quality of medical education is somewhat lacking.    The Committee,
therefore, strongly feels that there is a need for having a ‘Think Tank’ of eminent Professionals of both medical care and
medical education.   Such a body should, however, be solely involved in the work of assessment and analysis of medical
education  so as to provide various policies based on the academic knowledge and professional experience of its
members for its growth in the right direction. (Para 19.3)
POWERS OF UNIVERSITY/HEALTH UNIVERSITY
            The Committee is of the opinion that observations of local University  should invariably  be obtained before
permission being given for starting a new college/increasing the intake capacity/adding new courses.  Similarly, the
Committee finds no harm if University  representative is also part of the inspection team.   The Committee has been
informed that a Sub-Committee was constituted by the General Body of the Council to go into the establishment of
Health Universities.    The Sub-Committee has recommended discussion by a broader group in a workshop.  The
Committee hopes that the issues raised before the Committee with regard to Health Universities would also be taken
care of and a clear perception of the feasibility of Health University  would emerge as a result of discussion to be
undertaken by the broader Group. (Para 20.4)
ROLE OF NATIONAL LEVEL INSTITUTIONS
            The Committee feels that in  view of the weak financial position  of States, Central Govt. has to take an initiative
in this direction if referral character of All India Institutions is to be maintained.   The Committee is happy to note that
the Central Govt. has launched a pilot project this year for strengthening the diagnostic facilities of State hospitals.   The
Committee has been given to understand that this scheme is being implemented for the last two-three years.   States like
M.P., Haryana, Bihar, Tripura, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, UP, Kerala, Gujarat and J&K have already benefited from
this scheme during this period.   While appreciating the initiative, the Committee would like to emphasise that such
grants should also be strictly monitored by the Central Govt. so as to assess the  fulfillment of the objective of this
project. (Para 21.3)
The Committee strongly feels that Govt. institutions generating income should be allowed to retain such an
income in the maintenance and up-gradation of their institution.   If the whole income being placed at their disposal is
not possible, the Committee finds no harm in a specific percentage of income being retained by them.  This facility 
need not result in deduction of equivalent amount of funds  from their budget allocation. (Para 21.4)
The Committee therefore, feels that the Central Govt. should explore the possibility of establishing more
national level institutions. (Para 21.5)
The Committee observes that problem of faculty shortage is also being faced by premier institutions like AIIMS
and PGI due to one reason or other.   The Committee understands that besides     a number of posts lying vacant, quite a
few  professors are working on ad hoc basis.  Besides that, in the institutions   under the control of Central Govt.,
recruitment to all the four sub-cadres i.e. General Duty Medical Officers, Teaching Sub-cadre, Specialist Non-teaching
Sub-cadre and Public Health Sub-cadre  of Central Health services is  made  through UPSC.   The Committee has been
given to understand that this is a very long drawn affair.  Not only this, promotional avenues for all the sub-cadres of   
Central Health Services  are not of a satisfactory level.   The Committee hopes that after the  ongoing exercise of cadre
review is over,  things would improve for the better.   The Committee  is of the view that there is also a need for
evolving some system of co-ordination among the concerned authorities, i.e. UPSC, Directorate of Health Services/
Directorate of Medical Education and the concerned college. (Para 21.6)
JOINT CONSULTATIVE MACHINERY
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should pursue the setting up of such a mechanism
with all the State Govts/management of both national level and private institutions. (Para 22.1)
            The Committee is also of the view that a cell for receiving complaints and inviting suggestions from general
public and affected persons should be set up in the MCI to work as a watch-guard and also facilitate the functioning of
MCI. (Para 22.2)
PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY STUDENT COMMUNITY
            The Committee understands that a specific  time schedule for admission  to MBBS has been laid down by MCI.  

112th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/112threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:22]
The Committee finds that due to  delay in the admission procedure, training schedule gets disturbed and as a result,
instances are there that results are delayed.  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that MCI should strictly monitor
the adherence of  time schedule by medical  colleges all over the country.  (Para 23.2)
The Committee is of the view that the   development of coaching classes in some states in addition to the normal
colleges cannot be considered to be a healthy sign.   MCI should, therefore, undertake a review of this development in
concerned states and pursue the State Govts. to take required steps for  putting a check  to this unhealthy practice.    The
Committee feels that possibility of students of private medical colleges/younger institutions utilizing the library facility
available in Govt. medical colleges strictly on merit and without disturbing  students  of such colleges may be explored
in the larger interests of medical education.   The Committee is also of the view that a mechanism needs to be evolved 
for periodic review  of stipend payable to students and bringing about uniformity to the extent possible.   The
Committee would also like to point out that there is a need for standardization   of medical textbooks having a balanced
mixture of foreign and national components. (Para 23.3)
TEACHER-STUDENT RELATIONSHIP
The Committee feels that the situation should be  such that the teachers are able to share their experiences with
the students.   Teachers also  get an opportunity to evaluate the students better in such an environment.   The Committee
finds that  availability of video cassettes and internet access has vastly improved interactive learning wherever
available.   The Committee is of the view that steps should be taken for compulsory introduction of such hi-tech
facilities in all medical colleges  in the country. (Para 24.1)
MEDICAL RESEARCH
The Committee is of the considered view that steps should be taken  to step up research activities in the   Health
sector, with the active involvement of both public and private sector.   (Para 25.1)

PREFACE
 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf,  do hereby present this
Hundred Thirteenth Report of the Committee on Technical Education.
 
2.         Realising the importance of the subject of technical education, the Department related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Human Resource Development at its meeting held on the 21
st October, 1997, decided to examine the
subject with specific reference to the functioning of All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE).   To start with,
the Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Department of Education and prominent persons in the field of
technical education, including Secretaries of Technical Education and Higher Education of the States of Uttar Predesh,
Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Haryana.   However, subsequent to a couple of preliminary meetings, the Committee felt
that the subject needed to be examined in depth and, therefore, constitution of a Sub-Committee for the purpose would
be desirable.   Accordingly, an 11 member Sub-Committee on Technical Education with  Shri Rajnath Singh Surya,
M.P. was constituted.  Composition of the Sub-Committee is given at Annexure I.
 
3.         The   Sub-Committee was of the view that in order to properly assess the functioning of technical education in
the country, it would be necessary to undertake a few field visits to obtain first hand information.   The Sub-Committee,
accordingly, visited Bangalore, Hyderabad, Chennai, Port Blair, Kolkata, Pune, Mumbai, Goa, Uttaranchal,
Bhubaneswar and Lucknow and held discussions with representatives of technical institutions, universities  and State
Govts. and experts.   Finally, it also heard the officials of Department of Secondary Education and Higher Education 
and AICTE on the subject.
4.         The Sub-Committee  considered and adopted the Draft Report on the 6
th November, 2001.   The Committee at
its meeting held on 10th December, 2001 adopted the Report.

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
 1.1      Mark of civilization has always been seen through the progress of technical education.  It is instrumental in
making significant contributions to the     economic development of a country by way of manpower production and
relevant activities suiting to the needs of the industry and society and thereby adapting to the vast changes in the global
economy.
1.2       The beginning of formal technical education in India can be dated back to the mid 19
th Century. The major
policy initiatives in the pre-independence period included appointment of the Indian Universities Commission in 1902,
issue of the Indian Education Policy resolution in 1904 and the Governor General's Policy Statements of 1913 stressing
the importance of technical education, the establishment of IISc in Bangalore, Institute for Sugar, Textile and Leather
Technology in Kanpur, National College of Engineering (NCE), Bengal in 1905 and Industrial Schools in several

113th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/113threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:23]
provinces in early 1900s. Significant developments include setting up of the Technical Education Committee of the
Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) of 1943 and the Sargent report of 1944.  The All India Council of
Technical Education (AICTE) was set up in 1945 by Govt. of India   on the recommendation of CABE to stimulate,
coordinate and control the provision of education facilities which industrial development of the post-war period would
need. At that time, AICTE's mandate basically covered only programme in Engineering and Technology.
1.3       The growth of industries in the country just after independence also demanded the need for qualified
professionals in fields such as Business Management, Architecture, Hotel Management, Pharmacy, etc. Although the
diverse elements of Management, such as Commerce, Economics, Finance, Psychology and Industrial Sociology were
being taught for a long time, Management Education in a formal way commenced in India only in the fifties. The
Government of India decided in 1954 to set up a Board of Management Studies under AICTE to formulate standards
and promote management teaching institutions.   Although Architecture is covered under the Architects Act, 1972, for
better coordination of the professional course, Architecture Education was also placed under the purview of AICTE.
1.4       Hotel Management Education had a modest beginning with short programmes in Nutrition and Food Sciences
which started in late fifties. Four colleges were established in four major metropolitan cities between 1961 and 1964.
The National Council of Hotel Management and Catering Technology was set up in 1982-83 to which all the institutions
of Hotel Management run by the Government are affiliated.  Education in other professional fields such as Pharmacy,
Applied Arts and Crafts, etc. have also undergone similar development during the post independence period.
1.5       Technical Education programmes during the first three Five-Year Plans were devoted to expansion of technical
education to meet the growing demands for technical personnel at Diploma, Degree and Post Graduate levels. From the
Fourth Five Year Plan onwards, the emphasis was shifted to the improvement of quality and standards of technical
education.   This was done through implementation of the Quality Improvement Programme consisting of three major
components viz, (I) Provision for M.E./M. Tech. and Ph.D. programmes, (2) Establishment of curriculum design and
development cells and (3) Short-term training programmes. Meanwhile expansion of institutions and intake remained at
a low level in the Government, Private aided and University sectors. The policy shift during eighties towards permitting
involvement of private and voluntary organisations in setting up of Technical and Management Institutions on self
financing (non Govt. Grant) basis ushered in an era of unprecedented expansion of the Technical Education System, a
trend which has continued during Seventh, Eighth and Ninth  Five Year Plans.
II          PLANNED  DEVELOPMENT – ROLE OF AICTE
2.1       The long title of the All India Council for Technical Education  Act, 1987 reads as under:
            " An Act   to provide for the establishment of an All India Council for Technical Education with a view to the
proper planning and co-ordinated development of the technical education system throughout the country, the promotion
of qualitative improvement of such education in relation to planned quantitative growth and the regulation and proper
maintenance of norms and standards in the technical education system and for matters connected therewith."
As may be seen from the above,  proper planning and coordinated development of technical education throughout the
country and maintaining its quality in relation to planned quantitative growth is the mandate given to AICTE under its
Act.   The Committee, after undertaking extensive field visits and discussing the status of technical education in the
country with various experts in the field, is of the considered opinion that AICTE has failed to accomplish the mandate
given to it under the Act.   The Committee has found that there is no proper planning, proper assessment of technical
manpower, balanced development, coordinated approach, and quality maintenance regarding technical education.  
2.2       The  Committee has been given to understand that there is no uncontrolled growth in the field of technical
education in the country. The total intake capacity in AICTE approved Technical Institutions was only 6,40,737 in
August 2001 i.e. only 61 seats per lakh population which is still too  meagre as compared to international standards.   
As per a recent study, the number of Scientists and Technicians per 1000 population in India is only 3.5 as against 8.1 in
China, 29.5 in Brazil, 45.9 in Korea, 55 in USA, 76 in Israel, 86 in Germany and 110 in Japan.  While noting that
technical manpower in the country is less than the international standards, the Committee would like to point out that
there has been higher concentration of technical institutions in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka
and Maharashtra.  Such a development has given rise on the one hand to mushrooming growth of sub-standard technical
institutions in these States and on the other hand has led to lopsided development of technical education in the country.
2.3       The Committee observes that in the State of Tamil Nadu even though during the period 1997-98 to 2001-2002,
Govt. Engineering Colleges remained same (i.e. only 7),   the number of Self financing Institutions has gone up from 76

to 212.  In Karnataka, during the same period, the number of Govt. Engineering Colleges remained only 13 and Self
financing Colleges went up from 52 to 90.   In Andhra Pradesh, during the same period, whereas there was no increase
in the number of Govt. Engineering colleges (i.e.9), Self- financing Colleges  went up from 48 to 153.   Similarly, in
Maharashtra, Govt. Engineering Colleges during this period remained only 10, whereas number of Self-financing
Colleges increased from 102 to 141.      From the figures made available to it, the Committee is constrained to observe
that during the current year  there has been phenomenal increase in the number of engineering colleges in these States,
69 new colleges in Tamil Nadu, 26 in Karnataka, 58 in Andhra Pradesh and 13 in Maharashtra  have come up.  
Majority of institutions imparting training in other streams of technical education are also concentrated in these States
only.   In contrast, inspite of AICTE encouraging setting up technical institutions in other regions of the country, not
much progress seems to have been made.   Number of technical institutions has moved from 75 in 1999-2000 to 103 in
2001-2002 in entire northern region.    Position in North-Eastern region is very dismal with only one technical
institution coming up there.
2.4       The Committee in this context is of the view that for proper growth of technical education, focus of the
Department and AICTE should be on proper planning and coordinated development.   Concentration in certain pockets
has already given  rise to regional imbalance.   Therefore, focus should be on the country as a whole.    There is no
denying the fact that setting up of technical institutions  mainly depends upon the readiness/willingness of applicants
and their meeting the prescribed requirements and such initiatives have not been forthcoming particularly from N-E
region.   The Committee is of the view that the Department and AICTE should make all conceivable efforts for
encouraging both Govt. and private initiatives in setting up technical institutions in N-E region.
2.5       Another disturbing development as a result of concentration of technical institutions in a few states is that intake
capacity in different streams of technical institutions is not being utilised fully.   There are reports that a very large
number of seats remain vacant every year.    In most of the States, admission is made through a common entrance test
conducted by the State Govt.    On a specific query about the number of seats filled up during the last three years in the
States of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra, the Committee has been informed that data on
vacant seats is not made available to the Council.   Hence, it is not possible to analyse the details in this regard.  
Expressing its serious concern on such a situation, the Committee would like to point out that an objective analysis of
intake capacity and vacancy position in these States is very much required for checking mushroom growth of technical
institutions.
2.6       The Committee during its interaction with teaching community/experts/state authorities has been given to
understand that Computer Education and Information Technology are in much demand all over the country.    However,
students are not simply coming forward to take admission in traditional disciplines like Civil Engineering, Electrical
Engineering etc.   As a result, tremendous increase in the intake capacity in Computer Science and Information
Technology has been observed, particularly in self- financing institutions.   From the information made available to the
Committee, it is observed that maximum number of proposals received from different states by AICTE in 2000 for
starting new technical institutions in 2001-2002 and 2002-2003 pertain to MCA discipline.
2.7       The Committee  is of the view that  if a particular branch develops ignoring other branches of engineering,  a
situation  will come when we will have surplus manpower in that  branch and scarcity of manpower in other branches,
which are equally, if not, more important.   Such a situation would result in lop sided development of technical
education.
2.8       The Committee also observes that  with the ongoing recession in industry, demand for IT has shown a declining
trend.  Quite a few  sanctioned  seats in IT and Computer Science are remaining vacant.  The Committee, therefore, 
strongly feels that for a balanced development there should be a planned and coordinated development of every branch
of technical education. Courses in core areas like Civil/Electrical/Engineering etc are required to be continued and
updated by introducing specialization in keeping with the changing technological scenario.  The Committee is of the
opinion that while starting  Information  Technology and related courses, the requirements of various states need to be
kept in view so as to remove regional imbalances and disparity.
2.9       Committee's attention has also been drawn to a recent decision of the Apex Court (Bharatidasan University vs
AICTE and Others) which indicates that the Universities are not obliged to seek prior permission of AICTE to introduce
any technical courses in their departments and constituent colleges.   The Apex Court has further decided that the role of
AICTE with respect to Universities imparting technical education is recommendatory in nature.   The Committee has
been given to understand that this decision would lead to different norms for Universities and other Technical

institutions, different quality parameters and, therefore, different standards of education which would eventually result
in lopsided development of technical education.   The Committee feels that implications of the aforesaid judgement may
be studied in their entirety and remedial steps, if required, may be initiated.
2.10     The Committee is of the view that for planned development of technical education, accurate data regarding
demand and supply of technical manpower is necessary.  As per Section 10 (a) of AICTE Act, the  Council is
empowered to undertake survey in various fields of technical education, collect data on all related matters and make
forecast of the needed growth and development in technical education.  The Council has initiated a scheme for
collecting data and forecasting the demand and supply of technical manpower in the country through National Technical
Manpower Information System (NTMIS) which has established various nodal centres in the country.   The findings  of
NTMIS are made available to the user agencies including State Governments.    The Committee is, however,
constrained to note that at present NTMIS is not being effectively made use of  which  has  led to uncontrolled and
imbalanced growth of technical institutions, many of them being sub-standard.
2.11     It has been further informed that in April, 2000, AICTE had written to each State Government to prepare a
perspective plan for developing technical education in the state and for qualitative improvement of technical
education.    However, none of the States has given any perspective plan for development of technical education and the
Council has so far not been provided with any feedback from the State Govts. regarding the quality of technical
education, manpower requirement, employment opportunities etc.   The Committee is of the view that AICTE should
impress upon the State Govts. to furnish the required information at the earliest.
III        INCONSISTENCIES IN DIFFERENT PROCEDURES AND NORMS – REMEDIAL SUGGESTIONS
THEREFOR
3.1       During its field visits to a number of states and inter-actions with various functionaries, the Committee’s
attention was drawn to a number of inconsistencies in the policies of technical education in the country. The Committee
feels that unless  such lacunae are removed, a uniform policy and a balanced development  of technical education seem
to be a distant dream.
3.2       The Committee was informed that inspite of academic eligibility prescribed by AICTE for Degree and Diploma 
level courses, different States follow different academic eligibility criteria and there is no uniformity in the minimum
cut off percentage which creates confusion.  During  its study visit to Chennai, the Sub-Committee was informed that in
Tamil Nadu a minimum of 60% in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry individually and an aggregate of 70% at the
10+2 level is considered as entry criteria into the Professional courses.   However, in other States like Karnataka,
Kerala,  Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and UT of Pondicherry, they require a pass percentage of  50 % .   Due to this
differential eligibility criteria and other reasons, nearly 20,000 seats  in Tamil Nadu remained unfilled this year.  The
Committee strongly feels that there should be  uniformity at all India level for selection/eligibility criteria for admission
in different technical education courses as for as possible.   The Committee, therefore, recommends  that the
Department  and AICTE, alongwith State Governments, should work out common modalities in this regard.
3.3       The Committee's attention was drawn to the practice of different Universities in the country awarding degrees
under different nomenclature and resultant difficulty in establishing their equivalence.  A suggestion was, therefore,
made that AICTE should publish a list of such degrees with their equivalence to Degree in Engineering, PG Degree in
Engineering and Diploma in Engineering  which should be given wide publicity. 
3.4       The Committee observes that  various Technical Institutes/Boards  award degrees in technical education.  It
becomes difficult to establish the equivalence of such degrees for the purpose of admission and also for the purpose of
recruitment.  It was suggested that a State Council of Technical Education be set up in all the States of the country and
the Engineers who qualify in various examinations should get registered with SCTE for the purpose of admission to
Technical Institution for acquiring higher qualification as well as for the purpose of recruitment.  The practice which is
followed by Medical Council of India (MCI), Council of Architecture and Pharmacy Council of India may be made
applicable to the engineering graduates and Diploma holders.
3.5       On being asked about the feasibility of such initiative, AICTE clarified that it was not empowered to publish the
list of recognized degrees and its equivalence.  The UGC has the responsibility of publishing the list of recognized
degrees.  The equivalence is decided by the Association of Indian Universities for the purposes of higher education and
training whereas equivalence of degrees for employment is decided by the Board of Assessment under the Ministry of
HRD.  The Committee was given to understand that AICTE is referred to whenever recommendations are required in

respect of degrees which are covered under the ambit of technical education. 
3.6       The Committee has also been given to understand that  there is a lot of discrepancy in  AICTE norms and
standards in respect of educational qualifications  prescribed for various faculty positions in Engineering, Architecture,
Pharmacy and Polytechnics.  It was informed to the Committee that a Lecturer in the Engineering College needs 1st
class Bachelor’s Degree whereas a Lecturer in Pharmacy College & Architecture College needs 1st Class Master’s
Degree in the same pay scale.    The Committee is also surprised to note that discrepancy is also there in respect of
career advancement for the faculty members of Engineering College and Polytechnics.  Latest circular of AICTE
recommending the new Pay Scales states that a Lecturer requires eleven years service to get the selection grade without
improving any qualification, whereas a Lecturer in Diploma level institution requires a higher qualification, i.e. Master’s
Degree in Engineering in order to become eligible for selection grade.  In other words, teachers who are teaching the
diploma programme need higher qualifications as compared to teachers who are teaching the students in the Degree
Colleges.
3.7       The Committee feels that this is not a desirable position .  All such discrepancies need to be removed.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that AICTE should initiate a review of norms and standards laid down in respect of
educational qualifications prescribed for different categories of teachers of technical education and practice prevailing in
different institutions in the country.  Remedial action, wherever required, may  be taken at the earliest.
3.8       The Committee was also apprised that there was no uniformity in the admission schedules of different States. 
As a result,  students face difficulty while seeking admission in  different states.   Not only this,  at present different 
admission tests are conducted on different dates for admission to various technical institutions in the country.  
Sometimes,  it is observed that various  entrance test dates clash creating problems for the candidates and also putting  a
lot of financial burden on their parents.   In this context, it was suggested that a uniform/common entrance test may be
held for students seeking admission to different institutions on All India basis. Another suggestion made was that only
one combined entrance test for one stream of technical education may be conducted at All India level. 
3.9       The Committee, in this context, was informed that in the IIT, JEE, already IT-BHU and ISM-Dhanbad are
participating in addition to the IITs.  The ambit of IIT-JEE is being expanded from the year 2002 to include three other
premier national level institutions (NIFFI, IITT, IITM) that have been conducting their separate tests.  The Committee
was also  informed that the  Government is planning to hold an All India Engineering Entrance Examination (AIEEE)
for admission to undergraduate programmes in Engineering which will cover all Centrally funded technical institutions,
including Deemed Universities in the field of technical education.  All other institutions in the States that agree to
participate in this test may be included and gradually the Examination will be extended to all technical institutions in the
country.  The Committee hopes that  more and more States would participate in the Test and the Test may be conducted
at the earliest, preferably from 2002-2003 academic session.
3.10     As per Section 10 of AICTE Act, which defines Powers and Functions of the Council, there are varied functions
to be discharged by AICTE.   However, it has been observed that AICTE basically keeps itself engrossed  with the
function under section  10 (k) i.e. grant of approval for starting new technical institutions  and for introduction of new
courses or programmes in consultation with the agencies concerned.   However, other equally important functions like
undertaking surveys, coordinating for development of technical education in the country, promoting innovations,
research and development, formulating schemes for promoting technical education for women, handicapped and weaker
sections of society  have been neglected.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that AICTE should not restrict its
activities to granting approval or fixing norms, formulating guidelines for fees etc. but it should discharge its other
functions as well which are necessary for proper, coordinated and qualitative improvement of technical education in the
country as prescribed in the AICTE Act.   
3.11     The Sub-Committee, during its interaction with various experts, got an impression that AICTE has become
highly centralised and there is need for decentralisation of its powers among its regional offices.  The Committee also
feels that Regional Offices of AICTE  need to be strengthened by delegating more powers by the Head Office to avoid
delay and for effective and smooth functioning of the Regional Offices.  However, it would like to point out that
delegation of powers to the Regional Offices may be done only after sanction of permanent staff for the Council and its
Regional Offices.  The Committee would also like to point out that in view of tremendous increase in the number of
technical institutions in the Country  in the recent years, required strength of staff should be sanctioned for Regional
Offices. 
3.12     The Sub-Committee  during its field visits after interacting with different functionaries gathered  that the present

norm of 5 acres land in metropolitan cities and 25 acres in rural areas for establishing an Engineering College does not
seem to be practical.  In a Metropolitan City  like Mumbai it is very difficult to get the required land.  Even in rural
areas, due to land ceiling, difficulties were being faced.  It was suggested that the requirement of land at different places
should be realistic.  In metropolitan cities,  where land is too scarce, vertical construction could be thought of which
would require lesser land.  
3.13     It was also pointed out that fixed deposit of Rs. 50 lakhs remains blocked which can neither be used by
promoters nor by AICTE.  A suggestion was, accordingly, made that security deposit taken from institutions should be
refunded in case  of those institutions which have shifted to their own buildings so that the amount could be utilised for
further development of these institutions. Another suggestion made was that there should be option for either having a
fixed deposit or bank guarantee. 
3.14     The AICTE has,  however, clarified that the concept behind the charging of security deposit from an institution
is to ensure safeguarding of interests of faculty and students during the initial period and it is refunded after 10 years
when the institution is stabilised.   It has no connection with the rented or own building.   Bank guarantee in place of
security deposit may not serve the purpose of security deposit, the Council further clarified.
3.15     The Committee was also given to understand that proposal was also there to modify the norm of  student-teacher
ratio from 10:1 to 15:1.   Another relaxation  being proposed was that required faculty can be built up during the first
four years of institution being established.  Some percentage of visiting faculty  is also going to be  permitted.  In view
of the acute shortage of Ph.Ds  in the country,   relaxation of such qualification for being eligible for appointment as 
Reader/Professor in certain streams of technical education is also proposed.   The Committee, while not disputing the
justification  for such relaxation, would like to emphasise that standard of technical education should be maintained at
all costs.
3.16     The Committee notes that a Core Committee under the Chairmanship of the Special Secretary, Ministry of
Human Resource Development has been set up for modification of norms and standards, including requirement of land
and fixed deposit for technical institutions.  The Committee hopes that the Core Committee will finalise its Report at the
earliest and take a realistic and practical approach in the matter.
3.17     During its study visits, the Committee was given to understand that a number of  schemes, such as
Modernisation and Removal of Obsolescence (MODROB), Research and Development (R&D), Thrust Area
Programme in Technical Education (TAPTEC) etc.  operate under AICTE through which financial assistance is
provided to technical institutions.   However,  many of the Govt. as well as self-financing institutions were  unaware of
such schemes and consequently failed  to reap the benefits of such schemes.  On a specific query, the Council clarified
that all possible attempts to give publicity to various Schemes of Staff Development,  Institutional Development,
Research and Development through national and local newspapers,  AICTE  website and also through individual
correspondence with the States, Universities and institutions are being made.  Every year, more than 40 to 50 crores of
rupees are being spent under these schemes.   The Committee feels that AICTE should prepare a composite list of
financial assistance schemes under separate heads such as Schemes for staff Development, Institutional Development,
Research and Development and send it to various Institution directly.   In that way, it would give wider publicity to such
schemes than what is practised now.
3.18     The Committee   has been given to understand that  NRI quota in various institutions is very often misused
which gives a free hand to the management to charge exorbitant fees from students.   However, in the Government
Institutions where it is strictly adhered to, the seats remaining vacant as a result of non-availability of candidates under
this category, it comes as a discouragement. In this context, it was suggested that in case of NRI quota not being filled
up, there should be provision to convert it into `Payment Seat'.   AICTE in this respect clarified that as per Unnikrishnan
judgement (1993), the  Supreme Court has fixed a quota for NRIs to an extent of 5% of the total intake from amongst
the seats in payment seat category.   This is uniform throughout the country.   However, a Bench of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court considered applications of private managements in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka  and Tamil
Nadu to enhance NRI quota from 5%  to 15% as is prevalent in Medical Colleges.   The Bench has ordered that  the
respective State Governments  may decide whether 15% NRIs could be permitted under the NRI quota.
3.19     In regard to the misuse of seats under NRI quota, the AICTE has stated that the provision of NRI seats has been
long misinterpreted by  private institutions and universities.  The Council  has now clarified vide its circular dated 3
rd
October, 2001 that unfilled seats under NRI quota shall automatically revert to payment seat category.   The AICTE has
