Orissa respectively may be  the reason for non-release of funds to them under this scheme.   The Committee, however,
fails to understand the reasons for annual release of funds to UP inspite  of unspent balance of Rs. 57.10 lakhs lying
with the state.    The Committee is constrained to observe that no quarterly progress report is being sent by  Bihar.    The
Committee recommends that submission of regular quarterly reports may be insisted from all states in order to
effectively monitor the scheme.    The Committee would also emphasise that matter of unspent balance should be
vigorously  pursued with the concerned states. (Para 5.3)
            The Committee, despite various training and sanitization programmes for teachers, is deeply perturbed over the
general attitude and behaviour of teachers towards the students in recent times.     It regrets to note that there is a general
erosion in the devotion and dedication  of teachers towards their duties as compared in the past.    The noble bond of
teacher and the taught is entirely missing and commercialisation and parochialism have now taken its place.   The
Committee feels that production of good teachers is a great challenge before the country.   Good teachers are the makers
of the country.    All concerned will have to put their heads together to face this challenge otherwise the future of the
country will not be so bright as   hoped. (Para 5.6)
VI        NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT TO PRIMARY EDUCATION (MID-
DAY MEAL SCHEME)
            The Committee observes that situation is highly discouraging and disappointing in Bihar.  Out of the 57 districts
of undivided Bihar, in 15 districts there has been no lifting of food grains since 1998-99, in 26 districts no food grain
has been allocated since 1999-2000.  In the remaining districts also, lifting of food grains has been far below the
allocated  food grains. What is a cause of serious concern is that even these lifting figures furnished by the State Govt.
do not match with the off take figures furnished by the FCI.  The Committee finds that in Orissa, a declining trend is
there in the figures of food grains lifted since 1998-99.  In UP, situation is worse as during 2000-2001, against an
allocation of 36,51,135 MTs only 8,19,218 MTs were lifted.  Similar position is observed in MP also. The Committee
has been given to understand that there is no provision of staff for implementation of Scheme both at Central and state
levels with the result that there is nobody to take responsibility for sending reports from districts to states and states to
Centre.  The Committee takes a serious view of this. The Committee is also of the opinion that provision of food grains
instead of cooked meals defeats the very purpose of the scheme. (Para 6.3)
            The Committee notes that a Sub-group was constituted under the aegis of Working Group on Elementary
Education and Literacy for formulation of Tenth Plan and  it  has suggested major changes in the scheme.  The
Committee would, however, like to express its reservations about the recommendation of the Sub-group with regard to
expansion of the programme to cover the children studying in Alternative Schools.  The Committee is of the view that
the Mid-day Meal Scheme should be restricted to the formal schools for the time being.  Steps should be  taken to
effectively implement this scheme.  Efforts should also be made to provide cooked meal only under this programme. 
The Committee recommends that the changes suggested by the Sub-Group and the shortcomings/constraints noticed by
this Committee  be given due weightage when modifications under Tenth Plan are made.   The State Governments/UT
Administrations also need to be taken into confidence before revision of the Scheme. (Para 6.4)
VII       DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME (DPEP)
            The Committee was given to understand that the norms prescribed by the World Bank with regard to school
buildings are not flexible. The committee desires that it  may be reviewed. (Para 7.1)
            The Committee is not  convinced by the reply of the Department.  The Committee notes that as mentioned in the
CAG Report  records relating to the Programme maintained in the State Project Offices, District Project Offices of the
selected districts and Department of Education were test checked by Audit to assess the extent to which the programme
objectives were  achieved.  In addition, ORG-Centre for Social Research conducted a survey of 54 districts, 1081
villages, 280 Census Enumeration Blocks(CEB), 22 SCERTs, 150 BRCs, 153 CRCs, 1361 schools  across 14 States.

both quantitative (primary survey using pre-tested beneficiary schedules) and qualitative (in-depth interview with
programme functionaries) techniques. The Committee is of the opinion that observations of CAG need to be looked into

VIII     JANSHALA PROGRAMME
            The Committee is of the view that the  Scheme is in the initial stages of implementation and needs more time to
get the actual feedback about the scheme.  The Committee, however,  hopes that the observations made in the report of
the Bodh Shiksha Samiti will  help the Government in formulating its future strategy in regard to the Scheme.  (Para
8.3)
            As may be seen from the above, expenditure on the project in all the States is far from satisfactory.   The
Committee observes that implementation of the Scheme  in all the above States is very slow and urgent remedial
measures need to be taken by the Department as the scheme is scheduled to run for only 18 months more i.e. upto
March, 2003. (Para 8.4)
 
IX        MERGER OF SCHEMES:
            The Committee welcomes the initiative taken in this regard,  The Committee, however, recommends that all the
inherent flaws of the earlier schemes should not be reflected in the revised new schemes after merger of these
schemes            Therefore, the Committee  is of the view that wide ranging consultations  should be held with the State
Govts., who are the implementing authority before  arriving at a final decision. (Para 9.2)
X         SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN
            The Committee recommends that provision for girls hostels especially in far flung areas should be made one of
the components  of SSA before it is implemented. (Para 10.5)
XI        GIRLS' EDUCATION
The Committee hopes that all these measures will help in promoting girl education, which is still elusive. (Para
11.5)
XII      EDUCATION OF SC/ST CHILDREN
            The Committee notes the ambitious interventions of the Government which have now become the part of Sarva
Shiksha Abhiyan, Since the SSA is still in initial stage of its implementation, the Committee can only hope that these
efforts will yield the desired result.  However, the Committee feels and recommends accordingly that such
blocks/districts where the tribal women literacy (as in the case of Orissa where it is merely 1.8 per cent) is much below
should be identified and given special attention in the implementation  of the scheme. (Para 12.5)

CHAPTER-I

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY
GOVERNEMNT

RECOMMENDATION

4.8 To start with, the Committee suggests that there is a need to optimize all existing and available
physical facilities to control overcrowding. The Committee would emphasise the necessity for
opening more counters and creating space for OPD patients. Since overcrowding also results वीणा
lack of guidance and direction to patients and a patient friendly handling system, there is a need for
constant review of arrangements as to how for appropriate information and guidance are available to
patients and their relatives visiting the hospitals. In particular, constant vigilance is needed for a better
interface between clerical staff and patients visiting the hospitals.

ACTION TAKEN

4.8 The Ministry agrees with the observations. Hospitals are taking steps to ensure that proper
guidance and directions are given to patients, further that efforts are made for rationalizing the use of
space.

RECOMMENDATION

4.10 Another solution in this connection, according to the Committee, could be setting up of the OPDs
away from the main wing of the hospital, preferably in the same complex, with self-contained
essential test/diagnostic facilities to divert the patients seeking OPD attention from those needing
detailed investigation and treatment. The Committee is happy to learn that the AIIMS is already in the
process of setting up such OPD, away from the main hospital area, which would be provided essential
facilities for basic pathological tests required for primary care. Such OPDs, the Committee feels,
would not only reduce the congestion in the main hospital, but it would also release some working
space for physicians, etc.

ACTION TAKEN

4.10 The suggestion to set up OPDs away from the main wing of the hospitals will be kept in view
while considering the establishment of new OPDs as also the need for providing essential facilities
within easy reach to provide basic care quickly.

RECOMMENDATION

4.11 The Committee feels that conscious and urgent steps for reducing the waiting time and promoting
easily accessible and cheaper testing facilities would go a long way to mitigate, if not eliminate,
overcrowding in the hospitals. Increased waiting time, in the Committee’s opinion, is a direct
manifestation of overcrowding and in almost all the hospitals, the Committee found, that the waiting
period was very long, ranging from one hour to three hours.

ACTION TAKEN

4.11 The Ministry agrees with the observations. Efforts are being made to reduce waiting time and
to facilitate movement of patients.
RECOMMENDATION

4.12 The Committee agrees that it may be difficult to lay down a specific waiting time applicable to all
facilities and disciplines but it is not impossible for each hospital to evolve its own internal norms and
standards for each Department to reduce the waiting time to the maximum extent possible, after

2


studying the pattern of patients. An overall goal in each hospital could be to strive to reach a situation
where the patient should not have to be away from home for more than half a day in order to get OPD
treatment. From that objective in view, each hospital should work out how best and how soon this can
be achieved progressively over a fixed period of time. In fact, one half of a day at OPD is considered
adequate keeping in view the fact that patients will also have to spend extra travel and transactional
time in reaching the hospital and returning home. Alternatively, provision of two shift OPD may also
be considered.

ACTION TAKEN

4.12 Safdarjung Hospital has brought the registration time forward by half an hour i.e. instead of 9.00
a.m., it has been made 8.30 a.m; the OPD ends at 11.30 a.m. instead of 11.00 am. Thus, the
registration time has been increased by an hour. The position is reviewed by the hospital authorities
periodically.

RECOMMENDATION

4.13 With the growth of technology, more and more sophisticated tests would be needed to support
diagnosis and therapy and large investments are inevitable, particularly in prestigious hospitals. This is
partly the result of patient expectations from any premier institute where they expect and are
encouraged to expect better and more state of the art diagnostic and curative procedures. Such
procedures are not only high-tech but generally tend to be cost-escalating. In this context, it is the
duty of the leaders in the profession, especially those heading the Departments, to examine and assess,
through proper audit, whether technological procedures adopted are, in every case, necessary and
relevant to patients’ needs in our country. This judgement can be made only by the leaders within the
medical community itself, who can be relied upon to look into all aspects of prevalence and incidence
of diseases, its proximate determinants and the socio-economic background of patients. In many cases
of ordinary ailments, Indian Systems of Medicine could be equally effective, if not more, and may be
considered for expansion.

ACTION TAKEN
4.13. Noted for necessary action.
RECOMMENDATION

11. The Committee found that blood banks in most of the Central Government hospitals had no
moder facilities and equipments commensurate with the nature of services required today. In view of
the menace of killer disease like AIDS spreading through blood transfusion, the Committee
emphasises the need for providing adequate facilities for carrying out HIV tests in the Blood Banks of
each hospital immediately. It recommends that the Department should provide facilities for modern
Blood Banks in each hospital where fractionation of blood into its different components can be done
and transfusion of blood is made foolproof.

ACTION TAKEN

11. The Ministry has laid down standards for staff and standards for space for Blood Banks. The
essential basic equipment which are needed for the smooth functioning of the Bank has also been laid
down. The rules have been framed for grant of licence to process blood components from whole
human blood. Human blood components are prepared by the Bank as a part of the blood services.
Testing facilities for blood grouping, hepatitis, HIV, Malaria, etc. are available in the Blood Banks of
Central Government hospitals. The Blood Banks are inspected by Experts before renewal of licence.


The deficiencies pointed out are brought to the notice of hospital authorities for rectification. The
deficiencies ‘pointed out by the experts are removed by the hospitals.

From the 1* of June, 2001, screening for Hepatitis C has been mandatory for all Blood Banks
in the country and HCV Test Kits are being provided to all government and charitable blood banks.
Component Separation Units, where one unit of whole blood is separated into various components and
then can be used by a number of patients has been provided to AIIMS, Red Cross Blood Bank, GTB
Hospital and Armed Forces Transfusion Centre in Delhi.

RECOMMENDATION

13. An increasing number of cases of suspected ‘AIDS’ are being reported from various parts of the
country, particularly in metropolitan and major cities. There is, however, not enough awareness
among the people about this deadly disease. The Central Government hospitals, which are supposed
to be role models in such campaigns, do not appear to be serious about the problem.

13.1 The Committee, therefore, feels that the Central Government hospitals should at least now rise to
the occasion, keeping in view the gravity of the situation and launch massive campaigns against the
spread of this disease. These hospitals could bring out posters, leaf-lets, etc. and display them
conspicuously in the hospital premises for the benefit of the people.

ACTION TAKEN

(13 & 13.1). The Government has initiated a massive awareness campaign on Prevention and Control
of HIV/AIDS in the country using electronic, print and folk media. Each year Family Health
Awareness Campaign is being conducted which aims to generate awareness amongst rural and urban
slum populations on sexually transmitted infections including HIV/AIDS. The last round of Family
Health Awareness Campaign was held during the period April-June 2001 and the next round is
envisaged in the month of February, 2002. With the objective to equip the medical and para-medical
personnel in the management of HIV/AIDS cases in the hospital, a comprehensive training programme
is being implemented. The training programme also includes Central Government hospitals. State
AIDS Control Societies are providing IEC material to hospitals for display at prominent places in the
hospital.

RECOMMENDATION

15. Enough opportunities, the Committee feels, are not being made available to doctors to keep track
of the latest advancements in the medical sciences/technology, which is a fast developing discipline.
The Committee is of the opinion that doctors/ professors should be given adequate opportunities for
refreshing and advancing their knowledge and skill by interacting with their counterparts in advanced
countries. The Committee, therefore, feels that Government should take immediate steps for
providing adequate opportunities for this to doctors and faculty members. The
technicians/paramedical staff handling various sophisticated and modern medical equipments should
also be provided the required training with a view to imparting efficiency and precision in their work.

ACTION TAKEN

15. The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has been organizing training courses at various places in
India where doctors are exposed to the latest developments on the subject. The training is imparted in
identified training institutions spread over various parts of the country. Doctors are also sent on
WHO/Colombo Plan, Common-Wealth Fellowships etc. for training abroad. Medical Council of India
also conducts continuing medical education as also other agencies like Medical Colleges, National
Board of Examination, etc.


The technicians/para-medical staff are acquainted with the working of the equipment under the
supervision of the agency installing/servicing the same. In service training programme is being
conducted at Safdarjung Hospital in the area of CSSD, OT, Medical Records, Rehabilitation and STD.
RECOMMENDATION

18. The practice of Doctors/professors going on deputation, after having had costly and advance
training at government cost and coming back for taking promotion, came to the notice of the
Committee. The Committee deprecates the idea of doctors/ professors for having best of both the
worlds, as it is against the very ethics of medical profession. It, therefore, recommends that the
Department should take a serious view in these cases and discourage such practices.

ACTION TAKEN

18. This has been noted for necessary action. The suggestion will be kept in view while considering
extension of deputation of officers of CHS.

RECOMMENDATION

21. CGHS beneficiaries being located mostly in metropolitan cities, particularly in Delhi, where a
number of Central Government Hospitals are functioning, deserve a separate wing for them and their
dependants. The Committee found that CGHS wing, provided in the hospitals particularly in the
Safdarjung and Dr. RML Hospitals, are not functioning satisfactorily. It was complained to the
Committee that CGHS beneficiaries do not get adequate attention and the facilities for which they are
entitled to, even after they come duly referred by their dispensaries. A patient, on an average, has to
wait nearly two to four hours for getting examined by the specialists. This waiting period, the
Committee notes, is more than that in case of the OPD patients. The Committee is of the view that
procedure for consultation/tests for the CGHS beneficiaries, duly referred by their dispensaries, needs
to be reviewed and streamlined by the respective hospitals so as to provide them quick and efficient
services.

ACTION TAKEN

21. There are 87 Allopathic dispensaries functioning under the CGHS, Delhi/New Delhi which
provides OPD treatment to the CGHS beneficiaries and some of them also provide laboratory facilities
to the CGHS beneficiaries. Two or three dispensaries are attached to such dispensaries where
Laboratory facilities are available. Some of the laboratories have been upgraded by providing modern
testing equipments. Further few nodal centers have also been set up in the dispensaries to provide
specialist consultations services to the CGHS beneficiaries by attaching two or three nearby

ACTION TAKEN

(10.3 to 10.4).

Since its inception, the Institute has been continuously developing and evolving curricular strategies
for undergraduate teaching programme, some of which have served a role model for the rest of the
country. Some of the important changes introduced in the curriculum at the Institute which are either
followed by other universities or under active consideration of the Medical Council of India are as
follows

Earlier the duration of the first professional phase of MBBS _ course in all medical colleges used to
be two years. In AIIMS, the course was successfully reduced to one and a half years without
compromising with the quality of teaching. The Medical Council of India followed this example and
introduced the same duration in all medical colleges. Subsequently, the Institute further reduced the
first professional phase to one year. This has been incorporated in the recommendations made by the
Medical Council of India.

Right from the first batch of AITMS undergraduate in 1961, the rural posting of interns has been one
fourth of the total internship period. Most other Medical colleges introduced this pattern subsequently

26


\

AIIMS has been a leader in designing objective assessment procedures especially in the practical and
clinical assessment. Several medical colleges are in the process of following these modalities of
assessment.

The contribution made by the AIIMS in the undergraduate education has reached beyond the country.
AIIMS has played a singular role in developing the curriculum for a new college at B.P. Koirala
Institute of Health Sciences at Nepal.

One of the important objects of the Institute is also to produce teachers for medical colleges. It is well
known that a good doctor/researcher does not necessarily makes.a good teacher. Teaching requires
skills in communication and an understanding of learning needs and behaviour of the students. In
medical colleges in our country, the teachers are expected primarily to teach the undergraduate
students. It is imperative that the future teachers (viz. junior residents, senior residents, pool officers)
are given pedagogic experience through teaching of MBBS students. This was historically also an
important reason for initiating undergraduate programme at AIIMS.

Over the years AIIMS has developed excellent facilities and infrastructure for providing high quality
of undergraduate training. In the interest of evolving new patterns of medical education for the
country through experimentation in undergraduate curriculum (which is only possible at AIIMS
because of its unique statutory status), and for ensuring a high order of teaching skills for future

coordination with other hospitals for management and referral of patients. A proper referral system of
treatment and follow-up of both regular and casualty patients exists between Safdarjung Hospital and
AIIMS. The Committee is, however, constrained to point-out that these facilities are only on
paper. Instances of precious lives being lost due to some vital equipment being non-functional
continue to occur on a regular basis. Reality is that only those patients whose attendants can
manage some reference at the right place get the best medicare. The Committee is of the view
that such control rooms and coordination between the hospitals should be activated. Surprise
inspections by higher authorities can prove to be effective in this matter.

RECOMMENDATION

10. The Committee noted that the equipments available in different hospitals have not been properly
maintained. Repairs are not done promptly when they go out of order. The Committee feels that the
maintenance of equipments is very crucial as the patients face lots of problems if the equipments are
not repaired in time. They are fleeced by private labs/diagnostic clinics which charge exorbitant
amounts even for routine and normal tests. It has come to the notice of the Committee that patients are
referred to private labs/diagnostic centers for various tests on the pretext of equipments in the hospitals
being out of order and private diagnostic centers are allowed to import medical equipments at
concessional rates. The Committee, therefore, recommends that immediate steps be taken for
providing necessary infrastructure for getting the medical equipments repaired in a reasonable time.

ACTION TAKEN

10. The equipments used in the hospitals are very sophisticated and have often been imported. These
electronic equipments are got serviced/repaired by the authorized service engineers by entering into
annual service contract. The Ministry does not feel that it would be advantageous to create an
independent infrastructure to repair medical equipments as technology is advancing day by day and
the infrastructure created may become outdated. It will also be difficult to ensure accountability for
losses or pilferage or misuse. The present system of entering into annual repair/maintenance contract
ensures departmental responsibility. New equipment is purchased keeping in mind after sale service
as an important constituting factor in deciding the selection.

The hospital have also been asked to study the down time of expensive equipment and a variety of
measures have been suggested on the use of the equipment to see that it is used and maintained
efficiently.

Department of Electronics have in the meantime set up service centers and plan to expand the
activities of these centers.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is not inclined to agree with the contention of the Department that the
present system of entering into annual repair/maintenance contract ensures Departmental
responsibility. Reports coptinue to come about there being instances of equipments not being
maintained/repaired timely or sophisticated equipments lying unutilised. | The Committee
strongly feels that there is an urgent need for evolving an affective monitoring mechanism to
check such instances both at the hospital level and in the Department. Appropriate action in
this regard should be taken at the earliest.

39


RECOMMENDATION

12. The Committee is disappointed over the fact that the functioning of the family welfare units, in
almost all the hospitals visited by it, was very poor. For example, in PGIMER only five vasectomies
were done against 417 tubectomies in the year 1994 indicating the gender bias of the programme.
While 1156 conventional contraceptives were distributed, there was not even a single case of insertion
of uterine devices during this period. Position prevailing in other hospitals is more or less the same. It
was found that the infrastructure provided for the purpose was not being put to optimum use. Near
total lack of motivation and dedication in the staff was also noticed. The Committee is surprised to
note the indifferent and nonchalant attitude of the Ministry in regard to such a high priority aspect of
our social-economic development. It, therefore, recommends that family welfare units provided in the
Central Government hospitals be strengthened and activated immediately. More emphasis should be
laid on vasectomy as family welfare device and suitable incentive/motivations be provided.

ACTION TAKEN

12. Department of Family Welfare has informed that for implementation of the Family Welfare
Activities in the Central Sector Hospitals, the Department has sanctioned Post Partum Centres, Urban
Family Welfare Centres and sterilization beds.

Department of Family Welfare is making efforts to utilize the present infrastructure effectively and
efficiently. In this regard some of the Post Partum Centres in Central Government hospitals requiring
certain equipments were strengthened by supplying Operation Theatre and Labour Room equipments.
The performance of Family Welfare activities are being monitored through quarterly progress reports,
regional review meeting at the central level and through monthly co-ordination committee meetings
under the Chairmanship of Medical Superintendent at the hospital level. The Central/State
Government representatives also participate in the meetings. Government of India regularly request
the States/UT Government to convene these meetings and give feed back to Ministry of Health &
Family Welfare. Besides review of the performance, these meetings act as catalyst to address to the
difficulties of the staff.

Further in order to strengthen the Family Welfare activities, the Department has entrusted the National
Institute of Health & Family Welfare and Population Research Centres for carrying out an evaluation
study of the Post Partum Centre and Sterilization Beds Scheme respectively during 2001-02.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee has been informed that no report has been finalized yet by the National
Institute of Health and Family Welfare. Reason being that out of 1562 Post Partum Centres, only 265
Post Partum Centres have furnished the filled in questionnaire to National Institute of Health and
Family Welfare. Out of these 265 Centres, in-depth study of 180 Centres were planned by National
Institute of Health and Family Welfare during February, 2002. Similarly, out of Seventeen Population
Research Centres entrusted to conduct the concurrent evaluation of Sterlization Bed Scheme, only
three Centres have completed their work. The Committee is not happy with the slow pace of
progress. This shows the importance given to family planning activities by the very Centres
which have been set up with the purpose of population control. The Committee is of the firm
view that all efforts should be made for completing these studies at the earliest so that remedial
measures can be taken.

40


RECOMMENDATION

14.1 Epilepsy, in our country, is mostly being treated in Neurological centers of the major hospitals.
The facilities available for treating epilepsy patients in these hospitals, including AIIMS, are
insufficient and unorganized. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is an imperative need to
establish an Epilepsy Centre, to begin with, in New Delhi, which should aim at developing a holistic
approach for treatment of epileptic patients. The Centre should endeavour evolving a national policy
and also promoting research in the indigenous system of medicine to provide best medical care to the
epileptic patients. Once the Centre is developed, similar centers, either separate or branches thereof,
should be set up in other parts of the country.

ACTION TAKEN

14.1 The. management of epilepsy patients is being carried out at Dr. RML Hospital, Safdarjung
Hospital, Lady Hardinge Medical College and Associated Hospitals under Central Government. It is
also felt that a community care approach needs to be adopted for covering peripheral areas.

A Technical Committee headed by DGHS examined this issue and gave its report in September, 1996
which is reproduced below:-

“Epilepsy clinics would be set up in the bigger hospitals like Safdarjung, Dr. R.M.L., Lok Nayak
Jaiprakash, Guru Teg Bahadur and Deen Dayal Upadhayay Hospitals with a holistic approach to
treatment emphasizing on health education, and awareness for the disease.

Regional Centres should be established as per the need and demand. At present there is no need of an
autonomous institution. However, research activity should be emphasized and undertaken at the
various tertiary level institutions.”

The recommendations were circulated for comments of Govt. of Delhi, Ministry of Labour, Railways,
MCD and Central Government hospitals before taking a final view in the matter.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee notes that a Technical Committee headed by DGHS had given specific
recommendations with regard to treatment facilities of epilepsy patients in its Report submitted
in September, 1996. The Committee is, however, surprised to find that no follow-up actio:
seems to have been taken as comments from the concerned authorities are still awaited. The
Committee is of the opinion that the Department should vigorously pursue this issue so that the
requisite action is taken at the earliest.

RECOMMENDATION

16. The Committee found that cleanliness and hygiene in various hospitals are very poor. Choked
sewage and leaking water pipes were seen in some hospitals. Toilets were very dirty and stinking.
Garbage and disposed cotton, etc. were found lying uncovered. The Committee is deeply concerned at
such state of affairs as stagnated water and open garbage become breeding grounds for various
organisms. The Committee feels that hospital authorities are not paying adequate attention to this
aspect and recommends that immediate steps be taken to keep the hospitals clean and hygienic.

41


ACTION TAKEN

16. Senior level Medical Officers have been made responsible for oversecing the cleanliness of
hospital premises. The premises have been divided into zones and responsibility assigned to Sanitary
Inspectors for the upkeep of the premises and laboratories. Hospitals arrange cleanliness drives
periodically. Incinerators are being used for the disposal of biological waste like dead foetus, etc. and
other infected waste including physical material like syringes, needles, bottles etc. As regards non-
infected, non-hazardous waste, the NDMC/local bodies are responsible for its collection and disposal.
The hospital authorities have been liaising with local bodies for disposal of this waste. The matter is
also being taken up in the Ministry of Environment and Forests to bring the problem into focus and
give a direction to the hospitals, local bodies and other engaged in the task of hospital waste
management. Ministry of Labour has permitted for relaxation of rule for engaging private contractual
labour for sanitation work of the hospital, particularly for three Central Government hospitals, i.e. Dr.
RML Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and Lady Hardinge Medical College & Associated Hospitals for
the period upto February, 2002. The proposal for Safdarjung Hospital for engaging contractual labour
for sanitation works in the selected places of the hospital is under consideration.

Adequate attention is being paid by LHMC for the management of hospital waste. The cleanliness
and hygiene of the hospital is being improved and wherever necessary renovation of toilets has been
undertaken. Under the Comprehensive Redevelopment Plan, proposal for latest amenities for
sewerage, water supply and management of hospital waste have been incorporated.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee feels that even though some steps have been taken, a lot more needs to be
done _ in the area of cleanliness and hygiene in the hospitals. The action taken is not visible in
reality. There is absolute lack of coordination between the local bodies and hospital authorities
in removing waste from the hospitals. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that there is need
for regular and proper interaction between the two authorities. |The Committee is also of the
view that M/o Environment and Forests has a special role to play in waste management. The
Committee desires that the Department should take up the issue of waste management
vigorously.

The Committee finds that the Ministry of Labour has permitted for relaxation of rule for
engaging private contractual labour for sanitation work of Dr. R.M.L. Hospital, Safdarjung
Hospital and Lady Hardinge Medical College and Associated Hospitals for the period upto
February,2002. | The Committee has been given to understand that contract labourers are
engaged for sanitation work in Safdarjung Hospital and the experience is found to be
satisfactory. Similar proposal for Dr. RML Hospital and LHMC is under process. The
Committee hopes that Ministry of Labour has extended the permission for relaxation of rulz
beyond February, 2002.

RECOMMENDATION

16.1 The CPWD is responsible for the maintenance of hospital building, including operation
theatres and various wards. The Committee noticed that the upkeep and maintenance of hospital
buildings was very poor which needed urgent renovations. Some buildings, particularly in Safdarjung
Hospital, Dr. RML Hospital and Lady Hardinge Medical College and Associated hospitals were found
to be in an uninhabitable condition. When asked about the reasons, the Committee was informed that
due to absence of any check or control by the hospital Administration, the CPWD was not prompt.in
attending to the complaints. It was, therefore, argued, that either the hospitals should have their own
engineering departments or the CPWD units posted in the hospitals be brought under the
administrative control of the respective Medical Superintendents to expedite and improve the
maintenance work. The Committee feels that these suggestions deserve serious consideration by the

42


Department. The Department may appoint a Committee of experts to examine the present state of
buildings and suggest suitable measures.

ACTION TAKEN

16.1 The Ministry had taken up the matter with the Ministry of Urban Affairs and Employment for
transferring to Medical Superintendents the administrative control of CPWD Units posted in the
hospitals and responsible for the maintenance of the hospital buildings. The CPWD informed that
three separate divisions have been created to cater to the requirement of the Central Government
Hospitals exclusively. Besides this, the Executive Engineers have been regularly attending the
meeting called by the Medical Superintendents and the works are carried out as per the requirement.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee finds that the Ministry of Urban Affairs and Employment seems to have
reservation on the issue of transfer of administrative control of CPWD units posted in the
hospitals to the Medical Superintendents. The Committee is of the strong opinion that for a
proper maintenance of hospital buildings, CPWD units should be placed under the direct
supervision of Medical Superintendents. _ If that is not done, procedural delays would continue
to occur and upkeep of hospital buildings would remain unsatisfactory. The Committee,
therefore, reiterates that the Department should again pursue this issue with the Ministry of
Urban Affairs and Employment.

RECOMMENDATION

17.2 The Committee also found that the increase in the number of doctors over the years was much
more than the Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ staff. There is, no doubt, an acute shortage of such staff in all the
hospitals which ultimately is reflected in poor and truncated services. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that adequate number of posts-in Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ categories be provided after
assessing the requirement of every hospital at the earliest and the process of filling the posts at various
levels should be reviewed and streamlined so as to avoid unnecessary delays. Special efforts are
needed to ensure that vacancies of teaching staff and the doctors are filled up as soon as possible.

ACTION TAKEN

17.2 Proposal for creation of Group C & 0 posts are examined in the Ministry on the basis of
recommendations of Dte.GHS who have to follow the norms for creation of specific category of posts.
Staff Inspection Units and Work Study Units have been undertaking staff assessment in various
hospitals on the basis of work-load and working norms. Efforts are being made to speed up the filling
up of vacancies of teaching staff and doctors.

Another Committee under the Joint Secretary in the Ministry also inter-alia looked into the
demands of the staff and the recommendations for the creation of posts is under process.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITEE

The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department. The Committee feels
that creation of Group C&D posts does not commensurate with the work load. The Committee
desires that the process of creation of posts in Group C&D may be completed without any
further delay to provide efficient and quality service to the patients.

43


RECOMMENDATION

19. The Committee received a number of complaints about the rude behaviour of a section of doctors
and staff towards patients and of lower staff with doctors. It also noticed that, ‘generally, the
relationship between the employees and the hospital administration is not cordial. The Committee
noticed, during its visits, that there is a general lack of discipline and courtesy in various hospitals.
Irresponsible unionism has become ramparit amongst the employees of the hospitals which culminates,
quite often, in ‘bandhs’ and ‘strikes’. For example, PGIMER, Chandigarh, AIIMS and Safdarjung
have witnessed many such incidents in the recent past. The Committee noticed that there was no
effective grievance redressal machinery available in any of the hospitals.

19.1 The Committee is of the view that the problems between the administration and the employees
should get immediate attention as and when they arise and should not be allowed to deteriorate.
Disruption in hospital services is a very serious matter which should be avoided at all costs as it is
ultimately the human life that suffers.

ACTION TAKEN

19 & 19.1 The Office Councils have been functioning in the hospitals under the JCM Scheme with a
view to redressing the grievances of the employees. The Office Councils meet periodically wherein
recognized staff association nominates their representatives.

RECOMMENDATION

19.2 The Committee, therefore, feels that deterrent punishment, coupled with an efficient grievances
redressal system/mechanism like JCMs in government establishments. should be provided in each
hospital immediately so as to prevent the staff from taking recourse to strikes, etc. Equally important
is the need for an ‘Ombudsman’ type of machinery at each hospital for looking into patient
complaints. Further, the Committee would suggest that time has come for hospitals to subject
themselves to social audit of their assorted activities.

ACTION TAKEN

19.2 In view of the fact that public grievances committee have been functioning in each hospital for
looking into the complaints of patients and there is a public grievances committee in the Dte.GHS
headed by D.G., the Ministry does not favour the idea of “Ombudsman” type of machinery at each
hospital for looking into patients’ complaints.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee feels that the present system of Public Grievances Committee addressing
the complaints of patients is not working satisfactorily because the Doctors themselves are
members of the Committee against whom complaints are made. | The Committee therefore,
reiterates its recommendation for creation of 'Ombudsman' type of machinery. The Committee
is constrained to point out that there is absence of work culture in the medical staff of the
Government hospitals. They are often found lacking in polite behaviour, reception,
responsiveness and discipline. The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that there is an urgent
need of change in work culture among medical staff. In this connection, the Department may
take necessary steps to include attitudinal training in the in-service training programme of
health workers.

RECOMMENDATION

19.3 The Committee would also recommend early redefinition of the role and functions of Hospital
Management Boards. Norntally, these boards are intended to be responsible for smooth functioning of
all aspects of a hospital's working But then, its effectiveness and credibility are constrained by the

44


fact that they are often (as in AIIMS) composed solely of those responsible for providing hospital
services and attending to internal management and coordination issucs. Unless outsiders are also
associated with such hospital management boards, their credibility will not improve. nor will the issue
of patient care remain at the center of the scheme of things.

ACTION TAKEN

19.3 Including outsiders in the Hospital Management Boards is being examined with a view to
improve patient care. This is already being done in specific areas as ०.४. in the implementation of
Transplantation of Human Organ Act at the hospital level.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee has been informed that inclusion of outsiders has been tried in the hospitals of
Delhi Govt. and has not been found to be beneficial either for the patients or for the hospital
administration. The Committee is not inclined to agree with this viewpoint. The Committee
reiterates that effectiveness and objectivity of the Hospital Management Boards will only be
there if besides hospital functionaries, outsiders are also made their members.

RECOMMENDATION

23. The concept of geriatric clinics in India has not gained momentum although problems relating to
the aged/elderly people in the country are becoming more complex with the disintegration of joint
family system and the fast increase in the number of upper age people. There is a growing feeling of
insecurity, coupled with related health problems, amongst elderly people. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Government should take necessary steps to develop ‘geriatrics’ as a specialized
subject, and provide sufficient number of specialists and infrastructure for opening Geriatric Clinics in
all the Central Government hospitals.

ACTION TAKEN
23. The Dte.GHS has been requested to examine the proposal for setting up of Geriatric Clinics.

The recommendations of the Technical Committee set up by the Ministry, to consider inter-alia this
issue. was examined. The recommendations were circulated in October, 1996 for comments to the
Government of Delhi, Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Railways, MCD/NDMC and Central
Government hospitals before taking a final view.

No separate Geriatric Clinics have been set up in the Central Government hospitals though separate
counters, queues, seating arrangement etc. is provided to Senior Citizens.

As far as the problems of the aged are concerned, ESI Corporation has taken up setting up of Geriatric
Clinics in its Action Plan 2001-02. This will be followed up in coming years as well.

Railways have extended medical facilities to its retired employees in a scheme known as Retired
Employees Liberalized Health Scheme. This scheme provides medical care to the retired railway
employees at par with servingyemployees. As per feasibility, separate doctors, clinics, dispensing
counters, etc. have been provided in addition to comfortable waiting rooms in selected hospitals for
senior citizens. Medical officers and staff are being imparted training in geriatric care wherever
feasible.

45


The Delhi Government has not set up any Geriatric Clinics separately. However, Special Clinics on
Sunday for Senior Citizens of the age of 60 and above werc started in 9 hospitals under Govt. of NCT
of Delhi for two hours from 10 A.M. to 12 Noon in September, 1999 to provide services under
Medicine, Surgery, Orthopaedic, Gynaecology, ENT and Eye specialities supported with Pathological
tests and Radiological facilities. Senior Citizens are being given prefercial treatment in registration in
OPDs and at Medicine Counters in different hospitals.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is not happy to note that the proposal of setting up of Geriatric
still under examination of the Department even after expiry of more than six years and it has not
been able to take a decision regarding setting up of such clinics. The Committee expects the
Department to take an early decision in this matter.

RECOMMENDATION

24. The Committee is deeply concerned about inadequate facilities for treatment of poor patients for
major illnesses, especially those involving various complicated procedures. The Committee has noted
that (a) several major invasive procedures, ¢.g. cardiac surgery are too expensive for the poor people
(unaffordable even for middle class); (b) there is a wide disparity, amounting to almost a factor | to 3,
between private and public hospitals, even at the lowest priced public hospitals. For most of these life
conditions, the patient has to produce substantial private funds even after contributions are received
from the PM’s and CM’s relief fund, etc. and (c) the costs are unlikely to come down soon.

ACTION TAKEN

24. National Illness Assistance Fund has been set up with an initial contribution of Rs.5 crores. The
fund could be subscribed by individuals in India or abroad, corporate: bodies in private or public
sector, philanthropic organization and all contributions made to this fund is exempt from payment of
Income Tax under Section 80-G of Income Tax Act. The primary objective of the fund is to provide
financial assistance to patients living in States/ Union Territories, below poverty line in India,
suffering from major life threatening diseases, to receive medical treatment at any of the
superspeciality Hospitals/Institutes or other Government/Private hospitals. The financial assistance to
such patients would be released in the form of a one-time grant which will be released to the Medical
Superintendents of the hospitals in which the treatment has been/is being received. In a bid to speed
up the assistance to the needy patients, the scheme has been modified in January, 1998 to provide that
an advance payment of २5.10 lakhs be made to the Medical Superintendents of All India Institute of
Medical Sciences, Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital and Lady Hardinge Medical

College & Smt. Sucheta Kriplani Hospital, New Delhi, PGIMER, Chandigarh and JIPMER,
Pondicherry to enable immediate sanction of an amount upto Rs.25,000/- in each deserving case
reporting for treatment in the respective hospital/Institute. This amount would be replenished as and
when the report of its utilization are received.

All the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations have been advised to set up an Illness
Assistance Fund in their respective States/Union Territories. It has been decided that grant-in-aid
from Central Government would be released to each of these States/UTs (with legislature) where these
funds are set up. The grants-in-aid to States/UTs would be to the extent of 50% of the contributions
made by the State Governments/UTs to the State Fund/Society subject to a maximum of Rs.5 crores to
States with larger number and percentage of population below poverty line viz. Andhra Pradesh,
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Kamataka, Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and
West Bengal and Rs.2 crores to other States/UTs. The State/ UT level funds could also receive
contributions/donations from donors, as mentioned for National Illness Assistance Fund. The Illness
Assistance Fund at the State/UT level would release financial assistance to patients living in their

46


respective State/UT upto Rs. 1.5 lakhs in an individual case and forward all such cases to National
Illness Assistance Fund where the quantum of financial assistance is likely to exceed Rs. 1.5 lakhs.

It has been provided in the scheme that Union Territories which do not have a legislative assembly
will: be sanctioned a budget outlay of Rs.50 lakhs each from out of the National Illness Assistance
Fund as and when the UT Administration have set up an 1055 Assistance Socicty/Committce.

Budget provision of Rs.25 crores each had been made during the financial year 1998-99 and 1999-
2000. In 2000-01, a budget provision of R$.6.5 crores was made.

The States/UTs (with legislature) 1.6. Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh. Tripura, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil
Nadu, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Maharashtra, West Bengal. Kerala, Mizoram,
Rajasthan, Goa, Gujarat, Sikkim, Bihar and NCT of Delhi and Pondicherry have set up Illness
Assistance Fund. The States/UTs i.e. Assam, Haryana, Manipur. Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya,
Orissa, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Nagaland have not yet sct up the Illness Assistance Fund.

The National Illness Assistance Fund is provided to Dr. RML Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and
LHMC & Associated Hospitals to provide assistance to the poor and needy paticnts.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee feels that the states which have not set up National Illness Assistance
Fund may be persuaded to set up the Fund at the earliest, so that the poor patients living in
these states are able to take benefit out of the Fund. The Committee notes that even though the
Fund is in existence for quite some time not many poor patients are aware of its existence. The
Committee, therefore, desires that adequate publicity through the electronic/print media may
be given about this Fund.

RECOMMENDATION

24.1 While a point of view was expressed by some witnesses that procedure may not be a likely
priority for the poor, the Committee is not impressed with this argument. Urbanisation and its
attendant problems, considerable adulteration in food and drugs, tensions of a competitive modern life,
etc. are some trends increasingly affecting the rich and the poor alike, except that the poor are subject
to the double jeopardy of exposure to both infectious and non-communicable diseases. Therefore, the
Committee would suggest that the Ministry must urgently explore all appropriate sources of funds to
assist poor patients coming to AIIMS or other Central Government hospitals for treatment of specific
life threatening illness. If a mechanism can be set up, such as a National Catastrophic Illness
Assistance Fund, then resources can flow from all sources, including private charities and international
agencies and organisations. Besides, there can be many imaginative methods of requiring both
government and private hospitals of a certain size and even profit-making nursing homes to make
earmarked contributions to the fund. Procedures would, of course, have to be developed to create a
decentralized self regulating network of major participating hospitals to have early and quick help to
poor patients.

laboratory service charges in Central Government hospitals. The recommendation of the Committee
for setting up of a National Catastrophic Illness Assistance Fund under the Department of Health has

to para 24. *

47

The Committee is constrained to point out that public is not aware about the provision
regarding exemption of poor and indigent patients from payment of diagnostic and laboratory

information should also be made available at the Enquiry Counters of Central Government

that the work will be completed within nine months of starting of the work. The construction work

facilities to attendants accompanying the patients coming from outside Delhi have been

RECOMMENDATION

AIM 16. The Committee found the facilities/instrastructure in Nephrology Wards inadequate. The
Committee was informed that the existing facilities including beds in the wards, are just enough for
only one-fourth of the patients needing immediate admission. These facilities, the Committee learnt,
are shared by the patients of Urology also. As a result, even the serious patients and those requiring
dialysis, have to wait for weeks for admission,

health workers. (Para 19.2)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee is not inclined to agree with this viewpoint. The Committee reiterates

that effectiveness and objectivity of the Hospital Management Boards will only be there if
besides hospital functionaries, outsiders are also made their members. (Para 19.3)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is not happy to note that the proposal of setting up of Geriatric clinics is
still under examination of the Department even after expiry of more than six years and it has not
been able to take a decision regarding setting up of such clinics. The Committee expects the
Department to take an early decision in this matter. (Para 23)

74


COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee feels that the states which have not set up National Illness Assistance
Fund may be persuaded to set up the Fund at the earliest, so that the poor patients living in
these states are able to take benefit out of the Fund. The Committee notes that even though the
Fund is in existence for quite some time not many poor patients are aware of its existence. The
Committee, therefore, desires that adequate publicity through the electronic/print media may
be given about this Fund. (Para 24)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is constrained to point out that public is not aware about the provision
regarding exemption of poor and indigent patients from payment of diagnostic and laboratory
service charges in Central Government Hospitals . The Committee, therefore, recommends that
steps should be taken for giving wide publicity through the electronic and print media. Such
information should also be made available at the Enquiry Counters of Central Government
Hospitals so that needy patients can take the maximum benefit. (Para 24.1)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee observes that a number of Projects for providing accommodation
facilities to attendants accompanying the patients coming from outside Delhi have been
approved and are in various stages of implementation in Safdarjung Hospital, Dr. RML
Hospital, LHMC and AIIMS. The Committee recommends that all efforts should be made to
expedite the completion of these Projects. The Department may also explore the possibility of
augmenting these facilities wherever feasible. (25.1)

ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES, NEW DELHI
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is deeply disturbed to note the reply of the Department that AIIMS
which is a premier institute of the country is neither able to provide dialysis facility to all
patients approaching it nor is currently in a position to cope with the requirements of life long
dialysis for chronically ill patients on a long term basis. The Committee feels that while the
Department feels the necessity of strengthening the Nephrology unit, it is not serious in action.

The Committee, therefore, recommends that the existing Nephrology unit of the hospital
should be strengthened in terms of space, equipment and staff etc. at the earliest.(16.1&16.2)

POSTGRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL EDUCATION AND RESEARCH
(PGIMER), CHANDIGARH

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Department is silent about the Committee's recommendation with regard to revival
of JCM in the Institute. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that
the JCM be revived without further delay, if not already done. (Para 16 & 16.1)

JAWAHARLAL INSTITUTE OF POSTGRADUATE MEDICAL
EDUCATION & RESEARCH, PONDICHERRY
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee expresses its displeasure over the undue delay in the matter. It finds
that the proposal is still being processed at different levels. The Committee recommends that

75


the proposal may be finalized and implemented without further loss of time under intimation to
it. (Para 5)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is not in a position to understand why the employees are opposing the
grant of autonomy. The Committee feels that the Department may make all out efforts to allay
their fears about the issue of autonomy and convince them about the necessity of granting
autonomy. It hopes that a consensus would be reached soon. (Para 8)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

Though the Institute has taken some steps in this regard as compared to the staff
strength, the Committee, feels the additions made are miniscule. It desires that steps may be
taken to construct more quarters inside the campus itself. (Para 9)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee takes a serious view of the matter. The Committee would like to be
apprised of the reasons for delay in non notification of draft Recruitment Rules and how does
the Department propose to fill up the posts in the absence of these rules. It also desires that the
Recruitment Rules are notified without further delay. (Para 11.2)

SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is shocked to note that the authorities are not even aware, who is the
owner of the land, while they were pursuing the things with the M/o Defence and precious time
has been wasted in this futile exercise. The Committee is equally perturbed to note that money
has already been deposited for the said land, and the matter is still hanging on fire. The
Committee feels that the matter may be taken up on a regular basis at the highest level with
M/o Urban Development to hand over the possession of land without further delay since five
years have elapsed after the decision of the Committee of Secretaries. ( Para 6)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is perturbed by this casual approach and fails to understand the reasons
for envisaging a scheme in the early days of a Pian period, doing some preliminary exercise and
by the end of the Plan , simply dropping the proposal. (Para 17.1)
DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee desires that the matter may be pursued vigorously at the appropriate
level. (Para 5.3)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee expresses its dismay over the lukewarm approach of the Department.
The Department has failed to procure necessary equipment for improving the Burns and Plasti:

76



ward even after more than six years. The Committee desires that necessary action in this regard
may be taken without further loss of time. (Para 6)

LADY HARDING MEDICAL COLLEGE AND ASSOCIATE HOSPITAL
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee would like to be specifically apprised whether the entire encroachment
in the vicinity of the Hospital has since been removed. (Para 2.3)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee notes the reply of the Department. The Committee, however, is
skeptical whether all the lacunae in the hospital can be remedied by implementing the
Comprehensive Development Plan. Moreover, the Plan is in conceptual stage and will be
implemented in stages and some of the issues require immediate attention. Further, no time
frame has been set by the Department to start and complete the Plan. (Para 12.2)

ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF PHYSICAL MEDICINE & REHABILITATION
(AIIPMER), BOMBAY.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department. The report of the
Committee was submitted in 1995, while the proposal was sent to M/o Finance in March, 1999.
The Committee regrets to note that nearly after four years the proposal was sent. If
immediate action had been initiated, the present situation could have been avoided. (Para 3.1)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee notes the reply. However, the position would not have improved much
where in all the employees would have got residential accommodation. The Committee,
therefore, reiterates the recommendation made in its 31* Report. (Para 4)

PREFACE
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Hundred  Sixteenth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.42) of the Department of Health, 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2002-2003.
 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Health
and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held
on 28
th   March, 2002.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on
22
nd   April, 2002.

REPORT
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       Main objectives of the Department of Health are :
(i)
                  to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention, control and
eradication of communicable diseases;
(ii)                to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the medical
colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas;
(iii)               to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs;
(iv)              to provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people and to train the required number of
personnel for this purpose;
(v)                to take steps for better implementation of Health Care Programmes for tribal and other weaker sections
of the Society; and
(vi)              to collaborate with member countries of United Nations and International Agencies like WHO, UNICEF
in matters relating to health promotion.
1.2              The Department of Health incurs expenditure either directly or through various institutions and establishments
run by it and by way of grants given to autonomous and voluntary organizations.  Grants to States and Union Territory
Administrations are mainly for Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being implemented thorough the State
Governments and Union Territory Administrations.  They include national programmes for prevention, control and
eradication of diseases.
1.3              The Department finances, wholly or substantially, the following autonomous Institutions engaged in patient care

116th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/116threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:24]
and/or research;
(i)                  All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences, New
Delhi;
(ii)                Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh;
(iii)               All India Institute of Speech and Hearing, Mysore; and
(iv)              Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi
The following Schemes are financed by the Central Government on 100 percent basis:
(i)                  National Scheme for Prevention of Visual Impairment and Blindness including Trachoma;
(ii)                National Leprosy Eradication Programme;
(iii)               National Guinea-worm Eradication Programme; and
(iv)              National AIDS Control Programme.
            The Schemes on which the expenditure is shared between the Central Government and State Government on
50:50 basis are:—
(i)                  National  Malaria Eradication Programme (Rural and Urban);
(ii)                National Sexually Transmitted Diseases Control Programme;
(iii)               National T.B. Control Programme; and
(iv)              Kala-Azar Control Programme
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       Plan allocation for the Department of Health for 2002-03 is Rs. 1550.00 crores  showing an increase of 7% over
the Plan allocation of Rs. 1450.00  crores for 2001-02.  On a specific query  about the projected demand of the
Department for 2002-03, the Committee was informed that a plan outlay of Rs. 2009.60  crores was proposed.  
Additional allocation was meant for new initiatives emanating from the draft National Health Policy-2002, such as
distributing drugs to Primary Health Centres, Urban Health, setting up of a Medical Grants Commission.   The
Committee was, however,  given  to understand that the meager increase in 2002-03 would not be sufficient even for
maintaining the tempo of the existing programmes.
2.2       The Committee has observed that during the Ninth Plan period, every year Plan allocation has been less than the
projected demand of the Department, which has been  reduced without a break at the RE stage and even that reduced
allocation continued to remain under-utilised.  The Committee has been informed that major shortfall in expenditure
during the initial years of Ninth Plan was due to non-finalisation of procedural formalities observed in the case of
National Anti-Malaria Programme and National TB Control Programme.   Utilization of funds increased from 55% in 
1998-99 to 88% in    2000-01.   The Committee is, however, not fully inclined to agree with the explanation given by
the Department.   The Committee observes that the trend of under-utilisation has continued during the Ninth Plan  due to
variety  of reasons like non-setting up of required infrastructure  for implementation of various disease control
programmes, non-release of funds due to unspent balances lying with the implementing agencies, slow performance of
district societies, less number of proposals from NGOs, non-completion of required formalities etc.   During 2001-02,
the last year of Ninth Plan, Plan allocation of Rs. 1450.00 crores was reduced to Rs. 1320.00 crores at the RE stage, and
anticipated expenditure at the end of the year is Rs. 1300.00 crores.   The Committee hopes that all procedural
formalities under ongoing  and proposed Programmes/Projects during Tenth Plan have been completed so that optimum
and judicious utilization of allocated funds is ensured right from 2002-03, the first year of Tenth Plan. 
III.       CENTRAL   GOVERNMENT   HEALTH   SCHEME
3.1
              The Scheme was started in 1954 with the objective of providing comprehensive medical care facilities to
Central Government employees and their family members.  The Scheme which initially started in Delhi now covers 23
cities of which Bhubaneswar and Ranchi CGHS cater only to staff of Accountant General posted there and their
pensioners.
3.2
              Rs. 12.00 crores under plan has been  provided to  CGHS for 2002-2003.  The Committee notes that Plan

116th Report

allocation of Rs. 12.00 crores in 2001-02 had to be reduced to Rs. 9.00 crores at the RE stage.  Explaining the decrease,
the Department replied that the CGHS earlier had proposals for expansion of its services by opening more CGHS
dispensaries which involves  creation of new posts. Fresh proposals for creation of new posts  under CGHS can be
referred to the Department of Expenditure only after the recommendations contained in the SIU Report of November,
1999 are  fully implemented.  However, due to a stay on the recommendations contained in the SIU Report by CAT,
New Delhi, it was not possible for the CGHS to open more dispensaries by creation of new posts and this resulted in
less expenditure during the year 2001-2002. 
3.3       The Committee notes that it has not been possible to carry out the expansion programme of CGHS dispensaries
to new cities as was planned by the Ministry of Health during the Ninth Plan Period, due to the fact that the Ministry of
Finance had not agreed to the creation of new posts of setting up of new dispensaries  pending finalisation of the SIU
report on the functioning of CGHS dispensaries.  The Committee is deeply disturbed to note that provision of medical
facilities to the government employees which is a basic necessity  is trapped into avoidable legal wrangles.  The
Ministry should have taken up the matter with the Central Administrative Tribunal for early resolution of the case(s) so
that the expansion programme of dispensaries was implemented expeditiously.  The Committee, therefore, would like
the Ministry to look into this and submit a report to the Committee within a period of three months  of the action taken
and the present status of opening new CGHS dispensaries area-wise.
3.4       The Committee was apprised that in places where there are no Central Government-run hospitals, the facilities
provided for in-patient treatment to CGHS beneficiaries are woefully inadequate.  Very few beds are reserved for them. 
Consequently, the patients are put to avoidable inconvenience and have to seek treatment through private facilities
which are very expensive.  The Committee, therefore, would like the Ministry to look into this aspect and furnish details
of the facilities available to the CGHS beneficiaries in private-run hospitals for CGHS beneficiaries and measures taken
to augment the same.
3.5       The Committee notes that during 2001, the following inspections were carried out in Delhi by Zonal Additional
Directors :—

South Zone 34 26

West Zone 27 12+2

The feedback from the beneficiaries was mainly on the following points  : —
(i)
                  Shortage of medicines.
(ii)                Long queues on the counters.
(iii)               Lack of waiting space and furniture in some dispensaries.
(iv)              Lack of punctuality in a few cases.

          The Programme is in operation since 1962 and is integrated with the  General Health Services.  Revised
National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) based on WHO recommended  DOTs Strategy (Directly Observed
Treatment Short Course Chemotherapy) was launched in the country in March, 1997 with a soft loan from World
Bank.   Against the targeted coverage of 271.21 million population, under RNTCP  more than 430 million population
has already been covered.   The revised strategy is also being implemented in Andhra Pradesh and Orissa with the
assistance of DFID and DANIDA at a cost of  Rs. 109.93 crores and Rs. 31.95 crores respectively to cover a total
population of 100 million.
15.2     Plan Allocation under the T.B. Control Programme for BE 2001-2002 was Rs.122.00 crores which was
substantially reduced to Rs.100.00 crores at the RE stage. The Department has clarified that delay in the procurement of
anti-TB drugs to be supplied to various States/districts and non-procurement of binocular microscopes during the
financial year resulted in the reduction of funds meant for this purpose from Rs. 44.43 crores to Rs. 32.55 crores. 
Allocation  for grants to State/District TB Societies was also reduced from Rs. 56.00 crores to Rs. 42.50 crores.  Reason
being funds meant to be released to the new 120 districts under the expansion plan could not be fully released due to
delayed approval of the EFC and CCEA.   Surplus funds lying with some district societies was another reason for
reduction.   The Committee observes that this trend has been there during the entire Ninth Plan period.   As per the
figures  available with the Committee, out of plan allocation of Rs. 581.00 crores from 1997-98 to 2001-02, the total
expenditure incurred  as  on 22.2.02 is only Rs. 398.48 crores.   The Committee finds that achievement level of Physical
Targets  under Sputum Examination and Sputum Positive Detection has also  been much  below the fixed targets  during
the Ninth Plan period.
15.3     Last year, the Committee’s attention was drawn toward under-utilisation of funds released as Grants-in-aid- to
some State Govts. for procurement of anti-TB drugs for sputum negative cases.   The Committee apprehends that
situation may not have improved much.  The Committee is constrained to note Utilisation Certificates are  still awaited
from some State Govts. in spite of reminders.  Pending Utilisation Certificates, no further funds are being  released to
the State  Govt. for purchase of anti-TB drugs for sputum negative cases.  The Committee views this with serious
concern.   The Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the submission of Utilisation Certificates
with all concerned State Govts.

           The Committee notes that five different schemes for  involvement of NGOs have been envisaged and NGOs are
being involved in  various aspects of service delivery.   The  Committee would like to be apprised about States where

implementing one project of involving private practitioners in E. Delhi and further expansion of this Project is

16.2          Against a Plan allocation of Rs. 70.76 crores for NLEP during 2001-02, Rs. 75.00 crores have been provided for

the Centralised Media activities. 
16.3     The Committee notes that there has been optimum utilization of funds under the Programme during Ninth Plan.  
Against total allocation of Rs.388.00 crores, reported expenditure figures are Rs. 384.26 crores.  Similarly,  achievement
level of Physical Targets as per the parameters of Case Detection, Case Treatment and Case Discharge have been many
times more.
16.4     While appreciating the achievement level under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme, the Committee
observes that 60% of globally recorded  patients are in the country.  States of Bihar, Jharkhand, Chattisgarh, UP, Orissa,
W.Bengal and MP contribute 64% of the country’s case load, out of which Bihar alone contributes 24% of the country’s
case load.   The Committee observes that there is no dearth of funds under the Programme and a large number of NGOs
are also involved with quite a few reported to be doing good work.  Special focus under 2
nd Phase of World Bank
Assisted Project is also there on the eight high endemic States.   The Committee, however, feels that Bihar being  the

19.1 The Programme, started in 1982, envisages a community based approach to the problem.   Funds are provided by
the Govt. to the State Govts. and the nodal institutes to  meet the expenditure on staff, equipments, training, IEC
activities etc.   At present, District Mental Health Programme is under implementation in 25 districts in 20 States.
19.2  Against a  Plan allocation of Rs. 4.00 crores in RE 2001-02, allocation in BE 2002-2003 has been astronomically
increased to Rs. 27.00 crores.  The Department  has informed that an increased allocation has been made for 2002-2003
based on the Tenth Five Year Plan proposal which envisages apart from sustaining the existing District Mental Health
Programme,   adding more districts to provide assistance for upgrading the infrastructure and modernization of the
existing mental health facilities in mental hospitals and psychiatric departments of medical colleges; to undertake
research in the field of mental health and to develop, disseminate and use   IEC programmes at national level.
19.3  The Committee notes that shortage of trained psychiatric manpower and lack of awareness regarding treatment are
the two main barriers to the provision of mental health services in the country.  The Committee has been given to
understand that about 4000 clinical psychologists,  psychiatric  social workers  and  psychiatric nurses are working in
the country which is inadequate to meet the total needs of  persons  with mental disorders in the country.  The shortage
of psychiatric manpower is felt in all the States, specially in rural areas.  The Committee strongly feels that there is a
need for having systematic evaluation regarding Statewise requirement of manpower.  The Committee also observes
that mental health programmes are being implemented in a varying degree by different States.   The Committee has
been informed that the District Mental Health Programme is to be enlarged and made more effective covering the  entire
country during the Tenth Plan.   The Committee feels that there  is an urgent need for expanding the mental health
services.  While  appreciating the substantive allocation of funds for this programme for 2002-03, the first year of Tenth
Plan, the Committee would like to emphasise that there should be regular and extensive monitoring at all levels to
ensure optimum and judicious utilization of funds.
