 XX      PREVENTION  OF  FOOD  ADULTERATION  PROGRAMME
20.1  The subject of the Prevention of Food Adulteration is in the Concurrent list of the Constitution.  However, in
general, the enforcement of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is done by the State/UT. Governments.  The
Central Government primarily plays an advisory role in its implementation besides carrying out various statutory
functions/duties assigned to it under the various provisions of the Act.
20.2     Four Central Food Laboratories have been established under the Act, which work as appellate laboratories for
the purpose of analysis of samples of food lifted by the Food Inspectors of the States/U.Ts. and local bodies.  There are
82 Food Laboratories under the administrative control of various State/Union Territory Governments and Local Bodies.
20.3
             On being asked about experience of the Department in respect of administration of Prevention of Food
Adulteration Act and the Rules made thereunder, the Department has informed that some of the problems being faced
relate to inadequate enforcement at the level of the States.  There is a shortage of trained manpower, especially at the
level of food inspectors. Number of samples drawn for test and analysis has declined as also the cases in which
prosecutions have been launched or conviction obtained.  Capabilities of the State Food Laboratories are also required
to be augmented so that they can properly undertake analysis of contaminants.
20.4           The Department has also informed that the Government of India has been trying to assist the State Governments
by training of State Laboratory analysts and food inspectors and by supply of equipments to the laboratories.  The States
have been requested to increase their manpower for proper enforcement of the Act; to increase the budget to provide
proper facilities in the states laboratories and to utilize  the equipments provided by the Government of India properly;
to conduct investigational market surveys in a systematic way, with particular reference to items of mass consumption
and to keep a proper data bank of the results. 
20.5     From the feedback given by the Department, the Committee is left with no alternative but to believe that the
situation is indeed very grim so far as implementation of the   Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is concerned.   It
seems that with the load of so many Disease Control Programmes, this aspect of health management is  not getting the
due impetus from any State in the country.   The Committee is therefore, of the view that drastic measures are required
to be taken.   The Committee recommends that an overall review of Prevention of Food Adulteration Programme with
special focus on status of State laboratories, requirement of more labs and necessary staff therefor should be initiated
without any further delay.

The Committee, therefore, would like the Ministry to look into this aspect and furnish details of the facilities

th February, 2002.   It is understood that at

equipments amounting to Rs. 4.80 crores.   It seems that the Institute will have to wait upto the RE stage as the

based support for  outbreak containment out of resources available under NAMP  cannot be considered a sound
strategy.   What is required is a well-planned programme with separate funding for control of JE. (Para 14.3)

Positive Detection has also  been much  below the fixed targets  during the Ninth Plan period. (Para 15.2)
The Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the submission of Utilisation Certificates with
all concerned State Govts. (Para 15.3)

achieve the desired results.   What is required is an exercise to obtain the feedback from the local Public Representatives

random surveys/surprise inspections by Central teams.  Last year the Committee had desired that the Department should
take action for evolving a more effective monitoring mechanism.   The Committee strongly feels that mere taking note
of the advice regarding random surveys/surprise inspections does not serve any purpose.  The Department has to take
initiative  in this direction without any delay. (Para 15.5) 
The Committee strongly feels that in a country like India which accounts for nearly 1/3
rd of the global TB
burden, where every year there are approximately 22 lakhs new TB cases, and where one  person dies from TB every
minute and more than 5 lakhs every year, all the inherent  flaws in the Programme at all levels need to be eliminated at
the earliest. (Para 15.6)

The Committee notes that shortage of trained psychiatric manpower and lack of awareness regarding treatment are
the two main barriers to the provision of mental health services in the country.  The Committee has been given to
understand that about 4000 clinical psychologists,  psychiatric  social workers  and  psychiatric nurses are working in

that mental health programmes are being implemented in a varying degree by different States.   The Committee has
been informed that the District Mental Health Programme is to be enlarged and made more effective covering the  entire

services.  While  appreciating the substantive allocation of funds for this programme for 2002-03, the first year of Tenth

ensure optimum and judicious utilization of funds.       (Para 19.3)

PREFACE

Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Hundred-Seventeenth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.44) of the Department of
Family Welfare,  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2002-2003.
 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Family
Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department   on the said Demands for Grants in its
meeting held on 28
th   March, 2002.

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Census of 2001 had indicated the population of India as 1027 million with 531 million males and 496
million females.    In the decade  1991-2001, nearly 181 million persons were added to the population of India.  
Population increased at an annual exponential growth rate of 1.93 percent in the decade.  As per the latest Sample
Registration System (SRS) estimates, the annual growth rate of population is 1.74% (1999).  
1.2       The eight States of U.P., Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Uttaranchal, Chhatisgarh and Orissa,
which currently constitute nearly 44% of the total population of India, are projected to comprise 48% of the total
population in 2016.   In other words, these States alone will contribute an anticipated 55% increase during the period
1996-2016.    Demographic outcome in these States will determine the timing and size of population at which India
achieves population stabilisation.
1.3       The three most significant factors that can curtail the growth of population are increase in the use of
contraceptives, improvement in the mother’s health and survival of children.  All the programmes of the Department of
Family Welfare are accordingly planned and being implemented for pursuing a combination of these three issues.
1.4       During the Tenth  Plan the main approach of family welfare programme will be:
(i)
                  To assess the needs for Reproductive and Child Health (RCH);
(ii)                To provide need based ,client centered and demand driven RCH care;
(iii)               To strengthen the infrastructure for service delivery and bridging the gap in essential infrastructure and
manpower;
(iv)              Providing additional assistance to poorly performing districts and ensuring uninterrupted supply of drugs
and equipments;  and

1.7       The Committee understands that under the Community Needs Assessment Approach (CNAA), an action plan is
prepared each year at the district level based  on the need assessment done by ANMs of Sub-Centre at village level.  In
the beginning of the financial year, the health worker will first complete the house-to-house survey.  Based on this
survey, Eligible Couple Register is updated by the ANM.  The Committee has been informed that the State Govts. are 
impressed from time to time to ensure that the Sub-Centre action is got prepared for each Sub-Centre in the State.  The
Committee has its own doubts about the implementation of this annual exercise, which is most essential for successful
implementation of Family Welfare Programme, specially in the remote and inaccessible areas.  The Committee strongly
feels that surprise inspections in the performing as well as non-performing districts by Central teams/dedicated
NGOs/Social Workers can bring out the ground reality.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should initiate such an exercise in 2002-2003.

II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1              The Committee has been informed that allocation for the Department for  2002-2003 is Rs. 4953.83 crores
against Rs. 4232.38 crores in BE 2001-2002 which was  reduced to Rs. 3721.67 crores at RE stage.   This represents  an
increase of Rs. 721.55 crores over the previous year.
2.2
              Commenting on the allocation, the Department submitted that the Annual Plan proposal for the year 2002-2003
was Rs. 7590.56 crores.  However, an allocation of Rs 4953.83 crores was approved by the Planning Commission.  As a
result of cut in plan proposal, funding of the infrastructural units in the States will be the most affected.   Besides that, 
other schemes like contractual appointments under RCH Programme, adolescent health care, supply of Dai kits,
promoting institutional deliveries, civil works at Sub Centres, urban slum project and strengthening of primary health
care infrastructure, may also be curtailed.
2.3
              The Committee  has also been given to understand that during 2001-2002, a cut of 710.00 crores (plan) was
proposed by the Ministry of Finance on the basis of expenditure  incurred by the Department till October, 2001
(51.19%).   However,  subsequently an assurance was given by the Ministry of Finance that if 75% expenditure was
incurred by the Department by December, 2001, the cut made in the outlay will be restored.    However, despite meeting
the targetted expenditure and the representations made at the highest level, the cut of Rs. 710 crores was only reduced to
Rs. 510 crores.  
2.4              The Committee agrees in principle with the Department's contention of there being no case for resorting to a cut
of Rs. 700.00 crores at the RE stage in 2001-2002 by the Ministry of Finance.  The Committee also notes that total plan
allocation of Rs. 3700.00 crores in 2001-2002 is anticipated to be utilised. Actual expenditure figures are not available
at present.  The Committee, however observes that during 2000-2001, against a higher projected requirement, plan
allocation was Rs. 3500.00 crores which was reduced to Rs. 3200.00 crores at the RE stage.  Actual expenditure was
even less i.e. Rs. 3071.35 crores.  The Committee strongly feels that inview of much higher allocation of Rs. 4930.00
crores in 2002-2003, the Department should ensure that funds allocated under various schemes are utilised optimally
and strictly as per the action plan to strengthen its case of higher allocation.
III        RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
3.1
              The Rural Family Welfare Centres were set up at all block level PHCs sanctioned upto 1.4.1980 to provide
Family Planning and MCH Services in rural areas.  There are 5435 such centres functioning in the Country.  Besides
that, to provide basic health and family welfare services to the rural population 1,37,311 Sub-Centres  are currently
functioning out of which 97,757 Sub-Centres were funded by the Department till now. 
3.2              The Committee was informed that a Consultative Committee consisting of the representatives of the Planning
Commission, Department of Expenditure, States of Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan was constituted by
the Department in 1998.   The Committee examined the SWAP proposal between Rural Family Welfare Centres and
Sub-Centres and strongly recommended that in view of the importance of the rural Sub-Centres for the Family Welfare
Programme, and as the Rural Family Welfare Centres have lost their original identity and have become part of primary
health centre complexes at the block level, the Department of Family Welfare should assume the responsibility of
funding all 1,37,311 existing Sub-Centres.   In exchange, for accepting this responsibility the States should take over the
financial liability of maintaining the Rural Family Welfare Centres  (RFWC) numbering 5435.
3.3       The Department  also informed that the main purpose of the SWAP is to streamline the system of financing the
Sub-Centres. As the Sub-Centres were established by Central Government and State Governments during different time
periods it is difficult to assess the impact of the programme run by the Department.   Therefore, there was a need to
bring all the Sub-Centres under one umbrella for effective monitoring of the programme.   The Planning Commission
insisted  that a consensus be developed among the States on the issue of swaping these responsibilities between the State
and Department of Family Welfare.     The Committee in its 101
st Report had also recommended that the issue needed
to be discussed with the States/UTs before any decision was taken in this regard.  The Committee, however, notes that a
decision has already been taken to implement the SWAP proposal from 1.4.2002.  Therefore there  is no proposal for
requirement of Funds for RFWCs in the Tenth Plan.  Accordingly, no allocation has been made in BE 2002-2003.
3.4       The Committee is surprised to note that a final decision has already been taken by the Department inspite of
there being no consensus on this issue among the States.  According to the Department itself, outcome of
implementation of SWAP proposal will be that some states will be in an advantageous position by saving the funds and

117th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/117threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:25]
some States in a disadvantageous position.  For example, as per the information made available to the Committee,
whereas additionalliability in the case of Chandigarh will be only Rs. 7 lakhs, for West Bengal it will be as high as Rs.
17.74 crores.  The Committee wonders about the fate of Rural Family Welfare Centres in view of no allocation being
made by the Department in BE 2002-2003.  The Committee would, therefore, like to emphasise that the issue of
compensating the affected states should be sorted out at the earliest.
3.5       The Committee is sympathetic to  grievance of some of the State Governments  who will be placed
disadvantageously as a result of the proposal.  The Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously
pursue its proposal with the Planning Commission for compensating the affected states.   The Department should make
concerted efforts to fix a rational basis for distribution of liabilities amongst the State Governments so that no injustice
is done to any State.
3.6       The Committee notes that 22842 Primary Health Centres exist  in the country against the requirement of 25907
Primary Health Centres . However, there are only 5435 Rural Family Welfare Centres at present.   Hence, there is  a
need to open many more Rural Family Welfare Centres by the States.   Given the tight financial position of the State
Governments, the Committee feels that it is a great challenge for them. 
3.7       The Plan allocation for Sub-Centres for BE 2001-2002 was Rs. 675.00 crores which has been substantially
increased to Rs. 1909.00 crores in 2002-2003.   Commenting on the increase, the Department has informed that on
account of transfer of liability of 39,554 additional Sub-Centres, the requirement of the additional funds on this account
is Rs. 593 crores.   Adjustment of the funds according to SWAP proposal for Rural Family Welfare Centres now to be
funded by State Governments is Rs. 430 crore.  Thus an extra liability of Rs. 163 crores is to be borne by Central
Government.  Other  reasons for increase in BE 2002-2003 against BE/RE  2001-2002 are as follows:
(a)
     Revision of financial norms for pattern of assistance to States/UTs for Sub-Centre Scheme.
(b)    Increased salaries of staff of Sub-Centres in States/UTs following 5 th Central Pay Commission
recommendations.
(c)     Provision for payment of arrears to the State Governments of previous years which until now were being
provided from the scheme named Arrears.
3.8       The Department has informed that 137311 Sub Centres have been established against a requirement of 155455
Sub Centres as per 2002 projected population.   In Tribal areas, 21335 Sub Centres have been established against a
requirement of 26243 Sub Centres.   There are 22842   Primary Health Centres in the country against the requirement of
25907 PHCs and 3043 Community Health Centres against the requirement of 6479 CHCs, based on 2002 Projected
Population.
3.9       The number of Sub-Centres, PHCs and  CHCs required and shortfall as per 2002 projected population is given
below.
Centre Requirement Short fall

3.10     The Committee is constrained to note that the major defaulting States in respect of setting up of Sub-Centres are
Bihar, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Meghalaya, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Delhi. In
respect of PHCs these are Assam, A.P., Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Nagaland,
Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Delhi.  As far as CHCs are concerned, Assam, A.P., Bihar, Haryana,

3.11     The Committee is perturbed  to note that targets for setting up of Sub-Centres, PHCs and CHCs during Ninth
Plan seem to have been prescribed for namesake only.  The achievement level for the first four years of Ninth Plan

of Sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs.  The Committee also fails  to understand as to how such a large number of states have
failed to achieve the target of setting up of Sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs and therefore recommends that the Department

3.13     The Committee also observes that in many States, the number of established Sub-Centres exceeds the projected
requirements as per 2002 projected population.  Financial liability with regard to all existing 1,37,311 Sub-Centres is to
be borne by the Central Govt. from 2002-2003.  The justification of bearing the expenditure in respect of excess Sub-
Centres set up in different States by the Centre needs to be explored from all aspects.  Specially in view of the fact that
proposal of the Department for financing the establishment of new Sub-Centres under the 100% Centrally Sponsored
Scheme is pending with the Ministry of Finance and shortage of Sub-Centres is there in large number of States.
3.14     The Department has informed the Committee about the state-wise  requirement, sanctioned strength, vacancy
and shortfall in respect of ANMs and LHVs.  The figures given below show the number of ANMs required, sanctioned,

periods varying from 1994 to 2001.  In respect of some states like Bihar and Delhi it is 10-15 years old.   The
Department has informed that the updated data as on 1st January, 2001 is not available in respect of some of the States.  
The Committee laments at the lackadaisical approach of the Department in getting the data collected from various States

the Department had initiated the contractual appointments/hiring of additional/ ANMs at Sub-Centres primarily in weak
performing remote districts under the RCH Programme.  4200 additional ANMs have been appointed on contract basis
during the last three years.  The Committee can well imagine the vacancy position prior to that.  The Committee feels
that  ANMs and LHVs are the persons responsible for delivering Family Welfare Services to rural people and therefore
recommends that the Department should make concerted efforts to get  the posts of ANMs and LHVs  filled up at the
earliest in respect of the weak performing states.
IV        URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
4.1       Urban Family Welfare Centres are in operation since 1950 to provide Family Welfare Services in urban  areas.   
There are three types of Urban Family Welfare Centres viz. Type I, Type II and Type III depending upon the population
covered by them.   At present,  there are 1083 centres functioning in various States under the scheme to provide
outreach services, primary health care, maternal and child health and distribution of contraceptives.   The financial
assistance under this component is given for the salary of staff, contingency and rent as per approved norms.
4.2
              The plan allocation for Urban Family Welfare Services was  Rs. 67.50 crores in BE 2001-2002 which has been
increased to Rs. 109.80 crores  in BE 2002-2003.  The Department has informed that the additional provision made in
BE 2002-2003 is proposed to be utilized to meet the expenditure relating to (i) revision of norms; and (ii) increase in
salary component as per the following:
Salary                                       Rs. 106.09 crores

Rent                                         Rs.    2.90 crores

4.3              In order to improve service delivery outreach services of Primary Health Care, Family Welfare and MCH
Services in urban areas particularly in urban slums, Urban Revamping Scheme was introduced under which
Government have accorded approval for establishment of 936 Health Posts and 14 Family Welfare Bureau in various
States of the country so far.   Out of which 871 Health posts and 10 Family Welfare Bureau have been sanctioned so far.
4.4       The Committee in its 101st  Report recommended for reorganisation of Urban Family Welfare Centres separately
and not under urban RCH programme.    The Department has replied that  the Expenditure Finance Committee had
advised former  not to pursue the reorganisation of Urban Family Welfare Centres due to financial constraints and  the
same would be taken up under Special Schemes in the 10 th Five Year Plan.    The Committee is of the view  that for
improving outreach service delivery system in urban slums, reorganisation of Urban Family Welfare Centres should be
made at the earliest.    Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department should make adequate provision for
reorganisation of Urban Family Welfare Centres in 2002-2003.
V         REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME (RCH)
5.1       Reproductive and Child Health Programme is the flagship programme of Family Welfare, which combines
trinity of objectives viz. reproductive health, Child survival and fertility regulation. The Programme is primarily offered
through Primary Health Infrastructure.  The overall goals of the programme are to reduce maternal and infant mortality
and morbidity and unwanted fertility and contribute thereto stabilization of population.
5.2      Allocation for RCH project in BE 2001-2002 was Rs. 1126.95 crores which was reduced to 933.36 crores at the
RE stage.   Allocation for 2002-2003 has been further reduced to Rs. 800.53 crores.   Commenting on the reduced
allocation the Department has stated that the outlay for Polio Eradication Programme and vaccines for routine
immunization till 2001-2002 used to be routed through RCH programme.    The Planning Commission advised that the
Department  should club  all the immunization related activities under one head.   Acting on the advice of the Planning
Commission, the allocation for polio activities and vaccines for routine immunization related activities which stands at
Rs. 376 crores and Rs. 141 crores respectively have been separated from the RCH Programme which in-turn resulted in
decreased allocation  for RCH Programme in BE 2002-2003.
5.3      The Committee notes with appreciation the rationalization done by the Department in restructuring the RCH
Programme and feels that the Departmentshould, in the same vein carry similar rationalization/ restructuring,  
wherever possible, in respect of other programmes.

Ninth Plan.   However, utilisationof these funds has been very poor.   As per the figures made available to the

the end of Ninth Plan.   Balance amount of RS. 563.55 crores is lying as unspent balance with States/UTs.   While all
the States/UTs are defaulters, situation with regard to the following States/UTs is a cause of serious concern

VII       POST PARTUM PROGRAMME
Post Partum Programme is a maternity centered hospital based approach to Family Welfare Programme covering
550 Post Partum Centres at district level and 1012 Post Partum Centres at sub-district level hospitals.   The objective of
the programme is to provide antenatal,  natal and post-natal services to expectant mothers and also to provide Family
Planning Services, besides diagnosing early cases of cervical cancer.   An allocation of  Rs 135.00 crores was made for
Post Partum Programme in BE 2001-2002.   However, no allocation has been made for the year 2002-2003.   Giving
reasons, the Department has replied that the Planning Commission has decided to transfer the Post Partum Programme
to the States/UTs w.e.f. 1.4.2002.  The Committee would be interested to know as to the precise reasons that weighed in
favour of transfer of this Programme to the States/UTs.

8.1
              Allocation of Rs. 117.00 crores made under the head Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptive in BE
2001-2002 has been increased to Rs. 181.80 crores in 2002-2003.  Explaining the reasons for increase,  the Department
has informed that due to increasing number of younger couples, the demand for condoms under free distribution from
the States has been increasing and   in order to meet the enhanced demand, increased budgetary provision has been
proposed.
8.2       The Department has further informed that as regards allocation of additional quantities of conventional
contraceptives in the States, these would be allocated proportionately in relation  to utilisation and demand of the
respective States.   The unmet need in condom under free supply scheme is nearly 30% whereas in Oral Contraceptive
Pill (OCP) it is around 10%.   Attempts will be made to fill up these gaps.   The additional allocation would be required
for the purchase of the raw material for OCP which is no more available under external assistance and the same has to
be met from domestic resources.
8.3       In regard to the quality of Nirodh, the Committee has been given to understand that  19% users have rated it
under free supply scheme as okay,  75% as good and 6% have rated as very good.    The Committee feels that the
quality of condoms goes a long way in its acceptance by the users.    The Committee is also of the view that poor quality
may lead to unwanted pregnancy and reproductive tract infections.    The Committee,  therefore, recommends that the
Department should ensure that only the best quality of latex is used in manufacturing of condoms.

I           INTRODUCTION
The Committee notes with satisfaction that the percentage of coverage in 2000-2001 in respect of TT for
pregnant woman and BCG, Measles, DPT and Polio for infants have increased in comparison to the preceding year.
(Para 1.5)
The Committee notes that though there is a marginal increase in the case of sterilisation and C.C. users, the
number of IUD Insertions and O.P. users has decreased in the year 2000-2001 in comparison to 1999-2000.    The
Committee feels that in the case of sterilisation, the number of male sterilisation is much below the desired level and
recommends that the Department should take appropriate steps so that the participation of males is increased in Family
Planning methods.   (Para 1.6)
            The Committee understands that under the Community Needs Assessment Approach (CNAA), an action plan is
prepared each year at the district level based  on the need assessment done by ANMs of Sub-Centre at village level.  In
the beginning of the financial year, the health worker will first complete the house-to-house survey.  Based on this
survey, Eligible Couple Register is updated by the ANM.  The Committee has been informed that the State Govts. are 
impressed from time to time to ensure that the Sub-Centre action is got prepared for each Sub-Centre in the State.  The
Committee has its own doubts about the implementation of this annual exercise, which is most essential for successful
implementation of Family Welfare Programme, specially in the remote and inaccessible areas.  The Committee strongly
feels that surprise inspections in the performing as well as non-performing districts by Central teams/dedicated
NGOs/Social Workers can bring out the ground reality.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should initiate such an exercise in 2002-2003. (Para 1.7)
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee agrees in principle with the Department's contention of there being no case for resorting to a cut
of Rs. 700.00 crores at the RE stage in 2001-2002 by the Ministry of Finance.  The Committee also notes that total plan
allocation of Rs. 3700.00 crores in 2001-2002 is anticipated to be utilised. Actual expenditure figures are not available
at present.  The Committee, however observes that during 2000-2001, against a higher projected requirement, plan
allocation was Rs. 3500.00 crores which was reduced to Rs. 3200.00 crores at the RE stage.  Actual expenditure was
even less i.e. Rs. 3071.35 crores.  The Committee strongly feels that inview of much higher allocation of Rs. 4930.00
crores in 2002-2003, the Department should ensure that funds allocated under various schemes are utilised optimally

PREFACE
 
            I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Hundred – Eighteenth  Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.43) of the Department of
Indian Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy,  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2002-2003.
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Indian
Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other
Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 3
rd   April, 2002.
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 22nd   April, 2002.
 
NEW DELHI
April  22, 2002
Vaisakha 2, 1924 (Saka)

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy was set up by the Government of India as an
independent Department in March, 1995 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  The main objective of the
Department is to provide focused attention for the proper development and  propagation of ISM&H, namely Ayurveda,
Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and to fully utilise the potentials of these systems.
II          PERFORMANCE  DURING  NINTH FIVE  YEAR  PLAN
2.1       The thrust areas identified for intervention during the Ninth Plan period were as indicated below:-
Effective use of ISM&H systems for health for all and for better patient care system.
-
                      Upgradation of medical educational facilities and improvement in standards of ISM&H medical education.
-                      Focus on research and development efforts
-                      Increasing availability of raw material
-                      Setting up of National Institute for each system.
-                      Development/Strengthening of pharmacopoeial  laboratories and Strengthening of State Government
pharmacies
2.2       Keeping in view the thrust areas, the following schemes were prepared by the Department  for implementation
during the  plan period:-
-
                      Scheme for strengthening of Pharmacopoeia Committee on ISM
-                      Scheme of grant-in-aid for  development of ISM&H UG colleges
-                      Scheme of grant-in-aid for Re-orientation for in-service training programme

-                      Scheme of assistance to PG medical education in ISM&H
-                      Scheme of assistance to State Drug Testing Laboratories/Pharmacies
-                      Scheme of assistance for Extra-Mural Research Project through Research Institutions
-                      Setting up of Medicinal Plants Board
-                      Innovative Schemes for development of medicinal plants,
-                      Scheme on Information, Education and Communication
-                      Scheme of assistance for International Exchange Programme/Seminars/Workshops on ISM&H.
 
2.3              The plan allocation and utilization of funds during the Ninth Plan period (year wise)is indicated below:

Year BE RE Actual Expenditure
1997-98 32.30 32.80 33.04

2.4       From the above table, the Committee infers that  the  Department has fully utilised the allocated funds during the
first two  years of the Plan. Thereafter, the trend of BE allocation being reduced at RE stage and that too remaining
under-utilised started. The Committee was given to understand that tremendous increase in the Plan allocation for 2000-
01 as compared to previous year's allocation, put a strain on its absorption capacity. The Committee observes that
instead of there being any improvement in 2001-02, the last year of Ninth Plan, situation has worsened. The Committee
strongly feels that although the Department succeeded in getting enhanced allocation by projecting higher requirements
meant for expansion of ongoing Schemes and launching of many new Schemes, the Department failed to achieve both
the physical and financial targets during 2000-01 and 2001-02. The Committee notes that a large number of new
schemes were proposed to be launched during Ninth Plan period. However, so far as their implementation is concerned,
performance has been dismal.   In the last year of the Ninth Plan, i.e.2001-02, as many as eleven new schemes were
there, out of which some were yet to be finalised due to procedural bottlenecks and in the case of others, due to late
approval, schemes were yet to take off.
2.5       The Committee observes that as many as nineteen new schemes have been identified by the Department for
initiation during the Tenth Plan period. Scheme of CGHS Expansion in dispensaries is one of such Schemes. The
Committee is, however constrained to note that this Scheme was proposed to be launched during the Ninth Plan.  
However, for reasons unknown to the Committee, the Scheme was dropped during 1999-2000.  The Committee is
surprised to note that this Scheme is again included in the list of new schemes  to be launched during Tenth Plan.   In
contrast, fate of Schemes like 'Health for all through preventive and promotive Programme of ISMH', 'Speciality clinics
on ISMH',  ‘Indian Homoeopathy Pharmacy Council' and 'ISM Pharmacy Council’ is not known. The Committee hopes
that proper planning and preparatory exercise with regard to finalization and approval in respect of all these proposed
new schemes must have been done before making budget provision for the same in 2002-03. The Committee would like
to be enlightened in this regard.
III.      BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
            3.1       The total allocation both Plan  and Non-Plan taken together provided to the Department for the year
2001-2002 was Rs. 165.56 crores which was reduced to Rs. 134.84 crores at the RE stage.  However, the
Committee observes that while there has been minimal reduction in the non-Plan allocation at RE stage from
Rs.45.56 Crores to Rs. 44.84 Crores,  Plan allocation at the RE stage was reduced drastically from Rs. 120 crores
to Rs. 90 crores.  This year the Department has been allocated  Rs. 150 crores under Plan and Rs. 50.86 crores
under Non-Plan.
3.2
              The Committee notes that the Department has been given an increase of about 25% over the last year.  Asked to

comment about the increased allocation the Department informed  that whereas the projected demand was for Rs.
256.66 crores, the Department received only Rs. 150.00 crores. It was clarified that  whereas it was sufficient for
continuing the existing and ongoing activities of the Department, the  new schemes and programmes projected in the
Tenth Plan would be affected to some extent.
3.3
              The Committee notes that the allocation at RE 2001-02 was reduced by the Department of Expenditure due to
insufficient utilization of the budget in first nine months,  owing   to a number of schemes not cleared or delay occurred
in receiving clearance of concerned Ministries.  The Secretary while deposing before the Committee also  confessed that
the Department of ISM&H being  a  new and small department, it had  to conceptualise new schemes and programmes
and steer them through various administrative and financial clearances from the Planning Commission and Department
of Expenditure and indeed faced a lot of difficulty in translating them into implementable schemes. This phenomenon,
the Secretary admitted has led to lesser utilization of funds. 
3.4       The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Secretary that the Department is new.  It is seven years
since the Department has been created for the very specific purpose of promoting and developing indigenous Health
systems.  The Committee, therefore, feels that without  the adequate  initiative  and support of the Department, these
systems will not develop and the purpose for which the Department has been created will get defeated.  The Committee,
is, therefore, of the opinion that the Department should make all out efforts to utilise the fund  earmarked for the
purposes  for which they are meant.
IV.       AYURVEDA
4.1       The provision for Ayurveda under plan in BE and RE 2001-2002 was Rs. 12.96 crores which has been increased
to Rs. 15.81 crores.  On being asked, in what manner the additional allocation is proposed to be utilised, the Department
stated that the following provision has been made for the system:

              The Department informed that the additionality provided under Plan to National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur
will be utilised mainly for capital works  and to start more PG Courses in the Institute. Similarly, the additional
allocation proposed for the  Institute of Post Graduate Teaching & Research in Ayurveda, Jamnagar, Gujarat will be

4.3       The Committee regrets to  note from the above table that the CCRAS, Jamnagar was able to utilise only Rs. 40
lakhs out of Rs. 75 lakhs provided last year. Now the Department proposes to give Rs. one crore.     The Committee 
would  like to be apprised of the reason for lesser utilization by the Institute during 2001-02. The Committee is of the
view that concerted efforts should be made for optimum utilisation of funds during 2002-03.  The Committee desires
that PG courses proposed to be commenced in NIA, Jaipur and CCRAS, Jam Nagar be started  itself.             
4.4       On the question of misleading advertisements on Ayurvedic medicines appearing in newspapers/magazines
noticed by the Department and preventive action taken by the Department , the Committee was informed that a meeting
of the Drugs Consultative Committee of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani Drugs Technical Advisory Board was called on
30.05.01. It was attended by various State Licensing Authorities who were asked to send quarterly reports on the action
taken against the persons/companies violating the provisions of Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable
Advertisement) Act and Rules, 1954. Drugs Control Cell in the Department is also checking misleading advertisements.
Besides that, Monitoring  Cell is going to be activated with Adviser (Ayurveda) being asked to submit quarterly report
to the Secretary.
4.5       The Committee notes that in spite of a number of initiatives being taken by the Department, not much

file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/118threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:26]
improvement seems to have been made. This is evident by the fact that no specific action-taken reports on 160
misleading advertisements forwarded to State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka,
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, NCT of Delhi, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have been received in spite of reminders
being sent to them. The Committee notes with serious concern that during 2001-02 (upto 14.2.02), 122 advertisements
were sent to the  Government of NCT of Delhi with no response forthcoming. This is indeed a sorry state of affairs. The
Committee enjoins upon the Department to vigorously pursue the matter with the concerned State Governments,
otherwise the efficacy of Ayuvedic medicines would be questioned.       The Committee would like to be apprised of the
initiatives taken and the results thereof within a period of three months.
4.6       The Department also informed that it proposes to engage Non Government Organisation i.e. SAMVAAD
Agency for the specific purpose to scan popular local and national newspapers/magazines  wherein
misleading/exaggeration claims of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani advertisements are published and to forward to the
concerned State Govt. FDA/Drug Controller for taking action under Drugs and Magic Remedies Act.  The Agency will
cover 57 publications including 30 national publications in Hindi, English and other regional languages and the
advertisements will be forwarded to all the major states and UTs.  The Committee appreciates the proposed  initiative.
4.7       The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee informed that the Department has decided to establish a
state-of-the-art Ayurveda Hospital, beyond Sarita Vihar,  Delhi with specialized treatment facilities, for  which it has
paid the cost of 4.5 acres of land to DDA.It was proposed to  establish the hospital  in collaboration with the private
sector and the Department has invited `expression of interest’.  The Committee notes that this proposal seems to have
been initiated during 2000-01 and an expenditure of about Rs.217 lakhs was incurred during 2001-02. The Committee
feels that scrutiny of expression of interest may be completed soon  and steps may be taken to establish it at the earliest.
4.8       Elaborating on Ayurveda and its impact on other countries, the Secretary informed the Committee that there is
resurgence of interest in our system, as people prefer gentler form of treatment, plant based medicines without adverse
side effects.  In this regard, Gujarat Ayurveda University has entered into collaboration with several institutions abroad
for the development of Ayurveda teaching and research and an MOU has been signed with the Govt. of Russian
Federation.  Hungary has recognized Ayurveda and 40 Ayurvedic drugs are already in  use and have requested for
technical support for starting  Ayurveda teaching in three universities, the Secretary added.
4.9       The Secretary further informed that some problem was noticed in U.K., where Ayurveda system was
downgraded to category III implying thereby that Ayurveda has no scientific basis.   To dispel the doubts, a scientific
presentation was made last year before the House of Lords Sub-Committee headed by Lord Walton which resulted in  
Ayurveda being  placed in  category for single drugs. South Africa has also decided to amend their law to accept
Ayurveda medicines and they also propose to start under-graduate and post-graduate course in Ayurveda.
4.10     Further elaborating, the Secretary stated that a  number of medical schools in the USA are receptive to the idea
of introducing a capsule course on Ayurveda for sensitizing their medical students.   The World Health Organisation
recently held a consultation for finalization of guidelines for establishing Panchkarma centres in the countries of South
East Asian region. This will help establishment of Panchkarma centres in these areas. A consultation on methodology
for research and evaluation of traditional medicine was held in Hong Kong in which USA,UK, Germany, Japan, China
and several other countries participated. The Consultation was arranged to decide methodology for research in
traditional medicine which could provide wider acceptance in the participating countries.
4.11     The Committee notes that the Department has taken adequate steps to popularise the system of  Ayurveda in
different countries.  The Committee hopes that such  initiatives will continue in  future also.
4.12     The Secretary informed the Committee about the efforts being made by the Government for the popularization
of ayurvedic system of medicine in foreign countries.  While the Committee notes the efforts made by the Government
in this direction, but observes that adequate measures for providing ayurvedic system of treatment to  public at large and
to the CGHS beneficiaries in particular are not adequate.  The Ministry was asked about the measures taken for
promoting inter alia
 ayurvedic system of medicine by the Government to the interested beneficiaries of the CGHS.  In
response to that, the Ministry has stated that apart from Arya Vaidashala Kottakkal, Kerala, there are 32 other
institutions/centers imparting ayurvedic treatment in different cities of the country and the same are also recognized
under CS(MA) Rules for medical attendance and treatment of all Central Government employees and members of their
families.  However, the Delhi unit of  Arya Vaidashala Kottakkal, has not been recognized so far.
4.13     The Committee further notes that ayurvedic hospital at Lodhi Road is under CGHS, Department of Health. 

118th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/118threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:26]
Perhaps, the decision about recognition of other ayurvedic institutions/centers for CGHS beneficiaries lies with the
Department of Health.  The Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy was created in 1995.  It is,
therefore, surprising that the hospitals/other institutions of the Central Government providing ayurvedic treatment still
continue to be under the Department of Health.  The Committee fails to understand the rationale behind this.
4.14     As regards the standard of facilities at the Lodhi Road ayurvedic hospital, the Department has stated that the
facilities for ‘panchkarma’ treatment  at ayurvedic hospital at Lodhi Road  reportedly are not up to the mark due to
various reasons including unfilled up posts.  The Department in its reply has added that this hospital is under CGHS,
Department of Health.  The reply of the Department speaks volumes of the kind of step-motherly treatment that the
system of ayurvedic treatment is receiving by the Department of Health.  The Government’s stated policy for
propagating of Indian system of medicines appears to be only on paper and apparently no serious efforts are being made
by the Government to provide an alternative system of medicine, particularly to the CGHS beneficiaries.
4.15     The Committee feels that adequate steps have not been taken by the Government to provide ayurvedic treatment
facilities to the CGHS beneficiaries.  At the same time, no serious efforts are being made to strengthen the system as the
ayurvedic hospitals/centers continued to be under the Department of Health.  The Committee would, therefore,
recommend that all facilities of ayurvedic treatment should be transferred within a period of three months  to the
Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy so as to ensure their proper management. Further, the
existing Government CGHS dispensaries/hospitals should be upgraded and private hospitals/dispensaries such as Arya
Vaidashala Kottakkal, Kerala, and its Delhi branch may also be brought under the facilities of CGHS beneficiaries.  The
Committee also feels that the Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy should be headed by a professional
adoctor(vaidya) at Secretary level rather than a civil servant who may not be adequately familiar with what kind of
policies need to be formulated in this area.  This will also facilitate taking decisions for cultivation of herbs which are
the basic raw-material for manufacturing  of all these medicines.
V.        HOMOEOPATHY
5.1
              For Homoeopathy, the plan allocation was Rs. 8.27 crores in BE 2001-2002. It has been increased to Rs. 10.21
crores in BE 2002-2003.  The Committee has been informed  that the increase is mainly for the National Institute of
Homoeopathy, Kolkata.  The Department informed that an amount of Rs. 6.00 crores has been provided during the year
2002-2003, which is Rs. 2.00 crores more than BE of 2001-2002 and is meant for payment of construction cost to the
Central Public Works Department for the construction of staff quarters at the Institute.
5.2              The Committee, however, notes that against an allocation of Rs. 4.00 Crores for NIH in 2001-02, expenditure
reported upto February,2002 is only Rs. 2.91 Crores. The Committee observes that all the proposed activities for the
year could not be activated. Like  Laboratories could not be modernised to the required level as targetted. Similarly, no
progress seems to have been made on the proposal for starting courses for Dispensers/Pharmacists/Nurses of the
Institute. What is a cause for  more serious concern  is the issue of increase of bed capacity from 60 to 100. The
Committee has been given to understand  that steps have been taken to enhance the bed capacity to 80 at the first stage
followed by 100 later.
5.3       The Committee notes that  in this connection cadre review committee had suggested creation of 44 posts in
various categories including teaching and non-teaching.  However, the Department proposes to create 47 posts.  The
Committee would like to know the reasons for creation of 3 extra posts by the Department on their own when an expert
committee has threadbare discussed the matter.  The Committee would also like to know whether these extra posts are
on the teaching side or  the non-teaching side.
VI.       UNANI
6.1       Under the head Unani, on the Plan side,Rs. 10.84 crores was allocated in BE 2001-2002 which got reduced to
Rs. 8.84 crores at the RE stage.  However, in BE 2002-2003 an allocation of Rs. 10.50 crores has been made. 
6.2       Clarifying the reasons for this variation, the Department stated that an amount of Rs. 3.50 crores was allocated
for National Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore for construction of the building of the Institute. However, because
of some delay in starting the construction work, there were savings with the Institute from the previous year. As a result
of this and keeping in view the requirements of the Institute, the budget provision in RE was reduced to Rs. 1.5 crores. 
As a result of this, the plan budget for Unani Sector was reduced from Rs. 10.84 crores in BE 2001-2002 to Rs. 8.84
crores at RE stage.  However, theCommittee regrets  to note that the Department is silent on the issue of increase in
allocation and in what manner it  proposes to utilise the same.  The Committee, however, hopes  that the entire

allocation would be properly utilised by the Department.
6.3       Commenting on the progress made in the National  Institute of Unani Medicine, the Secretary stated that it is
making steady  progress. The hospital blocks, laboratory, library etc., would be handed over by October, 2002 and PG
courses in some disciplines are expected to be started in the next session.i.e.2002-2003.  The Committee desires that PG
courses at the Institute may be started in 2002-2003. The Committee further desires that the target for handing over the

6.4       On the question of settling the dispute of land at RRIUM, Karim Ganj, the Department submitted that the State
Govt. of Assam had allotted some land for construction of building for the Institute at Karimganj, Assam.  The land
allotted by the Govt. of Assam was disputed as the farmers went to court against acquisition.  Therefore, the Central
Council for Unani Medicine requested the Deputy Commissioner, Karimganj to allot another piece of land.  The Dy.
Commissioner has now informed the Council that they are identifying three sites for consideration for selection of a
suitable site.  Simultaneously, the farmers who had gone to court against acquisition of land are willing to withdraw. 
TheCommittee desires that the issue may be sorted out as quickly as possible, as it is pending  for quite a long time.
VII       YOGA
7.1       The plan allocation for `Yoga and Naturopathy’ which was Rs. 5.99 crores in BE 2001-2002 got reduced to Rs.
3.83 crores at the RE stage.  The allocation has been increased to Rs. 7.60 crores in BE 2002-2003.  Clarifying this
variation, the Department stated that due to delay in obtaining the clearance of Delhi Urban Arts Commission etc., the
proposed construction work of Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga could not be started leading to  reduction in the
Plan Allocation from Rs. 3.00 crores to Rs. 1.09 crores during 2001-2002.  As necessary clearance of Delhi Urban Arts
Commission is expected shortly, higher Plan allocation of  Rs. 4.50 crores has been made for Morarji Desai National
Institute of Yoga during 2002-2003. The Committee is of the view that construction work of MDNIY should start
without any further delay.
7.2       The Department further stated that as less number of new projects were found viable for implementation and
keeping in view the opening balance of Rs. 12.15 lakhs, the plan allocation for Central Council for Research in Yoga
and Naturopathy  was reduced from Rs. 2.00 crores to Rs. 1.75 crores during 2001-2002.National Institute of
Naturopathy has been given higher Plan allocation from Rs. 0.80 crores last year to Rs.0.90 crores this year due to
increase in its activities.
7.3       The Committee had, last year, recommended that yoga be made part of regular curriculum in all the schools all
over the country.  The Department has stated that it had taken up with the Ministry of Human Resource Development  to
incorporate teaching of yoga, naturopathy and other Indian Health Traditions in the school curriculum and the Ministry
was reminded on 22.2.2002 to intimate the steps taken in this regard. The Committee feels that no effective steps seem
to have been taken in this regard and  desires that the Department may pursue this issue  more vigorously with the
Ministry of Human Resource Development .
VIII      NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SIDDHA (NIS, CHENNAI)
8.1       Apprising the Committee about the progress in the case of National Institute of Siddha, the Secretary informed
the Committee that the project was pending for several years  and it  was finally approved in January, 2002.  An
investment of Rs. 47 crores is proposed to be made for PG teaching and research.  The Secretary also informed the
Committee that the expenses will be shared by the Centre and State in ratio of 60:40 in case of non-recurring and 75:25
in case of recurring expenditure.
8.2       On the question of popularizing Siddha  to other parts, the Department has stated that NIS, will help in
popularizing it, as many students from different areas will go in  for UG and PG courses and for research once the
institute is established.  The Committee feels that it could have been one of  the ways to popularise the system.    The
Committee is of the view that by publishing the efficacy of siddha medicines in vernacular  newspapers and also by
establishing more siddha dispensaries, the system can be made more popular.
IX        MEDICAL EDUCATION
9.1       At present, there are about 400 ISM&H colleges in the country.  However, standard of education in some of the
institutions is far from satisfactory and they are nowhere near the norms fixed by Statutory Bodies.  The Committee was
informed that high priority was given to this area.  About 56 colleges were assisted all over the country particularly for
teaching equipment, books, Journals and access to computers.

9.2       Commenting about the standards of ISM&H education and mushroom growth of ISM&H colleges, the Secretary
informed that a general concern has been expressed in various forums that they are being established without adhering
to laid down standard.  The Secretary stated that whereas the Department continued to support ISM&H institutions to
upgrade their facilities and the Central Council for Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy laid down minimum standards of
education and other regulations, the mushroom growth of sub-standard colleges continued.  So the Department is
contemplating legislative measures to check this unhealthy trend, the Secretary added.
9.3       To sort out this problem threadbare, the Department stated that a Sub-Committee of VCs  and representatives of
State Govts which  was formed to make necessary recommendations,  met on 22
nd July, 2001.  However the
recommendations of the Sub-Committee have not been received by the Department so far. The Committee feels that the
Sub-Committee should finalise its recommendations at the earliest so as to address to this problem urgently.  The
Committee hopes that the Department would be benefited by the recommendations of the Sub-committee in initiating
appropriate legislative measures in this regard.
X         QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS
10.1     Laying down the Pharmacopieal standards and quality control of ISM&H drugs is one of the priority  areas of
the Department.  The Secretary informed that Drug Standardization  received due priority during 2001-02.  Laying of
pharmacopoeial standards and preparation of formularies was also given adequate attention.  Substantial progress was
made in Ayurveda and Homoeopathy  where 40% and 65% pharmacopoeial work respectively has been completed.
Target has been fixed to complete all pharmacopoeial standards by 2005 and 35 laboratories are assisting the
Department in completing pharmacopoeial standards.  Pharmacopoeial Laboratory of Indian Medicine for Ayurveda,
Unani and Siddha and Homoeopathy Pharmacopoeia  Laboratory at Ghaziabad are being strengthened by augmenting
their infrastructure including technical manpower.  The construction work is expected to start in 2002-2003. The
Committee appreciates the steps taken in this regard.  However, the Committee feels that the Pharmacopoieal work
relating to Ayurveda needs to be further expedited, as only 40% has been done. 
10.2     The Committee is constrained to note that BE allocation of Rs. 42.00 lakhs and Rs. 26.oo lakhs for PLIM,
Ghaziabad and HPL, Ghaziabad had to be reduced to Rs. 8.00 lakhs and Rs. 23.00 lakhs respectively at the RE stage.
What is more shocking is that even against this reduced allocation, expenditure reported upto February, 2002 is only Rs.
3.58 lakhs and Rs. 19.79 lakhs respectively for the two laboratories .   The Committee notes that non-creation of new
posts and non-filling of some posts are the two main reasons for under-utilisation of funds. This situation has been
continuing for the last few years. The Committee fails to understand as to how in the absence of required staff, the
primary task of testing/analysis of drugs is being carried out in these labs. The Committee would like to be apprised
about the required and sanctioned strength of posts and vacant posts in both these labs. The Committee hopes that
construction work in both the labs would be started at the earliest.
10.3     The Secretary also informed that in order to improve the quality of drugs and public confidence, Good
Manufacturing Practices Rules were notified two years ago and will become law from 23
rd June, 2002 after a grace
period of two years.  The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules have  been amended to make an enabling provision to recognize
private laboratories as public test laboratories to expand the facilities for the testing of ISM&H drugs.  Schedule `K’ of
Drugs & Cosmetics Rules has also been amended to facilitate availability of 49 drugs in all licensed pharmacies/shops,
which was not the case earlier.  Essential Drugs List for Ayurveda, Unani and Homoeopathy are  circulated to state
governments and they are  advised that these be stocked in the dispensaries and hospitals. Welcoming this initiative, the
Committee is of the view that Department must ensure that the Pharmacies which are stocking  the homoeopathic
medicines must be certified by a person having necessary qualifications. 
10.4     The Secretary further  informed that Central Scheme for assistance to State Pharmacies and Drugs Testing
Laboratory to improve the capacity of states and to monitor the quality of products which is their statutory responsibility
has been implemented and in the last two years, 27 Pharmacies and 16 laboratories have been assisted  and a sum of Rs.
31.46 crores as grant-in-aid was released.  The Committee notes that this scheme was approved for only the last two
years of the Ninth Plan.  During 2001-2002 a budget provision of Rs. 18.50 crores was kept but the demands from the
States for assistance for pharmacy/DTL were not encouraging and the States which were assisted earlier did not come
up for second installment either.  As a result, only Rs. 11 crores could be spent out of Rs.18.50  crores during 2001-
2002.
10.5     The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons as to why the states did not even approach the

XI        NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS
11.1     The efficacy of most of the ISMH drugs is dependent upon the use of pure and genuine raw material obtained
from medicinal plants.  However, due to over exploitation, unscrupulous collection and denuding of forests, supplies
have been dwindling. 
11.2     Elaborating on the steps initiated in this regard, the Secretary informed the Committee that non-availability of
raw material of required purity and containing alkoids and essential oils etc. has been engaging the attention of the
Department.    Ministries and Departments of Central Government are separately addressing to conservation, cultivation
and research in medicinal plants areas.  Previously there was no agency to co-ordinate all functions and focus the plants
development for domestic consumption and exports.  Now  a Medicinal Plants Board has been set up under a
Government Resolution to co-ordinate all activities and draw up policy and schemes for all round development of this
sector.  The Board is assisting  various schemes and grant of Rs. 11.70 crores has been released.  The Committee is
happy to note that about 17 States have set up state level Medicinal Plants Board. The Committee desires that the
Department should persuade rest of the States /UTs also to set up medicinal plant board at the earliest to stop
adulteration and to make optimum use of available resources in their respective states/UTs.
XII       PUBLICITY
12.1     The Committee notes that the Department has initiated a number of steps to popularise ISM&H   313 blocks in
the country were selected for implementation of IEC Scheme through various NGOs.  The activities of the NGOs were
to organize community awareness, meetings, training workshops for ISM&H practitioners, health melas, organisation of
Yoga classes in primary schools and training of cultivation of medicinal plants.  Folders on Home remedies in Ayurveda
and Unani were sent to State Govts. for distribution to Panchayats to make the systems more popular at grass root level. 
Health Melas were also organized, in which  free  diagnosis and dispensing of medicines was also arranged.  First ever
comprehensive exhibition AROGYA, 2001, on Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy at Pragati Maidan, New
Delhi from December 15-18, 2001 in association with India Trade Promotion Organisation was organized which was a
great success.  6 NGOs were assisted in North East during 2000-2001.
12.2     The Committee was also informed that the Ministry of Tourism has agreed to propagate Panchkarma in hotels
for which guidelines have been already provided to them.  Ministry of External Affairs has also asked all Missions to
help propagate ISM&H. 
12.3     The Committee notes the steps taken in this regard.  The Committee feels that simply sending the folders on
Home remedies in Ayurveda and Unani to State Govts for distribution to Panchayats will not serve any purpose  unless
the folder is in vernacular language and the instructions printed in the folders are communicated properly. The
Committee, therefore, desires that a demonstration on how to prepare the home remedies may be held at the block level. 
The Committee also notes that a small booklet on ISMH for distribution in various fairs, conferences, seminars etc. has
been prepared and another detailed booklet giving in brief the status of the system including the achievements is under
print.    The Committee is of the view that these booklets should be widely circulated as and when printed and hopes
that these booklets will greatly help in removing doubt etc. about the efficacy and scientific approach of our systems.

13.1     The  Department informed that as per the guidelines conveyed by the Planning Commission, 10% of the plan
budget has been earmarked for the North Eastern States and Sikkim.  Accordingly, a lump sum provision of Rs. 15.00
crores in 2002-2003 has been made for North Eastern States and Sikkim.  The Committee notes that BE provision of Rs.
12.00 crores for North-Eastern region in 2001-2002 was reduced to Rs. 9.00 crores at the RE stage.  Expenditure
reported upto February, 2001-2002 is only Rs. 2.81 crores.
13.2     The Department has clarified that three Research Councils, namely, Central Council for Research in Ayurveda &
Siddha, Central Council for Research in Unani Medicine and Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy were asked
to frame new proposals for the North-East.  However, the Planning Commission has approved, in principle, research
project namely Research in Tribal Areas and North Eastern States.   But the approval came late in February and  hence it

            Preparation and maintenance of the Central Register of  Indian Medicine is one of the main objectives of the
Central Council of Indian Medicine.   The Committee observes that the Central Register pertaining to only six states i.e.
Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Haryana and Tamil Nadu out of the eighteen states where practitioners of
ISM are registered has been prepared so far and that too for varying period of time.    The Committee urges upon the

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
II          PERFORMANCE  DURING  NINTH FIVE  YEAR  PLAN
            From the above table, the Committee infers that  the  Department has fully utilised the allocated funds during the
first two  years of the Plan. Thereafter, the trend of BE allocation being reduced at RE stage and that too remaining
under-utilised started. The Committee was given to understand that tremendous increase in the Plan allocation for 2000-
01 as compared to previous year's allocation, put a strain on its absorption capacity. The Committee observes that
instead of there being any improvement in 2001-02, the last year of Ninth Plan, situation has worsened. The Committee
strongly feels that although the Department succeeded in getting enhanced allocation by projecting higher requirements
meant for expansion of ongoing Schemes and launching of many new Schemes, the Department failed to achieve both
the physical and financial targets during 2000-01 and 2001-02. The Committee notes that a large number of new
schemes were proposed to be launched during Ninth Plan period. However, so far as their implementation is concerned,
performance has been dismal.   In the last year of the Ninth Plan, i.e.2001-02, as many as eleven new schemes were
there, out of which some were yet to be finalised due to procedural bottlenecks and in the case of others, due to late
approval, schemes were yet to take off. (Para 2.4)
            The Committee observes that as many as nineteen new schemes have been identified by the Department for
initiation during the Tenth Plan period. Scheme of CGHS Expansion in dispensaries is one of such Schemes. The
Committee is, however constrained to note that this Scheme was proposed to be launched during the Ninth Plan.  
However, for reasons unknown to the Committee, the Scheme was dropped during 1999-2000.  The Committee is
surprised to note that this Scheme is again included in the list of new schemes  to be launched during Tenth Plan.   In
contrast, fate of Schemes like 'Health for all through preventive and promotive Programme of ISMH', 'Speciality clinics
on ISMH',  ‘Indian Homoeopathy Pharmacy Council' and 'ISM Pharmacy Council’ is not known. The Committee hopes
that proper planning and preparatory exercise with regard to finalization and approval in respect of all these proposed
new schemes must have been done before making budget provision for the same in 2002-03. The Committee would like
to be enlightened in this regard.(Para 2.5)
III.       BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
            The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Secretary that  the Department is new.  It is seven years
since the Department has been created for the very specific purpose of promoting and developing indigenous Health
systems.  The Committee, therefore, feels that without  the adequate  initiative  and support of the Department, these
systems will not develop and the purpose for which the Department has been created will get defeated.  The Committee,
is, therefore, of the opinion that the Department should make all out efforts to utilise the fund  earmarked for the
